FOREWORD 

THIS is a new history for high schools, conceived in the spirit of modern America and dedicated to worthy citizenship. It is an attempt to make clear to the student the fundamental history of American institutions: an effort to treat inspirationally as well as instructively such topics as the evolution of selfgovernment, the rise of commercial power, and the development of American culture. A study of this institutional aspect of our country's story is the most important socializing factor at our command for training our youth for citizenship. 

In keeping with its purpose, the text is organized to meet the needs of the modern classroom. The development is primarily topical, but cross-references and appropriate transitions plainly trace the chronological thread of the narrative. Political matters are subordinated to the treatment of America's social and industrial life. This is especially true for the period since the 

Civil War. The chief emphasis for that period is on the rise of the New South; the romantic occupation of the Great West ; the increased industrial efficiency; the growth of scientific knowledge and inventive genius; the tremendous development of education since 1880; the establishment of new esthetic standards; and the growth of a scientific philanthropy. 

Interwoven with the purely material facts of the nation's maturing is the story of American democracy, — the gradual but definite evolution from the imperfect colonial concepts, through the Jeffersonian and Jacksonian ideals, down to the more comprehensive and more broadly enlightened democracy of to-day. When the book emphasizes political contests it is for the purpose of showing more clearly what factors have been responsible for this enrichment of our democracy. Hence the emphasis upon the gradual extension of the franchise through iii

iv 

FOREWORD 

colonial times down to the victory of manhood suffrage in the Jackson era, and upon the later contest concerning votes for women. Hence, too, the treatment, upon occasion, of the improvement of democratic political machinery: the ballot in early New England; the convention and the committee system of the Jacksonian era; and the new primary system, with our other recent applications of direct democracy. Especially stressed are those democratic movements which are social as well as political, such as the farmer's struggle for better conditions and labor's notable progress in organization. 

The author has tried to keep constantly in mind that large classes and inadequate equipment are too often a problem for the teacher. The book is full, therefore, of teaching aids adapted to the varying capacities of the large and the small school systems. Illustrations, particularly, have been effectively and plentifully interlinked with the text. The maps are a special feature, rich in variety and exceptionally serviceable. Approximately four hundred illustrations are included as an aid to the teacher's guidance of the student. Frequent exercises and thought questions, time-order tests, and outline suggestions have been formulated on the basis of practical classroom procedure. The important matter of reference and library work is discussed in the pages immediately following. 

WILLIS MASON WEST

SUGGESTIONS TO TEACHERS 

PROBABLY no other part of the high school history course is so well adapted for giving pupils some idea of the use of source material as is the colonial period of American history. There are several good collections for this purpose. Professor Hart's small Source Book contains admirably selected material. Volumes I and II of the same writer's American History Told by Contemporaries cover the colonial and Revolutionary period to still better advantage. Sets of the Old South Leaflets are excellent. And the author of this textbook has prepared a Source 

Book in American History to 1789 designed especially as a companion volume to the first third of.this high school text. If any good collection of sources is available in sufficient quantity, a teacher interested in such work may profitably limit her class during the first ten or twelve weeks to the study of the text and of such supplementary sources, leaving the use of other library material to a later part of the year. 

It is undoubtedly well worth the time to give an occasional class period to the reading and discussing of some document such as the Records of the First Virginia Assembly, or the 

Connecticut Fundamental Orders, or some representative New

England town records, or the quaint and instructive Dorchester school code of 1646, or some one of the many records of Virginia county meetings on the eve of the Revolution. This requires, however, a copy of the source book for at least each two students. 

If there are only four or five copies in the library, part of the same benefit may be secured by allowing groups of students to prepare and present reports to the class upon such documents. Many other ways to relate the source material to the textbook story will present themselves. A pupil, or a group, may be asked to search a given document for valuable facts not stated in the 

---

vi 

SUGGESTIONS TO TEACHERS 

textbook. Or a student may be sent to the source to find authority for a statement in the text. If seemingly conflicting statements from different texts are presented in class, a source document will sometimes furnish material for judging between them or for reconciling them. 

Not the least important result of this work should be a recognition by the student of the fallibility of sources themselves. He should learn to distinguish the kinds of sources and to estimate their relative reliability for different sorts of information. Thus he may be brought to see that history, if a science at all, is a science of probabilities, not of mathematical or physical measurements. And the stronger students should thus come to see one special advantage of history in the high school course— namely, that it is practically the only subject there that gives the kind of training that we all have to apply in all our later relations with human society.

The author has been unwilling to overload the book with long lists of reading references unusable for most high school students or unattainable for most high school libraries. Especial attention is called to the device in Appendix III for aiding small schools in selecting library books, and to the way that device is followed up in all chapter reference lists by the use of a peculiar variety of type.

Topical studies are suggested at various points in the text. 

The index, also, by use of bold-face type, analyzes the text by topics, for the convenience of teachers who prefer that method. 

Teachers who follow the narrative method of presentation may wish to use this topical plan for review purposes. If they will note in the index when each title has its last page reference, they will be able to introduce that review at a fitting point, without leaving all such work to the close of the book.

ASIA 

During the crusades (1100-1300) Europe had learned to enjoy Asia's rich offerings of spices, sugars, cottons, and silks, so that for centuries a continuous procession of Oriental caravans linked 

Asia to the eastern Mediterranean. 

Genoa and Venice first got control of this trade, but in the latter half of the fifteenth century western Europe began to grow impatient of the Italian monopoly. Then, too, growing scientific knowledge was dispelling men's fears of the unknown seas. So the Atlantic seaboard countries sought new ways to 

Asia. Portugal found one to the south around Africa, while Columbus tried a still bolder road to the west, - and stumbled upon America in his path. 

Then for two hundred years the leading countries of Europe, especially Spain, France, and England sought eagerly to possess that New World. 70

THE AMERICAN PEOPLE CHAPTER I: AN INTRODUCTION THE EUROPEAN RIVALS FOR AMERICA (1600-1700) I. SPAIN IN AMERICA 

Spain was first in the field, because her sovereigns had backed the daring enterprise of Columbus. She had the sixteenth century practically to herself. Before its close, there were two hundred Spanish towns in America, with a total white population of more than 150,000. Unchallenged, Spain had set her grasp upon all South and Central America, save Portugal's Brazil. In North America she claimed huge regions, ill defined, known as Florida" and Mexico." The Pacific Ocean and the Caribbean were Spanish lakes, and the Frenchman or Englishman found trespassing upon those waters was likely to find a grave beneath them. 66 

Spain, however, had conquered faster than she could occupy. 

The Spanish Americans were scattered over an immense area, merely dotted with occasional settlements. Especially was this true in North America. Of all the Spanish towns only Santa 

Fe and St. Augustine (both small) were far enough north to lie within the present limits of the United States. 

Everywhere the conquerors dwelt as lords among vastly larger populations of submissive natives whom they had enslaved and Christianized. By the labor of those natives they drew agricultural wealth from the rich alluvial valleys near the coast, or guarded their uncounted herds of cattle and sheep that roamed over the "ranches" of the Argentine or of "New 

Mexico," or mined gold and silver from ancient diggings of the 

Incas and Aztecs.

EUROPEAN RIVALS IN AMERICA, 1600-1700 

The conquest had been marred by revolting cruelties, but, afterward, the relation between natives and conquerors was not harsh. Slavery always has its shames, but the enslaved natives were not overworked, except sometimes in the mines. 

Commonly the chivalrous 

Spanish gentlemen were kindly masters, ruling their hundreds or thousands of loyal dependents with patriarchal sway, much as they did their households. 

Finally, too, the government of Spain forbade further enslavement of the natives. Thereafter the Indians in the neighborhood of the Spanish settlements grew into a class of peons, much like the serfs that were still found in many parts of Western Europe.

In many a district, too, the only Europeans, for long, were missionary friars. 

Usually these gathered 

FRONT OF CARMEL MISSION 

Monterey. -near about the walls of a Mission a contented settlement of Indian converts, ruled their lives with gentle authority, and taught them to grow vineyards and olive groves and orchards. 

The common soldiers among the conquerors usually took Indian wives. From such mixture of blood there arose the many Spanish-American nationalities. Gradually the Spanish nationality itself was well-nigh lost in these though Spanish remains the language of nearly half the New World. 

Life in Spanish America was not progressive; but it was contented and leisurely, and for the masters it had a kind of

SPAIN IN AMERICA 

3 lordly stateliness. A landed proprietor rode and hunted over a vast estate, of which he himself sometimes hardly knew the bounds. With a mounted train of attendants he visited the nearest but still distant neighbors; and, in turn, entertained them with courteous ceremonial and magnificence. In no part of Spanish 

America did the people have any self-government. 

Even the great landlords, little monarchs as they were on their own domains, had no share whatever in the government of their country. Until after 1800, Spanish America was merely a group of subject provinces, ruled by appointed officials sent out from old Spain. Many of these Spanish governors were high-minded gentlemen, but their rule was bad because their first and almost sole duty was to make the provinces profitable to Spain. 

The precious metals of Mexico and Peru were not permitted to make those countries rich. Instead, they were drained across the Atlantic, in great "plate fleets," to enrich the king of Spain. 

The trade of the colonies, too, was made to enrich only the merchants of Spain. For two hundred years all commerce to and from Spanish America had to pass through their hands and through Spanish harbors.

To make sure that these despotic "Navigation Acts" were obeyed, trade with the outside world was limited to two American ports and to certain dates. Once a year a fleet sailed from Spain 

Detroit Publishing Company.

OLD SPANISH CATHEDRAL AT ST. AUGUSTINE.

SPANISH AMERICA, 1600-1700 

to Porto Bello (on the Isthmus), and another to Vera Cruz in Mexico. At each of these ports the arrival of the fleet was followed by a forty-day fair, to exchange the European imports for American metals, cattle, hides, and tropical woods. All other commerce, even between the different Spanish colonies, was forbidden on pain of death.

This arrangement increased many fold the cost of European goods to the colonist. At the same time, it robbed him of much of the value of his own products with which he had to make payment.

The cattle raised on the rich plains of the Argentine could reach a lawful market only by being carried across the continent to Peru, thence by sea to

Panama, again across the 

Isthmus to Porto Bello, and (one chance a year) from that port to Seville in Spain. Even into the eighteenth century, an ox at Buenos 

Aires was worth not more than a dollar, and a sheep only three or four cents (and this much only because some smuggling trade had grown up). The colonists, therefore, could not, in proper degree, buy the products of European civilization. Instead, they were forced back toward the barbarism of the natives. 

DRAKE'S Golden Hind, in which, after ravaging the coasts of Spanish-America, he sailed around the world in 1581 (page 14).

Spain's lordship in the New World had rested upon her mastery of the seas. Then in 1588 Sir Francis Drake and other famous 66 sea dogs" of England shattered the boastful "Invincible Armada" of

Spain in a mighty nine-day sea fight in the English Channel and the North Sea. That battle was a turning point in world history. It was one of the causes why the people in the Mississippi valley to-day speak English rather than Spanish. Spain's supremacy in Europe began to decline, and she ceased to expand in America. Other sea-board countries of Europe now felt free to try their fortunes in those parts where she had not already set her hold.

II. FRANCE IN AMERICA 

France seized upon the two great gateways to the interior, the St. Lawrence River system and the Mississippi. She estab lished her first permanent colony in 1608 at Quebec - which soon became the capital of a flourishing northern fur-trading colony known as "New France." By the end of the century she had come to hold also a vast domain known as Louisiana " (in honor of the French king). In this district, near the mouth of the central river valley, she built the rich colony of 

66 

New Orleans - joined in later years to the snows of Canada by a thin chain of trading stations and military posts, such as Detroit, Sault Ste. Marie, Vincennes, Kaskaskia, and Natchez (map facing page 99).

It is easy to point out certain French advantages. In the first place, the great French statesmen at home worked steadily to build a French empire in the New World, and among the explorers and governors in America many splendid and able men, like Champlain, Ribault, and LaSalle, were moved by the same patriotic hope. Next, and not less important, missionary zeal brought to New France numbers of fine-spirited and keen-minded priests. Then, both these priests and the able and tactful governors showed greater skill in dealing with the natives, and won greater influence over them, than any other Europeans did. 

On the other hand, New France lacked three essential things: a sufficient number of farm homes; independence in industry among the common people; and self-government. 

1. In Nova Scotia (or Acadie as it was called in French times) and along the banks of the St. Lawrence, little groups of unprogressive French peasants farmed the estates of great lords, to whom the French king had given the land, much as they had formerly farmed their lords' estates in Europe. Montreal and 

Quebec were gay with the balls of the noble seigneurs, whose wives and daughters copied as best they might the gay life of the Paris of their time. But there were no busy little towns, like those of 

New England, and no sturdy, independent farmers.

FRANCE IN AMERICA 

Except for some of the noble class, few French immigrants brought families with them. Many of them took Indian wives. 

The sons of these marriages did not take readily to regular labor. Instead, they turned to trapping and the fur trade, and tended to adopt Indian habits. The French government in Europe sought in vain to remedy this by sending over cargoes of "king's girls," and by offering bonuses for early marriages and large families. 

But even with this fostering, French colonization did not produce numbers. 

In 1754, when the final struggle for the American continent began, France had three times as many people in Europe as England had, but in America she had only a twentieth as many colonists! And these, except for the noble leaders and the missionaries, were largely reckless and roaming adventurers. 

While English colonists were building homes, the French mainly were building distant forts and trading posts. 

2. In her industries, too, New France was taught to depend, not upon individual enterprise, but upon the aid and guidance of a government three thousand miles away. Help was constantly asked from the king. "Send us money to build storehouses," ran the begging letters of Canadian officials; "Send us a teacher to make sailors"; We want a surgeon "; and so, at various times, requests for brickmakers, ironworkers, pilots, and other skilled workers. Such requests were usually 66 HA 

CORNER OF AN OPEN COURT in a building of the old French Quarter of New Orleans.

granted with the result that New France did not learn to walk alone. 

STRENGTH AND WEAKNESS 

3. 

The French colonists had no legislatures of their own and no town-meeting government - nor indeed could they have a public gathering of any sort without a special license. Even the regulation of inns and of pew rent, the order in which people should sit in church, the keeping of dogs and of cattle, the pay of chimney sweeps, were dealt with by ordinances of the governors at Quebec, who were sent over by the French king. "It is of the greatest importance," wrote one official, " that the people should not be at liberty to speak their minds." Worse even than that the peo- ple had no minds to speak. In 1672, Frontenac, the greatest governor of New France, tried to introduce the elements of self-government. 

He provided a system of "estates to advise with him, a gathering of clergy, nobles, and commons (citizens and merchants); and he ordered that Quebec should have a sort of town meeting twice a year to elect aldermen and to discuss public business. But the home government sternly disapproved all action by the people as one body, telling Frontenac to remember that it was 66 proper that each should speak for himself, and no one for the whole." So the plan was dropped- and the colonists cared so little for it that they made no effort to save it. 

FRENCH TRAPPER. 

III. WHAT THE ENGLISH FOUND IN AMERICA 

For a century and a half the English in America were confined to the Appalachian coast district. Their fringe of the continent was more like the European homes of the colonists

WHAT THE ENGLISH FOUND IN AMERICA 

than was any other large district in America. The lives of the 

English settlers, therefore, were less changed than if they had colonized the Mississippi valley or the Pacific coast. 

The Appalachian coast, however, does differ from the European coast of the Atlantic in two vital matters. 

1. The summers are hotter, and the winters colder, than in 

Europe. Unexpected fevers in one season, and unforeseen freezing in the other, ruined more than one attempt at settlement. Captain George Weymouth explored the region near the mouth of the Kennebec in the spring of 1605 and brought back to England reports of a balmy climate "like that of southern France," but the colonists who tried to settle there two years later (page 20) suffered cruelly from a winter like that of northern Norway. 

2. As one goes from north to south, the climate changes more swiftly in America than in Europe. Between Maine and Florida the English colonists encountered climates as different as they would have found in the Old World if they had spread out from Norway to Morocco - many times the variation they had known in their home island.

This difference in climate between North and South (along with certain differences in soil) made the natural products of one region very different from those of the other. The rich lands of the South, and its warm climate, were suited to the cultivation of tobacco or rice or cotton, in large tracts, by slaves or bond servants. The severe climate of the North made it difficult to raise anything but the common food crops, and the stony soil of that region called for more toil. Farming did not pay there except in small holdings, worked by the owner's family, along, perhaps, with a little trustworthy "help." But the magnificent pine and oak forests of the North, its countless little water-power sites, its many harbors, and the abundance of fish in its seas, invited to lumbering, milling, shipbuilding, trade, and fishing.

INFLUENCE OF GEOGRAPHY 

9 Owing to geography, then, our early colonial life was marked by sectionalism. North and South had each its distinct set of industries, and so came to have its distinct manner of living. 

Virginian Englishman and New England Englishman grew apart in habits and feelings and character. 

Moreover, communication from north to south was difficult, and this condition reinforced the tendency to sectionalism. 

Colony was divided from colony, or groups of colonies were divided from one another, by arms of the sea. Even when two colonies lay side by side, without intervening bays, there were still no roads from north to south. The main highways were the rivers, running from the mountains to the sea. So, as a rule, a colony found it about as convenient to hold communication with England as with its neighbor on either side. The people of the different sections had little chance to mix with one another as they do now. 

On the other hand, geography gave the English colonists one mighty advantage. Their territory was more compact than that held by France or Spain. The rugged Appalachians, singularly impassable for such low mountains (covered as they were with forests tangled with underbrush and vines), kept the settlements from scattering too widely and so weakening themselves. Four rivers broke the mountain wall the Potomac, Delaware, Susquehanna, and Hudson-Mohawk; but, without more engineering skill than that age possessed, only the Mohawk could be used as a road to the inner country. That route, too, was closed against the English for fifty years by the Dutch in eastern New York and afterwards by the formidable Iroquois 

Indians farther west. 

Compact settlement made it possible for the English colonists to establish their civilization as the scattered French or Spanish colonists could not, and to make more progress in industry. 

It also made possible the union of the colonies against England, when the time came. Nature, seemingly unkind to the English colonist, was really kinder to him than to his rivals.

IO WHAT THE ENGLISH FOUND IN AMERICA 

Three groups of Indian peoples held the country between the Atlantic and the Mississippi-together numbering fewer people than are found to-day in many a single city in that district. 

1. The Confederacy of the "Six Nations" of the Iroquois was the strongest native power for war. These tribes dwelt in compact, fortified villages in what is now western 

New York. 

2. The Gulf tribes (Choc taws, Seminoles, Creeks) had made the most progress toward civilization, THE "LONG HOUSE OF THE IROQUOIS 

several families under one roof, each with especially in agriculture; its own fire. but they were too far south and west to affect white settlement much until the beginnings of Georgia and Tennessee, toward the end of the colonial period. 

3. The roaming Algonkins were much the largest of the three groups, but also much the least united and least civilized. 

Thinly scattered in a multitude of petty and mutually hostile tribes, they "haunted, rather than inhabited, a vast hunting preserve" stretching from the Atlantic to the Mississippi and from the Ohio to the far north. To this group belonged nearly all the tribes with which the early English settlers came in contact. 

These scattered Algonkins were not powerful enough to endanger English settlement seriously. At the same time they were more savage and untamable than the gentler races of South America whom Spanish conquerors enslaved so easily. 

They did not make profitable slaves and so the English had little chance to mix with them. Then, too, they were dangerous enough to scattered settlements to help keep the early English colonies fairly compact. 

In various ways, too, they directly aided English colonization. They furnished the first settlements with the "Indian " that many a time saved from starvation, and soon they corn

INFLUENCE OF THE NATIVES 

II taught the English immigrant to raise not only this maize but also tobacco - which became his first important export and brought him his first wealth.

Colonies too far north to raise tobacco profitably found their first wealth in furs, especially in beaver skins, obtained cheaply from native hunters. Indian wampum at times made an important part of colonial money. 

Foresi trails, worn deep by the feet of generations of red men, became highways for white travel. And stations for the exchange of furs, where certain trails and Indian waterways met, became the sites of mighty cities, like Milwaukee, Chicago, St. Louis, Detroit, and 

Duluth. (See map facing page 99.)

WAMPUM presented to William Penn (page 92) to commemorate his treaty with the Indians. 

Maize was long the main food. European grain failed in the new climate season after season, until the colonist had learned to deal with the new conditions. Moreover, to clear and prepare the soil for wheat or barley took much time and toil. Maize was a surer and easier crop. 

When European settlement began, the Indians in America were raising at least a million bushels a year. They had learned to select the seed, to fertilize the soil, and to preserve the crop for winter by drying it in the sun or in earth ovens. They taught the colonists how to raise it, at need, without even clearing the forest merely girdling the trees (to kill the foliage) and planting among the standing trunks. It was no accident that this Indian grain came to be called "corn," the 

English name for grain in general. 

Many Indian tribes have wholly disappeared. Still there are to-day almost as many Indians in the United States as there were in the same territory three hundred years ago. At the census of 1920, about half of them (some 185,000) were still living in tribes on reservations. In 1924, however, all Indians in the United States (even those on reservations) were given full American citizenship by act of Congress. The Indian makes perhaps a third of one per cent of the present American people.

I. WHY ENGLISHMEN WANTED COLONIES SIR WALTER RALEIGH AT THIRTY- 

FOUR. A portrait ascribed to Zuccaro, now in the National Gallery at London. 

The first impulse to English colonization came from English patriotism. When Elizabeth's reign was half completed, little England entered upon a daring rivalry with the overshadowing might of Spain. Out of that rivalry, English America was born. Reckless and picturesque free-booters like Drake (cut on page 4) sought profit and honor for themselves, and injury to the foe, by raiding rich provinces of Spanish America.

More far-sighted statesmen, like Raleigh, saw that English colonies in America would be 

a great bridle to the Indies of the Kinge of Spaine," and began to try so to "put a byt in the anchent enymys mouth." 14

DIFFICULTIES OF COLONIZATION 

15 But to found a colony in those days was harder than we can well understand. The mere outlay of money was enormous for that time. Ships had little storage room. Freights were high, and the best accommodations were poorer than modern steerage. To carry a man from England to America cost from £10 to £ 12, or about $500 in our values (since money in 1600 was worth eight or ten times as much as now). To provide his outfit, until he could raise a crop, cost as much more. Thus to establish a family in America took some thousands of dollars.

WHY ENGLAND WANTED VIRGINIA 

The English crown founded no colonies, nor did it give money toward founding any. It did give charters to those men who were willing to risk their fortunes in the attempt. These charters were grants (1) of territory and (2) of authority over future settlers. Nearly all English colonies were at first proprietary. The proprietor might be an individual or an English corporation. In either case, the proprietor owned the land and ruled the settlers.

The first colonial charter was granted by Elizabeth, in 1578, to Sir Humphrey Gilbert. Gilbert made two brave attempts at a colony. The first was dispersed by the Spaniards before it was well under way. The second, in the spring of 1583, reached the Newfoundland coast. Gilbert's authority was recognized readily by the "thirty-six ships of all nations" already there for the fishing; but desertion and disease weakened the colonists, and in August the survivors sailed for England. 

Gilbert had sunk his fortune, and he himself perished by shipwreck on the return voyage; but his enterprise was caught up at once by his half-brother, Sir Walter Raleigh, the most gallant figure of that daring age. In 1584, Raleigh received a charter, copied from Gilbert's, and in the next three years he sent three expeditions to Roanoke Island on the Carolina coast. 

His explorers declared the new land "the most plentiful, sweet, fruitful, and wholesome of all the world," and the natives were affirmed to be "such as live after the manner of the golden age." But supplies and reinforcements were delayed by the struggle with the Spanish Armada (page 4), and when they did arrive the colonists had vanished without trace. 

Raleigh had spent a fortune (a million dollars in our values); and, though he sent ships from time to time to search for the lost colonists, he could make no further attempt at settlement. 

Still, despite their failures, Gilbert and Raleigh are the fathers of American colonization. They had inspired their countrymen with the feeling that the founding of colonies was an heroic and patriotic enterprise. Wrote Gilbert, "He is not worthy to live at all that, for feare or danger of death, shun- 

bos

neth his countries service and his owne honour." And with pathetic courage, when in prison and near death, Raleigh said, “I shall yet live to see it [Virginia] an Inglische nation.” 

The next advance came from a new kind of colonizing organization the great London Company of 1606. For twenty-five years attempts at colonizing America had failed because the life-and-death struggle with Spain in Europe drained England's energies. Worse was to come. James I (1603) sought 

Spanish friendship; and then indeed Englishmen began to feel their chance for empire slipping through their fingers. But splendid memories of "the spacious days of great Elizabeth" still stirred men's hearts; and, as a protest against James' dastard policy in Europe, enterprising Englishmen turned again to colonize Virginia - "this one enterprise left unto these days." 

PATRIOTIC AND MISSIONARY MOTIVES 

Raleigh had found part of the funds for his undertakings by forming a partnership with some London merchants. In 1606, to carry on the enterprise, some of these same merchants organized a stock company¹ and secured from King James a grant known as the First Virginia Charter.

In form, this London Company was a business enterprise, and some of the members perhaps cared only for money gains. 

But, like Raleigh and Gilbert, the great leaders cared more to build up the power of England. Some of them, too, had it much at heart to Christianize the savages. The clergymen who guided the Church of England (then recently cut off from Rome) could not rest content with "this little English paddock" while Rome was winning new continents by her devoted missionaries.2 

The London Company, in one main aspect, was a foreign missionary society-the first in the Protestant world- and this character brought it many gifts of money (West's Source Book, No. 26 c). 

¹ Stock companies were just coming into fashion for trading with distant lands, like India and Northern Russia. 

2 Hakluyt (page 15) could not help squirming under the Romanists' taunt “that they had bene the onlie converters of many millions of infidells.”

WHY ENGLAND WANTED VIRGINIA 

For many years, the Company had to struggle with discouragement and distress. Its pamphlets, urging people to buy stock, did not place emphasis on any hope of large dividends as we expect a prospectus of a commercial company to do but rather on the meanness and "avarice" of the man who would "save" his money instead of using it to extend English freedom and the kingdom of God. It was these high enthusiasms, far more than it was greed, that brought hundreds of the noblest of Englishmen to the rescue of the enterprise. 

So far we have considered only the motives of Englishmen who stayed at home, helping there to promote American colonization. Let us look now at the motives of the colonists. 1 In 1600, Englishmen needed room. True, the island had still only a tenth as many people as to-day; but, as industry was carried on in that day, its four millions were more crowded than its forty millions are now. 

For the small farmers, especially, life had become very hard; so these yeomen furnished most of the manual labor in the early colonies. Few of this class could pay the cost of transporting themselves and their families to America. Commonly they were glad to bind themselves by written indentures to become "servants" to some wealthy landowner. That is, these "indentured servants" mortgaged their labor for several years ahead, in return for transportation and subsistence, and perhaps for a tract of wild land at the end of their term.

Captains and capitalists, also, were needed in Virginia. These came from the English gentry class. Until the peace with Spain in 1604, many high-spirited English volunteers had been fighting Spain in the Netherlands, for Dutch independence. Other such youths were" gentlemen-adventurers" who, under leaders like Drake, had paralyzed the far-flung domains of New Spain with fear. To such men, and to many younger sons of gentry families for whom there seemed no career at home, America beckoned alluringly as the land of opportunity. The period, 1 West's Modern Progress, 182-184.

THE LAND OF OPPORTUNITY AND ADVENTURE 

too, like our own, was one of rapid rise in the cost of living; and the heads of some old families found themselves unable to keep pace with former associates. Some of them preferred the chance for leadership in the New World to the certain necessity of " taking in sail" at home. 19 None of these "gentlemen" were used to steady work, and they were restive under discipline; so sometimes they drew down abuse from strict commanders like the worthy Captain 

John Smith. Still they were of that "restless, pushing material of which the world's best pathfinders have ever been made." 

When they had learned the needs of frontier life, their pluck and endurance made them splendid colonists. 

No doubt, the chief loadstone for most early settlers of all classes was some wild dream of wealth (Source Book, Nos. 8-9). In the first colonies, too, the expectations of sudden riches were more extravagant than in later attempts, and led for a time to disastrous neglect of the right sort of work. Yet the motive was a proper one. It calls for no sneer. In a later century the same desire to better one's condition lured the descendants of the first settlers to people the continent from the Appalachians to the Golden Gate.

Moreover, the motive was not mere greed. The youth was moved by a vision of romance and adventure. He was drawn partly by the glitter of gold, but quite as much by the mystery of new lands bosomed in the beauty of unknown seas. Best of all, these motives of gain and of noble adventure were infused with a high patriotism. Englishmen knew that in building their own fortunes on that distant frontier, just as truly as when they had trod the deck of Drake's ship, they were widening the power of the little home island.

II. VIRGINIA A PROPRIETARY COLONY: 1607-1624 

Four points in the Charter of 1606 call for notice: 

1. The company of stockholders was divided into two subcompanies. One of these was made up mainly of Londoners,

VIRGINIA UNDER THE LONDON COMPANY 

and is known as the London Company. The other was made up of gentlemen from the west of England, and is called the Plymouth Company. These proprietary companies (page 16) were to remain in England. 

2. Until 1620 the name Virginia applied to all the region claimed by England on the Atlantic coast, between the Spaniards on the south and the French on the north. This tract then reached from Cape Fear to north of the Penobscot, and was about 800 miles long. Within it each company was to have a district 100 miles along the coast and 100 miles inland. The 

London Company's tract was to be located somewhere in southern Virginia, and the Plymouth Company's, somewhere in the north. 

3. The charter promised to settlers "the liberties, franchises, and immunities" of Englishmen. This clause (found in all 

English colonial charters) did not mean the right to vote: not all Englishmen had that privilege at home. It meant such rights as jury trial, habeas-corpus privileges, and free speech,so far as those rights were then understood in England. 

4. In England there was to be a Council for the double company, with general oversight. In each colony there was to be a lower Council appointed by that higher Council. The local 

Council was to govern the settlers according to laws to be drawn up by the king.

This plan of government was poor. There was no distinct line between the king's authority and the Company's, and administration in the colonies was left to an unwieldy committee. 

Nevertheless, under this crude grant, was founded the first permanent English colony. The Plymouth Company made a fruitless attempt at settlement on the coast of Maine (page 8), and then remained inactive for twelve years. But in December of 1606 the London Company sent out, in three small vessels, a more successful expedition to Virginia.¹

SETTLEMENT AT JAMESTOWN 

1607, and planted Jamestown on the banks of a pleasant river flowing into the south side of the bay. To avoid Spanish attack from the sea, they chose a site thirty miles up the stream. They were wearied by tiresome months of ocean travel, with cramped quarters, wormy food, and slimy water, and the green valley of the "James River" seemed a paradise- with its "faire meddows and goodly tall Trees, with Freshwaters" and its "beautifull strawberries foure times bigger and better than ours in England."

But the site of Jamestown was low, and the "faire meddows" proved to be fever-breeding swamps. The early years were a time of cruel suffering (Source Book, No. 19). Two thirds of the settlers perished the first summer, and the "First Supply," in the fall of 1607, found only 38 survivors. Indeed, for twenty years each new immigration lost, on the average, half its members the first season! 21 During the early years, the colony was one great "plantation." 

The company of stockholders in England were proprietors. 

They directed the enterprise, selected settlers, appointed officers, and furnished transportation, supplies, and capital. The colonists were employees and servants. They did the work, cleared forests, built rude forts and towns, and raised crops, facing disease, famine, and savage warfare. The Council at 

Jamestown were not so much political rulers as industrial overseers, or housekeepers on a large scale. 

The products of the settlers' labor went into a common stock. 

Lumber, sassafras, dyestuffs, and potash (from the logs burned in making clearings) were shipped to the Company to help pay expenses. Grain was kept in storehouses, to be guarded and distributed by the Council. Here, too, were kept the supplies from England, - medicines, clothing, furniture, tools, arms and ammunition, seeds, stock of all kinds for breeding, and such articles of food as meal, bread, butter, cheese, salt, meat, and preserved fruits.

The most interesting figure during the first three years was the burly, bustling, bragging, efficient Captain John Smith.

VIRGINIA UNDER THE LONDON COMPANY 

Smith finally usurped all the power of government, and his beneficent tyranny saved the colony from ruin. In 1609, however, he was injured by an explosion of gunpowder, and went back to England.

PORTRAICT 

The next winter was "The

Starving Time." The number of settlers had risen to more than three hundred, but spring found only sixty gaunt survivors. These embarked to abandon the colony, with slight chance of life whether they went or stayed, but at the river's mouth they met a fleet bringing reinforcements and supplies.

Meantime, the year 1609 had seen a remarkable outburst of enthusiasm in England in behalf of the sinking colony. 

Sermons and pamphlets appealed to the patriotism of the nation not to let this new England perish. The list of the Company's stockholders was enlarged, until it came to include the most famous names in England, along with good men from all classes of society (Source Book, No. 20). Each of 650 new members bought from one to ten shares of stock, at about $600 a share in our values. 

Then in 1609 and 1612 the Company secured new charters from the king, containing three important new grants. 

1. The territory of the Company was extended. It was made to reach along the coast each way 200 miles from Point Comfort, and "up into the land throughout from sea to sea, west and northwest" (map on next page). 

2. The Company in England became a democratic organization, choosing annually its "Treasurer" and Council (or, as we should say, its President and Directors); and the authority APTAYNE IWS NHO

There was still no hint of self-government. The Company in

Virginia had left anarchy behind, but she had not reached liberty. From 1611 to 1616, the governor was 

Sir Thomas Dale. This stern soldier put in force a military government, with a savage set of laws known as Dale's Code. Death was the penalty for repeated absence from church, for repeated blasphemy, for refusing to answer the catechism of a clergyman, and for neglecting work! The military courts, too, made use of ingeniously atrocious punishments, such as burning at the stake or breaking on the wheel. One offender, who was caught stealing food from the public storehouse, was bound to a tree, with a bodkin thrust through his tongue, and left to starve. An old Virginian historian fitly called the government very bloody and severe . . . in no wise agreeable to a free people or to the British constitution." Dale, however, did keep order and protect the colony from the Indians.

UNDER THE LIBERAL LONDON COMPANY 

At Dale's departure the colonists numbered 351. Of these, 65 were women or children, and nearly 200 were "servants.' 

There were only 81 free men. To each of these Dale had set off a small three-acre garden plot. This was wise—but it did not amount to a change to a system of private industry, as some writers say. 29 Now a revolution took place in the management of the London Company. That body had been seriously troubled by internal quarrels between opposing factions. In 1618, control passed finally to a progressive group led by the Earl of Southampton and Sir Edwin Sandys. These patriots had been struggling gallantly in parliament against King James' arbitrary rule in England; and they at once granted a large measure of self-government to the Englishmen in America over whom they themselves had authority. In 1619 this new management sent out Sir George Yeardley as governor, to begin a 1 new era.

With the arrival of Yeardley's fleet the number of settlers was raised to a thousand. They were still mainly indentured servants, and were distributed now among eleven petty plantations. These were mere patches on the vast wilderness about them, scattered along a ribbon of territory (nowhere more than six miles wide) curving up the James for a hundred miles. 

Yeardley at once introduced three fundamental reforms. 

1. He established private ownership. Each free planter received 100 acres of land; and each new planter thereafter was promised 50 acres for himself and 50 more for each person whom he brought with him. (For many years longer, all grants were in strips fronting on rivers up which sea-going vessels could sail since there were no roads but such rivers.) 

2. Martial law was set aside. Yeardley proclaimed, said a body of settlers, " that those cruell lawes by which we had soe longe been governed were abrogated, and that we were now 1 West's Modern Progress tells that story (pages 188–191) and explains also all other references in this volume to European events.

REPRESENTATIVE SELF-GOVERNMENT 

25 to be governed by those free lawes which his Majesties subjects live under in Englande." 

3. The settlers received a share in the government. A Representative Assembly was summoned, "freely to be elected by the inhabitants, . . . to make and ordaine whatsoever lawes and orders should by them be thought good and profitable.” 66 99 

This first Representative Assembly in America met at James town August 9,¹ 1619, and followed without hesitation the forms of the English parliament. It contained two delegates from each of the eleven little settlements. In the same house with these twenty-two "Burgesses," however, sat the governor and the seven or eight members of his appointed council SO this first Assembly was not purely representative. It passed laws against drunkenness, gambling, idleness, absence from church, and “excess in apparel," and it "established” the Church of England in the colony.2 __________________ Jury trial and representative self-government were established upon a lasting foundation in America in 1619, while Virginia was still the only English colony. These two bulwarks of freedom came as a gift; but once given, the Virginians resisted firmly all later attempts to withdraw them. They were not then known in any large country except in England; and they were not to take root in the colonies of any other country until more than two hundred years later. Their establishment in Virginia made them inevitable in all other English colonies.

The new management of the Company bestirred itself to build up the colony on the material side also. To supply the labor so much needed, Sandys sought throughout England for skilled artisans and farmers, and shipped to Virginia many hundred "servants" to work for the Company. Several cargoes of young women, too, were induced to go out for wives to the free settlers; and supplies of all kinds were poured into the colony with a lavish hand.

THE KING ATTACKS THE COMPANY 

To be sure, pestilence and hardship continued for a time, and in 1622 an Indian massacre left only eight hundred people in the colony though more than three thousand newcomers had landed within three years. But Virginia was soon to become prosperous. Two years later there were twelve hundred settlers again, distributed among nineteen plantations. The Indians had been crushed. The settlers were making fortunes in the new business of raising tobacco; and their homes were taking on an air of comfort. The period of experiment was past. 

Meanwhile King James had become bitterly hostile toward the liberal management of the Company. Sandys had been prominent in parliament in opposing the king. Indeed he was reported to be "the king's greatest enemye." An envious business associate testified, too, that Sandys had expressed a wish to make a free popular state [in Virginia] in which the people should have noe government putt upon them but by their owne consents." 

When Sandys' term as "Treasurer" expired, in 1620, the king sent to the " General Court" of the Company the names of four men from whom he ordered them to elect a new Treasurer.

The Company (some hundreds of the best gentlemen of England present) remonstrated firmly against this interference with freedom of election. So James yielded, exclaiming petulantly, "Choose the Devil, and ye will; only not Sir Edwin Sandys!

Sandys then withdrew his name; and the Company sent a committee to his friend, the Earl of Southampton - who was little more to the royal taste to inquire whether he would accept the office. "I know the king will be angry," said the Earl to his friends, "but, so this pious and glorious work be encouraged, let the Company do with me as they think good." 

Then, "surceasing the ballot," the meeting elected him " with much joy and applause, by erection of hands." Sandys was chosen Deputy Treasurer and remained the real manager. Two years later the king failed again in a like attempt. Small wonder

Since James could not secure control of the Company, he decided to take Virginia away from it. The Indian massacre of 1622 furnished him an excuse for interfering. He sent commissioners to the colony to gather information unfavorable to the Company's rule. They, however, found the Virginians warm supporters of the Company. The charter could be revoked, too, only by the English courts. But just at this time those courts had been made mere tools of the monarch; and in 1624 the king's lawyers secured judgment that the charter was void. 

Thus ended the London Company-"the greatest and noblest association ever organized by the English people." 66 

VIRGINIA BECOMES A PROVINCE " III. VIRGINIA AS A ROYAL PROVINCE 

In 1624, then, Virginia became a Royal Province. This meant three great changes. 

1. The old land grants from the Company to settlers held good; but all the territory still owned by the Company at its fall became crown land. Royal governors, therefore, made grants from it thereafter, much as the Company had done. Indeed, it soon became the custom to grant a hundred acres to anyone who would clear and cultivate the ground and pay a few shillings yearly to the crown as quit rent." 

In later times Virginia often claimed its "ancient bounds as described in the Charter of 1609 (page 23). That grant, however, had not been made to the colony. The king afterward gave parts of it to other colonies. 99 2. The colony now had to support itself. In fifteen years the 

London Company had spent five million dollars in caring for it, and most of the settlers believed it must die unless such fostering continued. In the next four years they sent four petitions to

VIRGINIA SAVES HER ASSEMBLY 

the king, urging him to continue such aid. But the king was quarreling with parliament about money enough to run the government at home. He, therefore, paid no attention to such prayers and the colony found that it could walk alone. 

3. The king now had complete control of the government of the colony. And, as the colonists feared that he would help too little, so, with more reason, they feared that he would govern too much as he was trying desperately to do in England. 

So Virginia waged a strenuous and victorious struggle to save her Assembly. In the spring of 1624, as soon as it became plain that the king was going to overthrow the Company, the Assembly had solemnly put on record its claim to control taxation in a memorable law "The Governor shall lay no taxes or ympositions upon the colony, its lands or goods, other way than by the authority of the General Assembly, to be levied and ymployed as the said Assembly shall appoynt." 

This was the first assertion on this continent of the English principle, "No taxation without representation." That same summer, however, King James appointed a governor and council to rule the colony-with no mention of an Assembly - and none met for five years. The Virginians made several requests for one, and in 1625 they sent Yeardley to England to present their desires. Yeardley told the king that only the grant of an 

Assembly could allay the universal distrust in Virginia, where "the people, justly fearing to fall into former miseries, resolve rather to seek the farthest parts of the World." (What "former miseries were meant?) 

Neither this threat nor other petitions met with a direct answer, but they produced results. In 1629, the new king, Charles I, appointed Sir John Harvey governor. Harvey was a "king's man." But he had been one of the royal commissioners to Virginia in 1623 (page 27) and apparently he had learned there that it would not be wise to try to rule the colony without an Assembly. Before leaving England for his governorship, he drew up for the king's consideration a list of seven "Proposi-

SUGGESTIONS AND QUESTIONS 

29 tions touching Virginia." One of these propositions asked for a representative Assembly as part of the government. 

The king was just entering upon an eleven-year despotic period of "No Parliament " in England (page 48), but, in his answer to Harvey, he granted the request. After that time formal directions to call Assemblies became part of each governor's instructions. The London Company had planted constitutional liberty in America; the settlers cherished it devotedly; and the careless royal government found it easier to use the institution than to uproot it. Virginia had won a glorious victory for all future America.

CHAPTER III MARYLAND:1 A PROPRIETARY PROVINCE 

Among the people of Lord Baltimore's colony, as among English-speaking people in general, one might observe a fierce spirit of political liberty coupled with an ingrained respect for law. - FISKE, Old Virginia. 

For Maryland, the plan of colonization was much like that of Raleigh's day. George Calvert, a high-minded gentleman, had been interested for many years in the expansion of England. 

He was a member of the London Company and of the New 

England Council (page 35).

Finally he took upon his own shoulders a separate attempt to build a colony. In 1623, he secured a charter from King James for a vast tract in Newfoundland, with authority to rule settlers there; and to this province he sent out several bodies of colonists.

It put the head of the Baltimore family in the position, practically, of a king over the settlers, but his vast authority was limited by one supreme provision (not found in the charter to Raleigh). In raising taxes and making laws, the proprietor could act only with the advice and consent of an Assembly of the freemen or of their representatives. (In Maryland this term "freemen" soon became equivalent to "landowners.")

This recognition of political rights for the settlers, in a royal charter, is an onward step in the history of liberty. 

The creation of the Virginia Assembly, and the devotion of the Virginians to it, had borne fruit. Between 1620 and 

1630, it became a settled conviction for all Englishmen (at last even for the court circle) that colonization in America was possible only upon the basis of self-government. 

The Assembly soon won more power than king or proprietor had meant it to have. The proprietors did not live in the colony. They ruled it through governors, whom they appointed and dismissed at will and to whom they gave such part of their own authority as they chose. The governor was assisted by a small council, also appointed by the proprietor. This proprietary machinery (governor and council) had been intended to be the controlling part of the government; but within twenty years, the Assembly became the center of authority. " (page 8),

CHAPTER IV THE BEGINNINGS OF NEW ENGLAND 

After all that can be said for material and intellectual advantages, it remains true that moral causes determine the greatness of nations; and no nation ever started on its career with a larger proportion of strong characters or a higher level of moral earnestness than the English colonies in America. - LECKY, England in the Eighteenth Century, II, 2. 

In 1620 some members of the Plymouth branch (page 20) of the old Virginia Company (roused by the success of the London branch) reorganized as "The Council resident in Plymouth ... for the planting of New England." Soon a royal charter gave this body all North America between the fortieth parallel and the forty-eighth (map opposite). 

This "New England Council," or " Plymouth Council," sent out no colonists. Instead, it sold or granted tracts of land to various adventurers who undertook to found settlements. 

Some small trading stations were established under such grants, and in 1623 there came a more ambitious attempt. Robert

Gorges, son of the most active member of the Plymouth Council, was granted lands near Boston harbor, with a charter empowering him to rule settlers there "according to such lawes as shall be hereafter established by public authoritie of the state assembled in Parliament in New England." The Council also commissioned Gorges "General Governor over all settlements to be formed in their vast territory. 

The Pilgrim colony at Plymouth (of which we shall soon. speak more fully) was already in its third year, under a government of its own. But it was still weak, and it had no legal authority for its self-government (page 41). Moreover, it lay close to the proposed home of the "general governor." Accordingly the leaders at Plymouth dreaded Gorges' coming and were soon rejoicing quietly at his swift going. 

35

BEGINNINGS OF NEW ENGLAND 

For Gorges, who was indeed a very gallant and honorable gentleman, at once brought to Massachusetts Bay a well chosen company containing several " gentlemen,"¹ two clergymen, and some scores of skilled farmers and artisans. After one hard winter, however, this promising colony broke up. The gentle Bradford, governor of Plymouth, wrote with unusually caustic humor that Gorges departed “ having scarce saluted the Cuntrie of his Government, not finding the state of things hear to answer his qualitie."

Successful Colonization in New England 

Waited upon Religious Zeal By this time many English ships had visited New England and brought back reports of excellent harbors and promising sites for plantations. They told, too, of splendid forests 2 and of a marvelous wealth of fish and furs. Indeed it is estimated that for six summer months of each year, at this period, some ten thousand English fishermen were drawn to those shores by the codfisheries. Still, so far, commercial motives had proved insufficient to build a permanent settlement. Success in that work was to come from a new force just ready to take up the task of colonization. 

This force was Puritanism. The "established" church in 

England was the Episcopalian; and within that church the dominant party had strong "High-Church" leanings. This

High-Church party was warmly supported by the royal "head of the church," — Elizabeth, James, Charles, in turn; but it was engaged in constant struggle with a large, aggressive Puritan element. 

Puritanism was much more than a religious sect. It was an ardent aspiration for reform in many lines. In politics, it stood for an advance in popular rights; in conduct, for stricter and 

1 If this term in its technical use in the seventeenth century is not clear from previous historical study, consult No. 1 in the Source Book. 2 Forests in that day were all that forests, coal mines, and oil wells are now- and the woods of England were already becoming exhausted, and were insufficient for the demands of English industry.

PURITANISM BECOMES A COLONIZING FORCE 

higher morality; in theology, for the stern doctrines of Calvinism, which appealed powerfully to the strongest souls of that age; and in church organization, for an extension of the "reformation " that had cut off the English Church from Rome. 37 Two groups of English Puritans stood in sharp opposition to one another, — (1) an influential element within the church (some of them Presbyterian in their inclination, and others rather more what we now call "Low-Church" Episcopalians) and (2) the despised Separatists outside of it. 

The first had no wish to separate church and state. They wished one national church of their own sort - to which everybody within England should conform. They desired also to make the church a more far-reaching moral power. To that end they aimed to introduce more preaching into the service and to simplify ceremonies, to do away with the surplice, with the ring in the marriage service, with the sign of the cross in baptism, and perhaps with the prayerbook. Most of them at this time seem to have had no very clear ideas about changes in the form of church government; but at least they did not regard government by bishops as a divine ordinance (as the High-Churchmen did). 

On the other hand, the Independents, or "Puritans of the Separation," believed that there should be no national church, but that religious societies should be wholly separate from the state. They wished each local religious organization to be a little democratic society independent in government even of other churches. It was a congregation of these Separatists who established the first successful colony in New England, and whom we are now to study as the Pilgrims at Plymouth.

THE PLYMOUTH PILGRIMS 

Next to the fugitives whom Moses led out of Egypt, the little shipload of outcasts who landed at Plymouth . . . are destined to influence the future of mankind. - JAMES RUSSELL LOWELL. 

CHAPTER V 

99 

The Pilgrims in Holland. To all other sects the Separatists seemed the most dangerous of radicals, mere anarchists in religion. They had been persecuted by Queen Elizabeth, and some of their societies had fled to Holland. In 1608, early in the reign of James, one of their few remaining churches — a little congregation from the village of Scrooby-managed to escape to that same land, "wher they heard was freedome of Religion for all men. a countrie wher they must learn a new language and get their livings they knew not how . . . not acquainted with trads or traffique, by which that countrie doth subsist, but . . . used to a plaine countrie life and the inocente trade of husbandrey."¹ 66 They first settled in Amsterdam, but had no sooner begun to feel safe in some measure, through toil and industry, from “ the grime and grisly face of povertie coming upon them like an armed man," than it seemed needful to move again, this time to Leyden. There indeed they enjoyed "much sweete and delightefull societie . . . in the wayes of God"; but they continued subject to such "greate labor and hard fare" that 66 many that desired to be with them . . and to injoye the libertie of the gospell . . . chose the prisons in England rather than this libertie in Holland." 

So, after twelve years in Holland, the Pilgrims decided to remove once more, to the wilds of North America. They 

¹ Quoted passages in this chapter are from Bradford's Plymouth Plantation when no other authority is mentioned. 38

PARTNERSHIP WITH LONDON MERCHANTS 

39 hoped, says Bradford, to find a place where (1) their children anyway would not have so hard a time to earn a living; where (2) their young people would not be exposed to the "loose morals" (as the Pilgrims thought them) of easy-going Dutch society; and where (3) their religious society would be less likely to die as the older members passed off the scene. 

Winslow (another Pilgrim historian) dwells also on a fourth motive. They wished, he says, to establish themselves under their own English flag-one of their griefs in Holland being that their children were drawn away from the English tongue and manners by intermarrying with the Dutch. 

Of all these motives, the religious one was no doubt the weightiest. In Holland there was no chance for their society to grow. But if they could establish themselves in a New World, " a greate hope and inward zeall they had of laying some good foundation for the propagating and advancing the gospell of the kingdome of Christ in those remote parts of the world; yea, though they should be but even as stepping-stones unto others for the performing of so greate a work." 66 From the London Company the Pilgrims secured a grant of land, and, by entering into partnership with another group of London merchants, they secured the necessary money. For many months, says Bradford, this opening business was delayed by many rubbs; for the Virginia Counsell was so disturbed with factions as no bussines could goe forward." But when Sandys and the Puritan faction got control in that Company (page 24), the matter was quickly arranged. (Brewster, one of the Pilgrim leaders, had been a trusted steward of a manor belonging to the Sandys family.) 

The seventy merchants who furnished funds subscribed stock in £ 10 shares. (Captain John Smith says that by 1623 they had advanced more than $300,000 in modern values.) Each emigrant was given one share for "adventuring" himself, and he might buy more shares if he were rich enough. For seven years all wealth produced was to go into a common stock, but from it the colonists were to have "meate, drink, apparell,

PLYMOUTH PLANTATION 

and all provissions." The partnership was then to be dissolved, and the common property divided. 

The arrangement was clumsy, because it involved a system of labor in common, but it was generous toward the settlers. 

Penniless immigrants at Jamestown became "servants (as friendless individuals) to work for seven years under overseers and at the end of the time to receive merely a little wild land. 

The penniless Pilgrims were "servants" for a time, in a sense; but only as one large body, and to a company of which they themselves were part. Their persons were controlled, and their labors directed, by officers chosen by themselves from their own number.

Two heart-breaking years had dragged along in these negotiations, and the season of 1620 was far wasted when (September 16) the Mayflower at last set sail. Most of the congregation stayed at Leyden, with their aged pastor, to await the outcome of this first expedition. Only the more robust embarked for the venture. The Mayflower carried 102 colonists, but more than half of them were "strangers" from London and its neighborhood. Among these recruits were such worthy spirits as Miles Standish and John Alden.

The immigrants meant to settle "in the northern part of 

Virginia." (See the map facing page 35.) But the little vessel was tossed by the autumn storms until the captain lost his reckoning; and they made land, after ten weeks, on the bleak shore of New England, already in the clutch of winter (November 21). The tempestuous season, and the dangerous shoals off 

Cape Cod, made it unwise to continue the voyage. For some weeks they explored the coast in small boats, and finally decided to make their home at a place which an English map had already christened Plymouth. 

Before landing, they adopted the Mayflower Compact. A charter from the Virginia Company had provided that they should be "governed by officers of their own choosing." The

66 grant, however, had no force outside Virginia." So, to prevent disorder from some of the strangers among them," who were already letting fall "mutinous speeches," they drew up and signed a "Compact," believing" that shuch an acte by them done might be as firme as any patent." 66 4I This famous agreement has sometimes been called, carelessly, a written constitution of an independent state. This it was not. It did not hint at independence, but expressed lavish allegiance to the English king. And it was not a constitution: it did not determine what officers there should be, nor how or when they should be chosen, nor what powers they should have. It does, however, resemble a preamble to a constitution. The signers declared their intention (in the absence of other authority) to maintain order by upholding the will of the majority of their own company (Source Book, No. 46). The American genius for finding a basis for law, at need, in the common will dates from these humble English settlers at Plymouth. 

The early years were a time of cruel hardship, a stern struggle for bare life. The first winter, in particular, was more severe than anything these unprepared Englishmen had ever dreamed of. Says Bradford: "Now, summer being done, all things stand upon them with a wetherbeaten face; and the whole countrie, full of woods and thickets, represented a wild and savage hiew. . . . In 2 or 3 months time, halfe their company dyed . . . wanting houses and other comforts; [and of the rest] in the time of most distres, ther was but 6 or 7 sound persons to care for all the sick." 

Of the eighteen married women who landed in January, May found only four living. Yet not one person of the steadfast colony went back with the Mayflower when she sailed for England that spring. In Holland they had carefully pondered the dangers that might assail them, and had highly resolved that "all greate and honorable actions must be enterprised and overcome with answerable courages."

False hopes of quick-won wealth from fish and beaver had had a part in starting the movement. But the inexperienced

PLYMOUTH PLANTATION 

Pilgrims were wholly unfit for the fisheries and the fur trade; and in any case they found at once that to set up a permanent colony, with women and children, demanded that they give all their energies for a long time to raising food and building homes. 

For long the governor's most important duty was to direct the work in the fields — where he toiled, too, with his own hands, along with all the men and the larger boys. 

The "supplies" expected from the London partners came, from year to year, in too meager measure to care even for the new immigrants who appeared along with them. Fortunately, during the first winter, the colonists found a supply of Indian corn for seed. A friendly native taught them how to cultivate it; and the old cornfields of the abandoned Indian villages saved them the formidable labor of clearing away the forest. The slow progress, even then, toward a safe supply of food is shown vividly in a letter from Edward Winslow to friends in England at the end of the first year: "We have built seven dwelling houses, and four for the use of the plantation [for common use, that is, as storehouses, etc.], and have made preparation for divers others. We set, the last spring, some twenty acres of 

Indian corn, and sowed some six acres of barley and pease. 

God be praised, we had good increase of [the] Indian corn, and of our barley, indifferent good, but our pease not worth the gathering."1 

Even among these "sober and godly men" the system of industry in common proved a hindrance: "For this communitie was found to breed much confusion and discontente, and retard much imployment that would have been to their benefite and comforte. For the yung-men, that were most able and fitte, . . . did repine that they should spend their time and strength to worke for other mens wives and children.

The aged and graver men, to be ranked and equalised in labours and victuals, cloaths, etc., with the younger and meaner sorte, thought it some indignitie and disrespect unto them. And for mens wives to be commanded to doe service for other men, as dressing their meate, washing their cloaths, etc., they deemed it a kind of slaverie; neither could many husbands well brooke it."

SETTLEMENT WITH THE LONDON MERCHANTS 43 

In the third year, famine seemed imminent. Then Governor 

Bradford, with the approval of the chief men of the colony, set aside the agreement with the London partners in this matter of common industry, and assigned to each family a parcel of land "for the time only." "This," says Bradford, "had very good success, so as much more corne was planted then other waise would have been. The women now wente willingly into the field, and tooke their litle-ons with them to set corne, which before would aledge weakness . . . whom to have compelled would have bene thought great tiranie."1

Finally the London merchants saw that they could never get back their full investment, and they notified the colony that they would agree to pocket a heavy loss if the settlers would guarantee repayment of the rest. By 1627, when the partnership was to have expired, the colony had begun a promising trade with the Indians for beaver skins. So Bradford, with seven other leading men, ventured to take upon themselves the English debt in return for a monopoly of this trade until the money could be raised. The merchants at once surrendered all other claims upon the colony. Then the lands, houses, and cattle were divided among the settlers as private property. 

All danger of failure was past. The political development may be treated under three heads: 

1. While still on the Mayflower, the Pilgrims chose John 

Carver for their governor. 

Carver died during the first spring.

The Pilgrims' first purpose was a democratic church (page 37). 

Since their church government was a little democracy, it was natural that their civil ¹ government also should be democratic. 

There was, however, another reason why government at Plymouth was a democracy. The little colony at first had no

More than in any other important colony, all the settlers came from the "plain people." Hardly one of them would have ranked as a "gentleman' in England. Bradford there would have remained a poor yeoman, and John 

Alden a humble cooper.

At the time some of the best among them thought this a misfortune. They had not set out to build a democratic civil government. Even Pastor Robin son lamented that they were "not furnished with any persons of spetiall eminencie above the rest, to be chosen into officers." 

If such eminent persons had been present, public feeling and English custom would no doubt have made them into an aristocracy of office. To-day we may rejoice that this little commonwealth was so democratic in its society that it had to be democratic in its government.

Plymouth never secured a royal charter, and its government remained upon the basis of the Mayflower Compact until King William III annexed the colony to Massachusetts in 1691. In

The colony grew slowly, counting less than three hundred people in 1630, when the great Puritan migration to Massachusetts Bay began. The Puritan colonies, then established, grew much faster and taught more important lessons in politics and economics. Plymouth had little direct influence, in either of these ways, upon later American history. It did have a large part in directing the other Puritan colonies toward church independency; but its supreme service, after all, lay in pointing the way for that later and greater migration. This the Pilgrims did. With right their friends wrote them later, when the little colony was already overshadowed by its neighbors," Let it not be grievous to you that you have been but instruments to break the ice for others: the honor shall be yours till the world's end."
