- WILLIAM STOUGHTON, Election Sermon at Boston in 1690. 

Commercial Beginnings.- Many groups of English merchants were engaged in the New England fisheries, and some of them had tried to establish stations on the coast. One 

London group finally became incorporated as The Company for Massachusetts Bay. In 1628 this Company bought from the 

New England Council the territory between the Charles and Merrimac rivers (extending "from ocean to ocean"), and during the summer it sent out sixty colonists under John Endicott (a well-known Puritan gentleman) to a station near Cape Ann. A few "old settlers" whom Endicott found there were at first inclined to dispute his authority, but finally they recognized him peaceably as head of the settlement — to which accordingly he gave the Hebrew name Salem (Peace). 

A year later (March 14, 1629) the Massachusetts Company secured a charter from King Charles. At the time this "First 

Charter of Massachusetts Bay" was merely a grant to the proprietary company in England. It confirmed their title to the land they had bought from the New England Council, and it gave them authority over settlers, similar to the authority possessed by other colonizing companies in England. 

The Company now busied itself in collecting supplies of all sorts and in seeking out emigrants of various trades. In May of 1629 it sent out its second expedition, of some two hundred settlers, led by Francis Higginson, a Puritan minister. Soon after, a Puritan church was organized in Salem. 47

MASSACHUSETTS BAY COLONY 

So far the history of the colony is like that of other commercial plantations. Most of the settlers were "servants." The chief men were Puritans because it was easier just then for an emigration to find fit leaders in England among the Puritans than among other classes; and the proprietary Company was Puritan, on the whole, because almost the whole merchant class in England was Puritan. But there is no evidence that any one was planning, as yet, to build a Puritan colony. Later in this same summer, however, a new colonizing movement began, with that special purpose.

This new movement was due to a new danger to Puritanism. 

Despite the strenuous efforts of the Puritans, the English Church was being carried farther and farther away from their ideals. Bishop Laud, the tireless leader of the High-Church movement (page 36), was warmly supported by King Charles. 

All high ecclesiastical offices had been turned over to Laud's followers; and his "High Commission" Court, with dungeon and pillory, was driving Puritan pastors from their parishes. 1 The Puritans had rested their hope upon parliament. They had a majority in the House of Commons; and with the meeting of the third parliament of Charles in 1628 their reform seemed on the verge of success. That parliament extorted the king's assent to the great "Petition of Right"; and then, in the winter of 1629, it began vigorously to regulate the church. 

But the king struck a despotic blow. March 2, he dissolved parliament, sent its leaders to the Tower, and entered upon a system of absolute rule. For eleven years no parliament was to meet in England. Religious reform and political liberty had gone down in common ruin, the end of which no man could see. 

The continent of Europe offered no hope. Every form of 

Protestantism there seemed doomed.2 Wallenstein's victorious troopers were turning the Protestant provinces of Germany into wilderness homes for wild beasts, and in France the great 

Richelieu had just crushed the Huguenots.2 

1 West's Modern Progress, 191-198. 

2 Ib., 161-165.

BECOMES A PURITAN COMMONWEALTH 

Accordingly, the more dauntless of the English Puritans turned their eyes to the New World. At Plymouth they saw a colony of Separatists, not large, but safely past the stage of experiment. Close by was the prosperous beginning of the 

Massachusetts commercial colony, controlled by a Puritan company in England and managed on the spot by well-known Puritans like Endicott and Higginson. How natural to try to convert Massachusetts into a refuge for Low-Church Puritanism, such as Plymouth already was for "Puritans of the Separation." 49 But the leaders of this new movement had no idea of becoming part of a mere plantation governed by a distant proprietary company, however friendly. They were of the landowning aristocracy of England, justices of their counties, and, on occasion, members of parliament. August 25, a number of them gathered, by long horseback journeys, and signed the famous 

Cambridge Agreement (Source Book, No. 58), promising one another solemnly that they would embark for Massachusetts with their families and fortunes, if they could find a way to take with them the charter and the "whole government." 

A proposal to transfer the government to America had been made a month earlier, at the July meeting of the Company in England. The plan was novel to most of the members, and it threatened them with financial loss; but in September, after long debates, it was approved.¹

The new men of the Cambridge Agreement now bought stock ; many old stockholders drew out; the old officers resigned (since they were not among those who wished to emigrate); and 

John Winthrop, the most prominent of the new men, was elected "governor." The next spring, Winthrop led to Massachusetts a great Puritan migration - the most remarkable colonizing expedition the world had ever seen. For the first time, too, a proprietary corporation removed to its colony. 

Indeed colony and corporation merged. Massachusetts became 

"corporate colony" and a Puritan commonwealth.

But in that summer, seventeen ships (counting Winthrop's twelve) brought two thousand new settlers. Then six new towns were started - Boston, Dorchester, Watertown, Roxbury, Lynn (or Saugus), and Newtown - which later became Cambridge. (Map facing page 71.)

But the immigrants of 1630 found conditions sadly different from their expectations. Two hundred returned home in the same ships that had brought them over, and two hundred more died before December. Immediately on his arrival, in fear of famine before the next summer, Winthrop wisely hurried back a ship for more supplies. Its prompt return, in February, was all that saved the colony. 

Meantime the deserters spread discouraging stories in England so that emigration to Massachusetts ceased for two years. In 1633, however, it began again. Soon the famous ship-money troubles in England ¹ gave it new impetus, and it went on, at the average volume of three thousand people a year, until the reforming Long Parliament met in 1640.¹ 1 

Thus the eleven years of "No Parliament " (page 48) saw twenty-five thousand selected Englishmen planted in New England. 

This was the "Great Migration" of 1629-1640. In that last year the movement stopped short. Says Winthrop, "The parliament in England setting upon a general reformation both in church and state . . . this caused all men to stay in England, in expectation of a New World " there. Indeed, the migration turned the other way, and many of the best of the New England Puritans hurried back to the old home now that there was a chance to fight for their principles again in England itself.

New England had no further immigration of consequence until after the Revolution. But this coming of the Puritans, during England's ten hopeless years, is one of the fruitful facts in history. 51 True, the twenty-five thousand were not all Puritans, and the Puritans were not all saints. Some little communities were made up wholly of rude fishermen. A Puritan historian tells how a preacher from another town, visiting Marblehead and praising the devotion of the people to religious principle, was interrupted by a rough voice, "You think you are talking to the people of the Bay: we came here to catch fish.” 

The best Puritan settlements, too, contained many non- 

Puritan "servants." Winthrop alone brought in his "household" some twenty male servants, several of whom were married. Many of this servant population had the natural vices of an irresponsible, untrained, hopeless class. On reaching America, too, they saw greater opportunity for free labor than they had ever dreamed; but they had ignorantly bound themselves to service through the best years of their lives. 

Brooding upon this led some to crime or suicide. 

The great body of the free immigrants had been shopkeepers, artisans, or small farmers. They were plain, uneducated men, who followed a trusted minister or an honored neighbor of the gentry class. In large measure they came to escape the pressure of poverty. They listened eagerly to Winthrop's argument:- 

... "This Land [England] growes weary of her Inhabitants, soe as man, who is the most pretious of God's creatures, is here . . . of less prise among us than an horse or a sheepe. Why then should we stand striving here . . . (many men spending as much labour and coste to . . . keepe an acre or tuoe of Land as would procure many hundred as good or better in another Countrie) and in the meantime suffer a whole Continent, fruitfull and convenient, to lie waste?" (Source Book, No. 59.)

Even the leaders themselves had other motives besides the religious one. They, too, hoped (at first) to better their

MASSACHUSETTS BAY COLONY 

worldly condition. Winthrop had been induced to emigrate, in part, by the decay of his fortune in England. As he explained, in the third person, to his friends, "His meanes heer are soe shortened as he shall not be able to continue in the same place and callinge [as before]; and so, if he should refuse this opportunitye, that talent which God hath bestowed upon him for publick service were like to be buried." Many others of the 

1630 migration had been deluded by "the too large commendations" of New England which the enthusiastic Higginson had sent back the year before (Source Book, No. 59 d).

Still when these dreams faded, the more steadfast spirits did not falter, but showed bravely the higher aims that moved them most. After the first hard months, Winthrop wrote to his wife (about to join him the next summer): 

Yet we may "I do hope our days of affliction will soon have an end. not look for great things here. . . . [But] we here enjoy God and Jesus 

Christ. I thank God, I like so well to be here as I do not repent my coming; and if I were to come again, I would not have altered my course though I had foreseen all these afflictions."

Men who had left stately ancestral manor houses took up life calmly in rudely built log cabins, and never looked backward. 

Famous ministers, who came from the loveliest parish churches in peaceful England, preached and gave the communion, and married, baptized, and buried, in bleak, barn-like “meetinghouses," where each male worshiper brought his musket, anc where the worshipers might hear the dreaded war-whoop break in upon their psalms. A shocking proportion of the babies died, year by year, in the harsh climate and draughty houses, and many brave, uncomplaining, overburdened women "but took 

New England on the way to Heaven."

Sparks from the mud-plastered fireplaces and chimneys set many a fire. Winthrop's "Journal" speaks repeatedly of such loss home, barn, hay, and stock, often in the dead of a winter night. Wolves killed the calves of this or that settler a serious disaster when most stock had still to be brought from England. Men, and sometimes women, were

THROUGH HARDSHIPS TO SUCCESS 

53 lost in short trips through the woods, and found frozen to death. Inexperienced fishermen were caught by storms and swept away to sea. Amid all this, the men of the gentry class kept up as much as they could of the old English stateliness. They trod briar-tangled forest paths, clad in ruffles, silk hose, long cloak, and cocked hat, and solemnly exchanged garments, in token of friendship, with painted savages who now and then stalked haughtily into the villages to dine with the chief men.

After the first winter the colony was never in real danger of absolute ruin, and slowly it worked its way to a rude comfort. In 1670 a Boston schoolmaster tells us how

From the first, there were many kinds of work. Every free inhabitant, besides his village lot, had his hundred acres or so of land; and the "gentlemen " soon tried - not very successfully to farm larger plantations with indentured servants. 

These land grants, large or small, were true freeholds," free even from the small " quit rents" that were the rule in Virginia. 66 The stony soil forced the settlers at once to take up other work, also, besides farming. Each family raised a few pigs, to supply the pork-barrel- and the straying and trespasses of these unruly brutes caused much annoyance. 

As soon as

EARLY MASSACHUSETTS 

possible, men began also to breed cattle. The fisheries furnished some profitable export to England, to help pay for European supplies. From the woods that reached to their doors, the settlers' axes fashioned staves and clapboards both for home use and for export. Mills to grind grain appeared here and there, where streams provided water power. In the second year, New England's famous shipbuilding and coasting trade began, when Winthrop launched The Blessing of the Bay — a small schooner, which traded for furs with the Indians and with English settlements along the coast, from the Kennebec to the Connecticut. 

Very early some primitive iron works began to extract iron from the easily worked bog deposits, and to cast simple implements. 

In 1646 the Massachusetts General

Court gave a patent to John Jenks for improvements on the clumsy scythe, which gave that tool its modern form. Brick kilns were among the early industries. The first sawmill appeared by 1635 near Portsmouth in New Hampshire; and soon at many points such mills were turning the forest about them into rough lumber, while, at clearings remote from water power, the logs were burned into potash. (Potash in that day was indispensable in manufacturing woolen goods and glass and soap, and large amounts were sent to Europe. See pages 21, 36.)

ARISTOCRACY VS. DEMOCRACY 

It was not easy to stretch the charter of a merchant company into a constitution for a commonwealth. The charter provided that all important matters should be settled by the stockholders (freemen) in four General Courts each year. Only

THE STRUGGLE FOR DEMOCRACY 

55 men twelve freemen of the corporation had come to America of strong character and prudent judgment. They were all of the gentry class, and before leaving England they had chosen themselves magistrates (governor and "Assistants "). They had authority, therefore, to rule the two thousand settlers and make laws. Their first meeting in America fixed the wage of laborers, forbidding a carpenter or mason to take more than two shillings a day. 1 From the first a democratic movement challenged this oligarchic government. At the General Court in October, 1630, a little group of magistrates was confronted by more than a hundred sturdy settlers asking to be admitted freemen. 

This was a united demand for citizenship by all heads of families above the station of unskilled laborers. To refuse was to risk the wholesale removal of dissatisfied colonists. 

In this dilemma, the shrewd leaders tried to give the shadow and keep the substance. They postponed action on the application until the next spring. Meantime they passed two laws -in violation of the charter: first, that the Assistants, instead of the whole body of freemen, should make laws and choose the governor; second, that the Assistants (without any reëlection) should hold office during good behavior, instead of for only one year as the charter ordered. Then (May, 1631) they admitted 

116 new freemen, having left them almost no power. The new freemen submitted to these usurpations for a while because they did not know clearly what their rights were. The charter was locked in Winthrop's chest, and only the magistrates had read it. 

The chief founders of New England had a real dread of democracy.¹ 

John Cotton, the greatest of their clerical leaders, wrote:- 'Democracy 

I do not conceive that God did ever ordain as a fit government for either church or commonwealth. If the people be governors, who shall be governed?" The great Winthrop, too, declared that democracy has "no warrant in Scripture," and that "among nations it has always been accounted the meanest and worst of all forms of government." 

1 An oligarchy is government by a few. Government by a large upper class is aristocracy. In a democracy all the people have equal rights.

EARLY MASSACHUSETTS 

The first effective protest against this oligarchic rule was "the Watertown Protest." After good English precedent, it grew out of an attempt at "taxation without representation."” 

In February, 1632, the Assistants voted a tax for fortifying the colony. Watertown's share was fixed at eight pounds. The minister of Watertown (who had already had some trouble with the Assistants on religious matters) called the people of his town together and secured a vote from them "that it was not safe to pay moneys after that sort for fear of bringing themselves and posterity into bondage." " 1 66 

Governor Winthrop summoned the men of Watertown before him at Boston and rebuked them for their " error." The culprits were so overawed that they "made a retraction and submission . . . and so their offence was pardoned." On the walk back to Watertown through the winter night, however, the error seems to have revived, and during the next months there must have been much secret plotting and sending to and fro among the towns.2 A week before the next General Court, Winthrop warned the Assistants that he had heard the people intended to come to the assembly and ask that the Assistants be chosen anew every year, and that the governor be chosen "by the whole court, and not by the Assistants only." (The charter made both these rules, as the freemen must have heard.) 

Winthrop's warning aroused much excitement among the magistrates. But when the Court met, the freemen calmly took back into their own hands the annual election of governor and Assistants as a matter of right. Then, in accordance with the Watertown Protest, they voted that thereafter each town should choose representatives to act with the magistrates in matters of taxation.

Two years later (1634) came a further peaceful revolution.

This began as a protest against "special privilege." The 

Assistants had made laws to favor their own class - trying repeatedly to keep wages down to the old level in England¹ (page 55), and ordering that swine found in grain fields might be killed. (The poor man wanted his pig to find its living in the woods, but the rich men were not willing to fence their large fields.) 66 

The common freemen determined to stop some of this class legislation." In April, 1634, Governor Winthrop sent out the usual notice calling all freemen to a General Court in May. 

Soon after, on a given day, two men from each of the eight towns (page 50) came together to Boston and asked to see the charter! 

How this first "people's convention " in America was arranged - by what secret journeys and conferences and plottings there is no record. After reading the charter, the " convention" called Winthrop's attention to the plain fact that the making of laws belonged properly to the whole body of freemen (now some 200), instead of to the nine Assistants. Winthrop told them loftily that the freemen did not have men among them "qualified for such a business." He suggested, however, that perhaps they might once a year choose a committee to make suggestions to the Assistants. 

The governor felt sure that as his "Journal" shows this condescension had quieted the trouble. But when the 

General Court met (May 14), three deputies appeared from each of the eight towns and calmly took seats with the Assistants, claiming power not merely to suggest laws but to make them. 

The Assistants did not venture to dispute this claim. Representative self-government was established. 

1 Winthrop speaks often of the high cost of food and other necessities, as compared with English prices, though he was honestly dismayed that carpenters should ask more than the old English wage. But free land, near and abundant, soon made all wage laws absurd and unenforceable. A carpenter, ordered to work for too low a wage, became a farmer - and so helped to keep up wages for other working men.

EARLY MASSACHUSETTS 

The aristocrats had put forward John Cotton (page 55) to preach the "election sermon" with which the Court opened. 

Cotton "showed from the Word of God" that magistrates should hold office for life — unless deposed for cause, after public trial. The answer of the freemen was to demand a ballot, instead of the usual" erection of hands." Then they dropped Winthrop from the office he had held for four years, fined some of the Assistants for having used too much power, and admitted 81 new freemen whom the Assistants the day before had refused to admit. 

The Court then made the revolution permanent. It decreed that every General Court in future should consist (like this one) of deputies chosen by the several towns and of the governor and Assistants. Only such Courts could admit freemen, lay taxes, or make laws. At the opening of the May Court each year, all freemen might be present, to choose governor and Assistants.

For the most part, the old rulers took these changes in good part. Winthrop, after recording his defeat, adds magnanimously, "This Court made many good orders." (In 1636, in time of danger, Winthrop again became governor, and was then reëlected almost every year until his death, in 1649.) 

Massachusetts had grown from an Oligarchy¹ into a Representative Aristocracy.¹ 

It was not a Democracy.¹

There was even more aristocracy in society than in government. The people were divided into five distinct classes: gentlemen, who alone had a right to the title Master (Mr.); skilled artisans and freeholders, the backbone of the colony, usually addressed as "Goodman " Brown or Jones; unskilled laborers, for whose names no handle was needed; servants, who usually passed finally into the class of artisans ; slaves, of whom there were soon a few, Negro and Indian. 

Gentlemen were set apart from the lower orders almost as distinctly as Lords in England were from gentlemen. In early 

1 See explanation of these terms on page 55.

A REPRESENTATIVE ARISTOCRACY 

59 Massachusetts, one family out of fourteen belonged to this aristocracy. Ordinary people had to show respect to these social superiors, and the laws gave them some special privileges.

For instance, in 1631, Mr. Josias Plaistowe was convicted of stealing corn from the Indians. His servants who had assisted, under orders were condemned to be flogged; but the court merely fined Plaistowe and ordered that thenceforward he should be called "by the name of Josias, and not Mr., as formerlie." This last was equivalent to degrading an officer to the ranks. For another offense, Josias would no doubt be whipped, like an ordinary man. The aristocracy were always exempt from corporal punishment by custom; and in 1641 this exemption was put into written law ("Body of Liberties," No. 43; in 

Source Book). 

66 66 There was also a legal class distinction as to dress. In 1651, in striving to preserve this, the court declared its utter detestation . . . that men or weomen of meane condition should take uppon them the garbe of gentlemen by wearing gold or silver lace or buttons. or to walk in great bootes, or woemen of the same rancke to weare silke or tiffany hoodes,” and it imposed a fine of "tenn shillings for every such offense." 

The franchise, too, was far from democratic.

The voting 

freemen were a small part of the free men. The restriction was partly on religious grounds: the Puritan leaders were determined to keep political control in the hands of their own theological faction. The General Court of 1631, which admitted the first new freemen (page 55), ordered that thereafter only church members should be made freemen. as This did not mean that all church members could vote many standard histories seem to imply. It meant merely that voters were to be selected only from church members. Unskilled laborers, servants, even slaves, might be admitted to the churches, but never to full citizenship. Only about one man out of four voted at any time in colonial Massachusetts.

EARLY MASSACHUSETTS III. GROWTH OF POLITICAL MACHINERY 

The Court of 1634 voted by ballot when it unseated Winthrop (page 58). A secret vote protected the voters from being overawed by the aristocratic magistrates. 

Ballots had never been used before in a political election in America. Business corporations in England, however, often voted so (page 26), and nothing could be more natural than for the Massachusetts settlers to use the device as soon as a real contest arose. After 1635, the Court of Elections was required by law to use "papers" in choosing magistrates.¹ 

The ballot also makes it easy for more people to vote. They can vote near home, instead of having to come together at some central place as the Massachusetts voters were doing at their 

Court of Elections. 

The men of Massachusetts soon found a way to take this advantage of the new way of voting. (1) In March, 1636, the 

General Court ordered that the freemen of six outlying towns might send "proxies" to the next Court of Elections. (2) During the next December a special election had to be called (because the governor had resigned); and for this election, “in regard of the season," any freemen were authorized to send their votes in writing. (3) The next spring (1637) this way of voting for governor and Assistants was made permanent. This use of the ballot was an American invention. 

This brought another reform. Now that men no longer came together from the different towns to Boston to choose magistrates, but voted instead in their home towns, it was necessary to know in advance from what candidates the choice was to be made. Some new way of making nominations became necessary. So Massachusetts invented the American plan of 

¹ At this time the Court voted on only one office, and one candidate, at a time, and the man already in the office had to be voted out before any one else could be considered. In 1643, since many voters could not write, a new law ordered that kernels of corn be used in place of written ballots: white kernels to signify election; other colors, rejection.

FIRST AMERICAN TWO-HOUSE LEGISLATURE 61 

a nominating convention, made up of delegates from the several towns, meeting some time before the regular election. 

Within the first five years the English jury system was adopted in full. In the first summer in Massachusetts, a man was found dead under suspicious circumstances. The magistrates appointed a body of sworn men to investigate. This coroner's jury accused a certain man of murder. That man was then brought before a trial jury of twelve men. All this was merely in accord with custom in England. 

In 1634, however, a law of the General Court did establish jury trial, and a year later a law provided that a jury of inquest (grand jury) should meet twice a year, to present to the court all offenders against public welfare. 66 The next important fruit of the democratic movement was the division of the legislature into two Houses. For ten years after the revolution of 1634," the General Court sat as one body. 

But it was made up of two distinct "orders." The deputies were chosen each by his own townfolk, and they held office for only a few days. Often they were artisans or farmers. The 

Assistants had many additional meetings for judicial business and to aid the governor. They had to know some law, and they served without pay. Only "gentlemen" were qualified for the office, or could afford to hold it. 

Naturally, friction was incessant. At the first clash, in the second Court of 1634, the Assistants claimed "a negative voice," or veto. To grant this would be to give as much voting power to the aristocratic minority as to the democratic majority. 

But the plan was finally adopted after the ministers had been brought forward to argue for it. 

During the controversy, a pamphlet by Israel Stoughton of Dorchester attacked the claim of the Assistants with what 

Winthrop calls "many weak arguments." The Assistants called Stoughton before them, forced him to recant,

EARLY MASSACHUSETTS 

ordered his book burned (probably not for its "weakness"), deprived him of his elected office of deputy, and forbade him to hold any office for three years! (Winthrop had written a pamphlet in favor of the veto power, and the magistrates saw no wrong in public argument on that side.) 

The Assistants had now won much the greater weight in the legislature. They were a small disciplined body. They could agree upon plans before the Court met, and could act as a unit in the meeting, much better than the deputies could. They also monopolized debate: it was hard for individual deputies to confront men of such social superiority and such political ability. The deputies saw that they would gain dignity and influence if they sat by themselves. So, in 1644, the General 

Court separated into two "Houses."

This was the first two-House Legislature in America.¹ The immediate occasion for the division was a quaint three-year dispute over a poor woman's pig, which had strayed into the pen of a rich merchant and had been slaughtered by him. Says 

Winthrop, "There fell out a great matter upon a small occasion." 

Three law suits about this pig came before the General Court which was often a law court as well as a legislature. Each time the deputies sided with the washerwoman, while the Assistants voted for the gentleman. The bitterness roused by this long dispute helped at last to bring on the division. Then, too, when 

Assistants and deputies found it hard to live together in peace under one roof, the two-house parliament in England suggested a way out.

The story of this famous code illustrates the iong strife between Assistants and deputies in the General Court (pages 61-62). At first the Massachusetts 

Assistants often punished for acts which no previous law had declared punishable, inventing penalties to match their own idea of the offense. The common people, Winthrop says, "thought their condition very unsafe while so much power rested in the discretion of the magistrates," and soon demanded written laws.

The Assistants for several years evaded the demand. Twice they appointed a committee to draw up a code of law; but both committees (made up of Assistants and “gentlemen ") failed to report. Finally in 1638 the democratic faction in the General Court secured a new committee, made up partly of democratic deputies. This body invited suggestions from the freemen of the several towns (an early instance of the "initiative "), and at length made a bulky report which was then referred to two clergymen (John Cotton and Nathaniel Ward); and in 1641, upon this basis, each of these gentlemen presented a complete code. The more democratic one, by Ward, was then adopted. 46 This early code made splendid progress upon contemporary English law. 

The first entry (pictured on this page) provided that no punishment should be imposed by any magistrate except by virtue of some express law. Monopolies were forbidden. An accused man was guaranteed the new privilege of challenging" the jurors who were to try him. In England, under the common law of the time, a man might whip his wife, if only he used a stick no thicker than his thumb. But the section of this code entitled Liberties of 

Women'' contained the advanced provision, "everie marryed woeman shall be free from bodilie correction or stripes from her husband, unless it be in his owne defense uppon her assalt." 66

THE NEW ENGLAND TOWN 

63 "towns." Many of the colonists had come in congregations, led by honored ministers. Each such group wished to keep together near its "meeting house," where there were two or more services during the week besides the Sunday worship. 

But after all the chief reason why New Englanders were villagers, instead of dwellers on scattered plantations or farms, is to be found in the soil and climate, and in the kind of work that they therefore had to take up. New England farms, we have explained, had to be small to be profitable; and small farms made it natural for the owners to settle in villages, such as they had been accustomed to in the Old World, each with its tilled fields stretching away at convenient spots near by. The other early New England industries (lumbering, fishing, shipbuilding) likewise called for groups of workers — who also, accordingly, settled in villages. 

The first eight towns (page 50) were on the coast. After 

1634, new towns sprang up, along the rivers, farther inland, as at Lexington and Concord. Whenever a group of settlers wished to start a town, they had first to get permission, and a grant of territory, from the General Court. At first the General 

Court also appointed justices and constables for each settlement and tried to attend to its other local business. But from the first, too, on special occasions, the people of a town met to discuss matters of interest, as at the famous Watertown meeting of 1632 (page 56). During the first four years, such a gathering might be called by a minister or other leading man just before the people dispersed from the Thursday "sermon" (the ancestor of the Protestant midweek "prayer meeting ").

Then in 1633 Dorchester ordered that there should be a regular monthly town meeting to settle town matters (Source Book, No. 

66). Watertown followed this example the next spring; and soon each town, old or new, fell into line. Each town, too, chose a town clerk to keep records of the "by-laws" passed at the meetings, and elected a committee ("the seven men,' nine men, ‚""the selected townsmen," "the Select Men") with authority to manage town affairs between the meetings. ","the

EARLY MASSACHUSETTS 

Government by town meeting and selectmen,¹ ther, grew up out of the needs of the people and out of their desire to manage their own affairs. Soon the General Court gave its approval to the system. The central legislature still gave a town its territory and its name, and required it to maintain "trainband" (a local militia company), school, roads, and certain police arrangements. Sometimes it imposed fines when a town failed in any of these things. In theory, the town possessed only such authority as the central government delegated to it. - - In practice, great independence was left the town. The town meeting appointed all local officers, not merely selectmen and clerk, but school trustees, hog reeve, fence viewer, constable, treasurer, pound keeper, sealer of weights and measures, measurer of corn and lumber, overseer of chimneys, and overseer of the village almshouse. For most of these officers it alone defined all the powers and duties. It divided the town lands among the inhabitants (such a part as it chose to divide), and it fixed the size of building lots, a quarter-acre, an acre, two acres, or five. It passed ordinances regarding the town fields and pastures, the keeping up of fences, the running of cattle and hogs, the term of the school and its support, the support of the church, and of the town poor. 

All the people in a town could come to town meeting and could speak there (Source Book, No. 78), but not all could vote. At the base of society in every town there soon came to be a class of "cottagers," or squatters, who were permitted to live in the place only at the town's pleasure and who could not acquire land there, nor claim any legal right to the use of the town “ commons for pasture.

Servants whose terms of service were up usually passed at first into this class. The people in a town who held full town citizenship were known as inhabitants." A 

"6 66 cottager" or a new settler could be "admitted inhabitant" by vote of the town. In practice, all the "gentlemen" in a town and all the industrious artisans and freeholders were so admitted. 

1 This term came to be written "Selectmen," but the New Englander still pronounces it "Select Men."

Thus the town government became more democratic than the central government. More men took part in it, and they acted directly, not through representatives. This town government, too, touched the life of the people at more points than did the central government. 

GOVERNMENT BY TOWN MEETING 

This town democracy had disadvantages. Action was slow, and was often controlled by ignorance or by petty neighborhood jealousies. 

But it gave a constant and unrivaled training in politics to the whole people. Thomas Jefferson called the New England town meeting "the best school of political liberty the world ever saw." Fifty years later, Tocqueville (a wise and friendly French student of our institutions) declared in like vein, "Town meetings are to liberty what primary schools are to science." 

V. THE UNION OF CHURCH AND STATE 

In England the High-Churchmen had reproached the Low- Churchmen with being secretly Separatists. The Low-Church 

Puritans repelled the charge indignantly, and, to prove their good faith, joined vehemently in denouncing the Separatists.

Thomas Hooker was one of the greatest of the Puritan clergy. 

Before he came to America, while a fugitive in Holland, he was called a Separatist. But he claimed to have an extreme aversion" to that sect, and he wrote, "To separate from the faithful assemblies and churches in England, as no churches, is an error in judgment and a sin in practice." 66 Still, when the Massachusetts Puritans reached the New World, they did soon separate wholly from the English Church, refusing even to recognize its ordination of clergymen. On the other hand, they did not separate the church from the state, as Plymouth did, nor did they make one congregation independent of another in church government. Indeed the leaders cared for the state mainly as an agent to protect their religious doctrines.

The union of state and church was secured by three distinct devices: (1) no one was allowed to vote (no matter what other qualifications he had) unless a member of a Puritan church; (2) no church was permitted except those authorized by the

EARLY MASSACHUSETTS 

government; and (3) many matters of civil government were referred by the General Courts to the clergy. 

The Massachusetts leaders aimed to build (in their own words)" a City of God on earth." They believed they could do this by setting up an aristocratic theocracy: a government, that is, by the best among them, who should then rule according to the law of God. The experiment was noble, but it had peculiar dangers. Those same leaders were too likely to be sure that they were" the best," and that they alone knew just what that law was.

We understand better to-day that no body of men are good enough, however zealous and well-meaning, to rule the minds and souls of other men. The plan was certain to degenerate into bigotry and persecution. 

Indeed, the Massachusetts plan forbade religious freedom. 

A man like Winthrop felt that he had sacrificed home and ease in order to try out a vital experiment in society. He could not try it fairly, he believed, unless he drove out from his "City of the Lord" those who differed from him. He and his friends had come to the wilderness to find a chance to build their ideal state as they saw fit, where there should be none with right to hinder them. They did not mean now to let "intruders mar their work. (Source Book, No. 84.) 

So the Massachusetts government assumed power both to refuse unwelcome immigrants and also to expel troublesome minorities that grew up among their own number. In the first fall after Winthrop's arrival, two "gentlemen" from England came to Massachusetts by way of Plymouth. They were introduced by Miles Standish; "but," says Winthrop, "having no testimony [no evidence as to their religious character], we 

Iwould not receive them."

Then in the following March, the Assistants shipped back to England six men at one time, without trial, merely upon the ground that they were "unmeete to inhabit here"; while for years there were occasional entries in the records such as: "John Smith is ordered to remove himself from this jurisdiction for divers dangerous opinions which he holdeth."

RELIGIOUS PERSECUTION 

Such cases help us to understand two more famous expulsions. 

1. Roger Williams was one of the most powerful and scholarly of the great Puritan clergy. He had rare sweetness of temper, but, along with it, a genius for getting into bitter controversy. 

He was broad-minded on great questions, but he could quarrel vehemently over fantastic quibbles. As one critic well says, he lacked sense of proportion. He could regard the questions of grace after meat and of religious freedom as equally important. The kindly Bradford describes him as possessing "many precious parts, but very unsettled in judgment," and again: "I desire the Lord. to show him his errors and reduce him into the way of truth, and give him a settled judgment and constancy in the same; for I hope he belongs to the Lord." 

Driven from England by Laud, Williams came to Massachusetts in the supply ship in the winter of 1631 (page 50). He was welcomed warmly by Winthrop as "a godly minister," but it was soon plain that he had adopted the opinions of the Separatists. He preached against any union of church and state, holding that the magistrate had no right to punish for Sabbath-breaking or for other offenses against "the first table" the first four of the Ten Commandments or to tell any man what to believe. 

Only a man's church, he held, could discipline him in these matters. Indeed, he preached complete liberty of conscience, or "soul-liberty," as he liked to call it. This idea was like dynamite to the Massachusetts plan.

ROGER WILLIAMS' STATUE at Providence. Note the title of the book he holds.

Williams had become pastor of Salem. Just at this time Salem wanted more lands. The court of Assistants paid no public

EARLY MASSACHUSETTS 

attention to the request, but let it be known privately that, if the town expected the grant, it had best dismiss Williams. On his part, Williams was referring to the other churches of the colony as "ulcered and gangrened," and calling the clergy "false hirelings."

An opportunity soon offered to get rid of him. All land in 

America, he urged, belonged to the Indians until bought from them. He denied the title of the colony, and said the king had told "a solemn lie" in the charter in claiming right to give title. 

Such words, if left unpunished, might embroil the little colony with the home government. The magistrates seized the chance to get rid of the firebrand (and at the same time to show loyalty to the king) by ordering Williams back to England. 

On account of the bitter winter, the order was suspended until a better season for sailing. But when the magistrates learned that Williams meantime continued to teach his Separatist doctrines, an officer was sent to place him on board ship. 

Forewarned secretly by Winthrop (who felt much kindness for him), he escaped to the forest, and, with many hardships, found his way to the Narragansett Indians. The next spring (1636) a few followers joined him, to found the colony of Rhode Island. 

2. Anne Hutchinson is described by Winthrop (who hated her) as a woman of " ready wit and bold spirit." She was intellectual, eloquent, and enthusiastic. Her real offense seems to have been her keen contempt for many of the ministers and magistrates. She held religious views somewhat different from the prevailing ones, but Winthrop once confessed that "only men of good understanding" could see what the differences were. 

Indeed, he added, the two parties might easily have been reconciled if hard feelings had not already been aroused. 

Williams had been disposed of easily; but the Hutchinson dispute divided the colony for many months into two almost equal parties. Finally, the small "orthodox" majority, to crush the minority, resorted to cruel persecution and to not a little trickery. On trumped-up pretexts, sympathizers of Mrs. 

Hutchinson were expelled from the General Court, and five

RELIGIOUS PERSECUTION 

(These exiles, with many leaders of her faction were banished. followers, at once started new settlements in the wilderness parts of Rhode Island and New Hampshire.) 69 Soon, the colony found itself involved in other despotic persecutions. The several thousand Presbyterians and Episcopalians in Massachusetts, even when men of property, were shut out from all political rights. Their repeated petitions for relief were contemptuously refused or ignored, and they were even compelled to attend service in the established Puritan churches. 

In 1666 some Baptists tried to set up a church of their own in Boston and met together for divine worship, instead of going to the established church. The Massachusetts courts sternly rebuked this "high presumption against the Lord," and punished the offenders by heavy fines and imprisonment. (The still more cruel persecution of Quakers in Massachusetts belongs to a later chapter.) In all this denial of religious liberty, the Massachusetts Puritans were not ahead of their age, as they were in so many ways. But neither were they behind it. The famous 

Long Parliament (page 50) protested that it did not favor toleration: "We do declare it is far from our purpose to let loose the golden reins of discipline and government in the church, to leave private persons or particular congregations to take up what form of divine service they please. For we hold it requisite that there should be throughout the whole realm a conformity to that order which the laws enjoin." Still a few far-seeing men did reach to loftier vision. In 1641 Lord 

Brooke¹ wrote in an essay on religion: "The individual should have liberty. No power on earth should force his practice. 

One that doubts with reason and humility may not, for aught I see, be forced by violence. Fire and water may be re- ... 

¹ Lord Brooke, with Lord Say, thought for a time of settling in Massachusetts. See Source Book, No. 75. After giving up this plan, the same two 

Puritan nobles tried to establish a colony in the Connecticut valley, where Saybrooke was named for them.

EARLY MASSACHUSETTS 

strained; but light cannot. It will in at every cranny. Now to stint it is [to-morrow] to resist an enlightened and inflamed multitude. . . . Can we not dissent in judgment but we must also disagree in affection?" Meantime in Rhode Island Roger

Williams was making "soul liberty" the foundation of his social experiment.

CHAPTER VII OTHER NEW ENGLAND COLONIES The birthplace of American democracy is Hartford. — JOHNSTON. 

Let us never exercise power over men's consciences. - ROGER WILLIAMS. 

By 1640, when the great Puritan migration came to an end (page 50), there were five colonies in New England besides Plymouth and Massachusetts. English proprietors had founded fishing stations on the coasts of Maine and New Hampshire, and these settlements had been reinforced by Hutchinson sympathizers from Massachusetts. In 1638, a new Puritan migration from England began the New Haven group of towns-a colony closely resembling Massachusetts, but with less material for an aristocracy and with even more disposition to rely upon the Old Testament as a guide in government. 

The two remaining colonies, Rhode Island and Connecticut, represented new and fundamental American ideas. Roger 

Williams in Rhode Island was the apostle of modern religious liberty; and Thomas Hooker in Connecticut was the apostle of modern democracy.

I. RHODE ISLAND 

99 Williams founded the town of Providence in the spring of 1636 (page 68). From the Indians he bought a tract of land, and deeded it in joint ownership to twelve companions “and to such others as the major part of us shall admit into the same fellowship. 

Later comers signed an agreement to submit themselves "only in civil things" to orders made for the public good by the town fellowship, in which they were freely granted an equal voice. ("Civil" is here contrasted with "ecclesiastical." See page 44.) 

71

RHODE ISLAND AND RELIGIOUS FREEDOM 

The point to the agreement is that the people did not purpose to let the government meddle with religion. Williams believed it possible to keep order without compelling uniformity in religion. He compared a state to a ship, where all (passengers and seamen) must obey the captain in matters of navigation, though all need not attend the ship's prayers (Source Book, No. 90).

Then, in 1663, when the colony received its first royal charter (page 82), this fundamental idea was made yet more explicit: 

"Whereas it is much on their hearts," says a preamble, quoting the petition of the colonists, “to hold forth a livelie experiment that a most flourishing civill state may stand . . . with a full libertie in religious concernments," accordingly, "noe person within the sayd colonye, at any tyme hereafter, shall bee any wise molested, punished, disquieted, or called in question, for any differences in opinione in matters of religion, and [i.e. provided he] doe not actually disturb the civill peace." 

The practice of the colony, too, kept to this high level. During 

1656-1657, powerful Massachusetts complained, and finally threatened force, because little Rhode Island sheltered Quakers who might then swarm forth to annoy her neighbors. Williams disliked Quakers; but he now replied that they ought to be punished only when they had actually disturbed the peace, and not merely for being Quakers. "We have no law," ran his noble argument, "to punish any for declaring by words their minds concerning the ways and things of God" (Source Book, No. 92).

For a time this colony did become a dumping ground for turbulent cranks from all New England. But with clear-eyed faith Williams and his friends persisted in their "livelie experiment"— until at last they proved that religious freedom need not interfere with orderly government. 

II. CONNECTICUT 

Three Massachusetts towns had been foremost in the struggle against aristocracy, - Watertown, Dorchester, and Newtown. 

Some instances of Watertown and Dorchester democracy have been given (pages 56, 63). With regard to Newtown, it was said that the people there "grew very jealous of their liberties"

CONNECTICUT AND DEMOCRACY 

soon after Thomas Hooker (page 65) became their pastor. 

In 1635-1636, the people of these towns made a new migration to the Connecticut valley, to try their democratic experiment. 

The inspirer of this movement was Thomas Hooker, who became to Connecticut even more than Cotton was to Massachusetts. 

These two leaders were widely different in their lives. Cotton belonged to the aristocratic 

English gentry. Hooker's father was a yeoman. He himself had been a menial 

sizar when a student at Cambridge University, and his wife had been a ladies' maid.

By birth and association, as well as by conviction, he was a man of the people. 

Over against the aristocratic doctrines of Massachusetts leaders (page 55), Hooker stated admirably the case for democracy. Winthrop wrote to him that democracy was "unwarrantable" because "the best part is always the least, and of that best part the wiser part is always the lesser." Hooker replied: "In matters . . that concern the common good, a general council chosen by all, to transact business which concerns all, I conceive most suitable to rule and most safe for the relief of the whole." Winthrop and Cotton taught that the magistrates' authority had divine sanction. Hooker preached a political sermon to teach that (1) "the foundation of authority is laid in the consent of the governed"; (2) "the choice of magistrates belongs to the people"; and (3) "those who have power to appoint officers, have also the right to set bounds to their authority." 66 

THOMAS HOOKER'S STATUE AT HARTFORD. 

73

CONNECTICUT: DEMOCRACY 

For a time the three Connecticut towns kept their Massachusetts names. Later, they were known as Hartford, Wethersfield, and Windsor. From the first each town managed its own local affairs, and, in 1639, a central government was provided by a mass meeting of the inhabitants of the colony. This gathering adopted a set of eleven "Fundamental Orders the first written constitution " in the modern sense. 

66 The plan of government was much like Massachusetts', but more democratic. The governor held office for one year, and could not serve two terms in succession. He had no veto. The 

General Court could not be dissolved except by its own vote; and it could be elected and brought together, on occasion, without the governor's summons. It could also "call into question "magistrate or governor, and even (in modern phrase) "recall" him. The franchise was never restricted to church members, as in Massachusetts. At first, any one whom a town allowed to vote in town meeting could vote also in the General Court of Elections. Then in 1659 the General Court set up a small property qualification for voting. 

Connecticut did not reject union of church and state. Hooker believed in a Bible commonwealth as zealously as Cotton did, though he understood his Bible differently on political matters. 

The governor had to be a member of a church, and the first code of laws, in 1650, authorized the government " to see [that] the force, ordinances, and rules of Christe bee observed in every Church according to his word." Indeed, the preamble of the 

Fundamental Orders states that the first purpose of the government is to maintain "the discipline of the churches which according to the truth of the gospell is now practiced amongst us.” 

III. THE NEW ENGLAND CONFEDERATION 

The New England colonies were exposed to constant danger from the Dutch in New Netherland and from the Indians. In 

1642, civil war broke out in England between king and parliament, so that no protection could be hoped for thence (and quite as important neither was any interference from England

THE NEW ENGLAND CONFEDERATION 

75 to be feared). So, in 1643, Massachusetts, Connecticut, New 

Haven, and Plymouth organized the Confederation of New England, to deal with foreign dangers and their common interests. (Rhode Island and the New Hampshire towns asked in vain for admission to the Confederation. Massachusetts would have no union with "that sewer," as her leaders politely styled Rhode 

Island, or with the "heretics" and democrats of New Hampshire.)

This union was the first movement in America toward that federal growth which was finally to join all our commonwealths into the United States. It disappeared, however, before the end of the century, partly because two of the members were absorbed wholly in two others (pages 82, 85) and partly because Massachusetts (the most powerful member) “nullified” the federal congress when she thought it unfair to her.

PART II ENGLISH AMERICA, 1660–1763 CHAPTER VIII THE STRUGGLE TO SAVE SELF-GOVERNMENT 

From 1620 to 1640, quarrels between king and parliament had kept the English government from paying much attention to what went on in the colonies. In 1641 those quarrels grew into civil war. Parliament and Oliver Cromwell defeated the king and beheaded him, and, from 1649 to 1660, ruled over England. This Puritan government was called the Commonwealth. It had a tenderness for the Puritan colonies, and it did not last long enough anyway to interfere seriously in American affairs. In 1660 came the Restoration: weary of Cromwell's military rule, the English people called to the throne Charles II, son of the dead Charles I. The government of the Restoration at once showed a warm interest in colonial affairs.

I. EXPANSION BY CONQUEST AND BY GROWTH 

The years 1660–1690 saw a tremendous expansion of colonial territory. In 1660 the English held two patches of coast one about the Chesapeake, the other east of the Hudson - with a total population of about 60,000. The two districts were separated by hundreds of miles of wilderness, in which two small dots might mark a little Dutch settlement on the Hudson and a few hundred Swedes at the mouth of the Delaware. 

For more than twenty years, no new English colony had been founded. 

Thirty years later (1690) the English colonies formed an unbroken band from the Penobscot to the Savannah. To the south of Virginia the Carolinas had been added (1663); to the north of Maryland appeared the splendid colony of Pennsylvania (1681); while New York, New Jersey, and Delaware had become 

English by conquest. All the colonies, too, had broadened their

77 area of settlement toward the interior. Population had increased fourfold, rising to 250,000. 

This growth meant thousands upon thousands of new farms, won acre by acre from the stubborn forest - each such farm a new American home with an epic story of heroic work and daring. For the older areas it meant larger towns, new churches, larger schools, and, at the ports, the busy building and cheerful launching of thousands of new ships and fishing schooners, with the ceaseless ring and rasp of shipwright's hammer and saw on every creek and bay along hundreds of miles of coast. 

This transformation from patches of settlement to a continuous colonial empire brought home to English rulers the need of a more definite colonial policy. After the Restoration of 

1660, the king set up a "Council for Foreign Plantations," to see 66 that the several collonies bee drawn into a more certaine and uniform waie of Government." Later this Council became the 

Board of Trade. It contained many famous men, hard-working and well-meaning; but they were ignorant of the affairs, and out of touch with the people, that they were trying to rule. They aimed mainly at three things: (1) uniformity and economy in the colonial government; (2) better military defense against French and Dutch and Indians; and (3) new commercial regulations. 

The trade regulations between every European country and its colonies were then based upon "the Mercantile Theory" a mistaken idea that all European thinkers of that day had about wealth. Real wealth, it was thought, consisted only of gold and silver. Then a country, without mines, could get rich only by selling more goods than it bought. If a French farmer bought a useful farm horse from Germany for twenty pieces of silver, everyone felt that France was poorer, and Germany richer, by that amount! That both might be richer from the trade didn't occur clearly to anyone.

This false idea about trade gave rise to false ideas about the value of colonies. Nobody thought it worth while to have colo-

ENGLISH AMERICA, 1660-1690 

nies (apart from the chance of precious metals) except (1) as a source of goods not produced at home, and (2) as a sure market for home manufactures. So each colonizing country adopted 

66 navigation acts" to restrict the trade of its colonies to itself. 

By modern standards, all these restrictions were absurd and tyrannical; but it is only fair to say that the English system was more enlightened, and far less selfish and harsh, than that of Holland or France or Spain (page 4). 

As a regular system, the English restrictions began in 1660 with the "First Navigation Act." This law had two purposes. 

1. One was semi-military, to increase the shipping of the empire. Until this time, most European goods, even most 

English goods, had been carried to the colonies by Dutch vessels. 

England's navy had sunk low. But the safety of the island and of her colonies rested upon command of the seas. In that day, trading vessels were easily turned into war vessels; so to build up a merchant marine was the easy way to be sure of a war navy at need. Accordingly, this law provided that all trade between 

England and her colonies should be carried only in ships owned, and, for the most part, manned, by Englishmen or colonials.¹ 

This part of the Act was highly successful. The shipping of England and the colonies doubled in the first eighteen years. Nor did this part of the law in any way discriminate against the colonies: it directly benefited them, creating the great shipbuilding industry of New England. 

In less than twenty years the colonies were selling ships to England. By 

1720 Massachusetts alone launched 150 ships a year, and the shipbuilders of England were petitioning parliament, in vain, for protection against this invasion upon their ancient industry. In 1760 a third of all ships carrying the English flag had been built in America - and no small part were owned there. Massachusetts had then a ship for each hundred of its people. The carrying trade of the empire also passed largely into the hands of New Englanders. 

1"... ships which truly . . . belong to the people of England or Ireland or are built of and belonging to any of the said Plantations or Territories and whereof the master and three fourths of the mariners at least are English." The word "English" always included the colonials, and it was specifically defined in this sense by a supplemental Navigation Act two years later (Source Book, No. 100, a, and note).

EARLY NAVIGATION ACTS 

79 2. The law somewhat restricted exports. Sugar, tobacco, cotton, wool, ginger, and dyewoods were to be carried from a colony only to England or another English colony. These "enumerated articles" were all semi-tropical. New England could still send her lumber,¹ furs, fish, oil, and rum to any part of the world—if only they were carried in her own or English ships. 

Tobacco was the only " enumerated article " produced for export at that time on the mainland of North America; and for the restriction on tobacco, England gave an offset. She forbade her own citizens to raise tobacco (as they had begun to do), or to import it from foreign colonies. This gave Virginia and 

Maryland a monopoly of her market.

The import trade was first restricted by the Navigation Act of 1663. That law ordered that all European goods must pass to the colonies only through English ports. The design was to keep colonial trade from falling into the hands of other European countries; but, to guard the colonists against paying double taxes, a rebate of the English import duties was allowed on all continental goods reshipped for the colonies. 

In 1660, tariff duties both for the colonies, and for England, had been imposed on a long list of goods. In the colonies, however, this Act was always practically a dead letter. 

There was no proper machinery to enforce it; and whenever the restrictions were seriously troublesome, they were evaded by smuggling.

This was as far as the system went until after 1690. (1) The subtropical colonies could export their products only to England or other English colonies; (2) all imports to all colonies must come through England; (3) all ships in the colonial trade must be English or colonial. 

¹ Trees more than two feet in diameter a foot from the ground were reserved, in theory, for the royal shipping. But this restriction was little regarded in practice by American lumbermen. 

2 This part of the law was adopted mainly with a view to the English West Indies. In 1697 Jamaica alone had more commerce with England than all the continental colonies together north of Virginia.

NEW ENGLAND, 1660-1690 

A Massachusetts ship could still carry any product of that colony to any part of the world, exchange for goods there, carry these goods to England, and then "reship" them for an American port, or exchange them for other European goods in the 

English markets. Says Channing: "It is impossible to say whether the net result of this system. . . was in favor of Great 

Britain or the colonies." (For the more tyrannical "navigation" laws of the next century see pages 100 ff.)

(American Nation), or Channing, II, 1-13. There are clear treatments of the navigation laws in Harlow's Growth of the United States, 80-84, and in Greene's Foundations of American Nationality. 

II. NEW ENGLAND, 1660-1690 

Charles II (page 76) found himself beset with a storm of complaints against Massachusetts. In 1656, Quakers had appeared in that colony. Four, who persisted in returning after banishment, had been hanged, and several others (women among them) had been flogged brutally. Quakers in England appealed to the new king, and he ordered Massachusetts to send all imprisoned Quakers to England for trial. The Massachusetts leaders (to prevent such open interference with their courts) chose instead to empty the jails and drop the persecution.

The decent feeling of the mass of Massachusetts people had already practically put an end to the death penalty. Five Quakers had been condemned to death. But Governor Endicott had secured the last two convictions only by brow-beating judges and juries, and at each execution a force of soldiers had been necessary to prevent a rescue. The decree of death against the fifth man was never carried out, because of this popular feeling. Afterward a milder persecution was renewed with the king's approval. Quakers were liable to imprisonment and flogging in all the colonies except Rhode Island, as well as in England. 

These Quakers were not the sober brethren of later times. "It was a little hard," as Lowell says, "to know what to do with a woman who persisted in interrupting your honored minister in his sermon, calling him Priest of Baal, and breaking empty bottles over his head" (in sign of his emptiness). Nowhere else, however, was a death penalty inflicted, and nowhere else did Quakers become so extremely troublesome. It was persecution (in part, at least) that made them fanatics. 

---

THE PINE TREE SHILLINGS 

The king learned, too, that during the Commonwealth Massachusetts had usurped the right to coin money (the famous Pine Tree Shillings) and that she had given shelter to two of the "regicide" judges who had passed sentence against his father. Worst of all, perhaps, the Bay

Colony had openly disre garded the Navigation Acts. 

In 1661 its General Court had even adopted a resolution styling the law "an infringement of our rights."

Charles was indignant, too, that the English

Church was not permitted in this English colony. ՄՐ NEW Ис 81 165 2 XII

For the moment Charles contented himself with demanding (1) that an oath of allegiance be taken in Massachusetts; (2) that the Episcopalian service be permitted; and (3) that the right to vote be given to all 

Episcopalians who were "of competent estate." The colony complied with the first of these reasonable demands, ignored the second, and evaded the third. The General Court did provide that a man might be made a "freeman" without belonging to a Puritan church, if his good character were testified to by the minister of his town and if he paid a ten-shilling tax. But the 

Puritan ministers gave few such certificates to those outside their own folds, and few men paid so high a tax. 

Connecticut, New Haven, and Rhode Island had never had authority from England to set up governments; and the inhabitants had never secured any English title to their lands. 

Now that order was restored in England, something had to be done about this; and all three colonies promptly sent agents to England to secure royal charters. 

Connecticut and Rhode Island were amazingly successful, retaining almost all of their old self-government (Source Book, Nos. 97, 98). In neither colony did the king get authority to

NEW ENGLAND, 1660-1690 

appoint the governor or any other important officer. With good reason these charters (which the colonists themselves had really drawn up) were cherished and venerated. At the time of the American Revolution they became State constitutions, and they continued in force, practically without change, until 1818 in Connecticut and until 1842 in Rhode Island. The remarkable liberality of these grants was due partly to the careless good nature of Charles in the early part of his reign; partly to an enthusiasm just then for the colonies among English officials; and partly to the king's willingness to build up the other colonies to offset the stiff-necked Bay Colony.

New Haven was too much like Massachusetts to find favor, and she lay too close to Connecticut to be fit for a separate colony. So her territory was included in the grant to Connecticut. 

Governor John Winthrop of Connecticut, son of the Governor Winthrop of Massachusetts. (See a letter from son to father in

With Massachusetts the king continued to have trouble. 

In particular, Episcopalians there still complained that they were robbed of civil and religious rights as they had been for thirty years. So in 1664 Charles sent royal commissioners to

New England to straighten things out. The commissioners first conquered New Netherland from the Dutch - with whom Eng- 

---

land was then at war. Connecticut, Rhode Island, and Plymouth then gave them grateful welcome, but Massachusetts still showed them scant courtesy and even defied them. 

The commissioners returned home in chagrin, their work unfinished, and recommended that the Massachusetts charter be taken away. 

But the next year a victorious Dutch fleet, after sweeping the English navy from the seas, sailed up the Thames with a broom at the flagship's masthead. Then followed the plague and the great London fire. The Colonial Council (page 

77) did repeatedly order Massachusetts to send an agent to

England to arrange a settlement. The colony procrastinated long and skillfully until, in 1675, it was weakened by the famous Indian outbreak known as King Philip's War. Just at that time, too, the king, having made himself more powerful at home, was ready to act more vigorously toward the colonies. 

So, in 1684, the highest English court declared the charter of 

1629 forfeited and void.

THE ROYAL COMMISSION OF 1664 

The Board of Trade had decided that to have so many small governments in America was a bad arrangement, and so they had drawn up a plan to unite Massachusetts, Plymouth, and the Maine and New Hampshire towns, under one royal governor. They would have been glad to include Connecticut and Rhode Island in the scheme, and so unite New England into one royal province. But, unlike Massachusetts, the smaller colonies had given no excuse for legal proceedings against their charters.

Still, when Charles died, in 1685, the new king, James II, forced that consolidation through. He appointed Sir Edmund 

Andros governor-general of all New England, and ordered him to set aside the charter governments of Connecticut and Rhode Island by force. The Board of Trade, too, had planned an elected legislature for this New England province; but James tyrannically struck out this provision, leaving the government despotic.

James also extended once more the territory of the new province. He was already proprietor of New York and New Jersey

NEW ENGLAND, 1660-1690 

(page 91); and these colonies were soon joined to New England, under the rule of Andros-half of English America without a shadow of self-government!

Andros was a bluff soldier. He was commander of the troops he brought with him and of the colonial militia; and, with the approval of an appointed council, he had power to lay taxes, make laws, administer justice, and grant lands from the public domain. He saved the province from serious Indian peril, but on other matters clashed violently with the people. 

He insisted, to the bitter wrath of the Puritans, that Episcopalian services should be held on part of each Sunday in one of the Boston churches, until an Episcopalian church could be built. He also compelled landowners to pay small fees for new titles.¹ But the serious thing was the total suppression of self-government. Andros ordered the old taxes to be continued. 

Some Massachusetts towns resisted, and at Ipswich a town meeting voted that such method of raising taxes "did infringe their liberty as freeborn English subjects." The offenders were tried for "seditious votes and writings." The jury was packed, and browbeaten into a verdict of guilty; and citizens who had dared gallantly to resist tyranny were imprisoned and ruinously fined.

This absolute government lasted two years and a half. 

Massachusetts was getting ready to rebel; but under ordinary conditions a rising would have been put down bloodily. 

Thanks to the "Glorious Revolution" of 1688 (when Old

England drove James from the throne) the New England rising when it came was successful and bloodless. 

In April, 1689, the news reached Boston that James II was a fugitive, and that the new king, William of Orange, had invited all boroughs in England, and all officials unjustly deprived of charters and positions by James, to resume their former 1 For this there was much excuse. The colonies had often neglected the forms of law in granting lands, and had been careless in recording grants. 

To avoid future confusion, Andros provided for accurate surveys, and gave the old holders new deeds carefully recorded.

powers. The colonists assumed that this sanctioned like action by them. The people of Boston and neighboring towns seized a war vessel in the harbor, imprisoned Andros, and restored the charter government. Connecticut and Rhode 

Island also revived their former charters. 

THE SETTLEMENT OF 1691 

William III would have been glad to continue part of the Stuart policy in America. He wished, so far as possible, to consolidate small jurisdictions into large ones, and to keep the governor and judges in each colony dependent upon himself. The Connecticut and Rhode Island charters stood in the way of a complete rearrangement of this sort because the king's lawyers assured him that those grants still held good-since the legal proceedings against them had never been completed. Massachusetts did not fare so well. Her charter had been formally surrendered. The colony strove skillfully to obtain a re-grant of the original patent, but the best it could do was to accept a new one.

The Charter of 1691 created a government for Massachusetts more like that of Virginia than like that of Connecticut. 

1. The crown appointed and removed the governor. 

2. The Assembly nominated the Council, but these nominations were valid only after the governor's approval. 

3. The governor could adjourn or dissolve the Assembly at will; and he held an absolute veto upon its acts, while the king reserved also the right to a further veto. 

4. The higher courts were appointed by the governor; and appeals to the king were provided for. 

5. Religious freedom for all Protestant sects was promised. 

6. The franchise was placed on a property basis. All men owning land of forty shillings yearly value, or having forty pounds in personal property, became voters. 

The last two provisions in great measure overthrew government by a religious sect. The first four made Massachusetts a royal province. At the same time, Maine, Plymouth, and Nova 

Scotia were joined to Massachusetts.

THE COMING OF THE CAVALIERS III. VIRGINIA, 1660-1690 

During the years 1649-1660 (page 76), many of the defeated royalist gentry in England turned their faces toward the New World as the Puritans had done in their hour of gloom a generation earlier. At the Restoration, the royalists who were still in England expected to get back the lands they had lost; but large numbers were disappointed in this hope, and the movement to America then received a further impulse. Nearly all this emigration went to Virginia. Between 1650 and 1670 the population of that colony rose from 15,000 to 40,000. 

This migration made Virginia "the Land of the Cavaliers." 

It brought the Harrisons, Lees, Masons, Madisons, Marshalls, Monroes, Nelsons, Nicholases, Pages, Peytons, Pendletons, Randolphs, Wythes, Washingtons, and other gentry families, soon to become famous in the "Old Dominion." Virginia had already had a noble history; but it was this Cavalier migration which, a century later, flowered into her splendid galaxy of Revolutionary patriots, and, a little later still, justified her in her proud title "Mother of Presidents."

The party epithets, Cavalier and Roundhead, should not blind us to the close likeness between the gentry elements in Massachusetts and Virginia. The Cavaliers were less inclined to strike out new ways in church and state than the Puritan leaders were; but they were not graceless hangers-on of the court, as enemies pictured them. Most of them were highminded gentlemen, who had loved liberty only a degree less than they had feared anarchy — robust, dauntless, chivalrous, devout. They belonged to the same social class and had much the same habits of thought as the Winthrops and Hutchinsons of the Bay Colony and as the Hampdens and Eliots in England - with whom, indeed, they had stood shoulder to shoulder through a generation of constitutional struggle and from whom they had separated at last with mutual grief, when the great war came, dividing brother from brother. 

Still, for a time, this immigration caused bad government. 1

During the Commonwealth, Virginia had been almost a republic. Its Assembly had elected governor and council, and had taken from the governor all power over its sittings, along with the veto power.

At the Restoration the colony became again a royal province. The king appointed as governor Sir 

William Berkeley, an ardent royalist. Berkeley at once resumed the veto and the right to call, dissolve, or adjourn the Assembly. 

It had always been the rule to have an Assembly chosen at least once in two years. In 1660, the wild enthusiasm of

Cavalier immigrants for the restored king filled a new Assembly with the most hotheaded of the Cavaliers. By an arbitrary stretch of power, Governor Berkeley kept this unfit body alive (without new elections) for sixteen years just as his royal master in England was doing at that same time with his reactionary Cavalier Parliament. Berkeley was an old man, tortured by disease, arrogant, peevish, vindictive — an easy tool for a ring of greedy favorites. His long administration (16601677) was a period of misgovernment and reaction.

A law of 1670 took away the right to vote for Assemblymen from all but landowners ("householders "); ¹ and in local government, also, the people lost nearly all their old rights. Since 1632 the county had been the unit for choosing delegates to the Assembly and for raising and spending local taxes. It also passed "by laws" of considerable importance. Until the Restoration these things: were done in the county court, a meeting of all free White males. After 1660 such powers were turned over to a Board of eight "Justices" in each county, appointed by the governor from important landowners. Other men could still come to the county courts as spectators, but they were left no power except to cast a vote in the election of a new Assembly. 

Along with this political reaction went many other serious
