VIRGINIA, 1660-1690 

faults. Taxes were exorbitant, and were spent wastefully. 

There was much unjust "class legislation," such as the exemption of Councilors and their families from taxation. The sheriffs and other law officers (appointed by the governor) charged oppressive fees for simple and necessary services. The people were robbed by vexatious trade monopolies that the governor granted to his favorites.

The 40,000 inhabitants of 1670 included 2000 Negro slaves and 6000 White bond servants (Source Book, No. 104). Several thousand ex-servants who had not acquired land remained as laborers on the plantations of their former masters. The rest of the population consisted of a few hundred large planters and a large body of small planters. Discontent was chronic in the servant class; and now the small planters also were restive. 

They were practically unrepresented, and they felt rightly that they were overtaxed and discriminated against. 

These conditions led to the first "Rebellion" in America. 

An Indian rising brought the popular dissatisfaction to a head. 

Berkeley's inefficient government let the rising go on without check. Finally the savages ravaged an outlying plantation of 

Nathaniel Bacon, an energetic young planter. Bacon raised troops and punished the Indians terribly in two campaigns, but Berkeley declared the young captain and his followers rebels, because they had secured no commission from the government. 

This quarrel between Bacon and Berkeley blazed into a civil war in which the valiant Indian fighter suddenly became a democratic hero. Finding arms in their hands, Bacon and his party tried to use them for social reform. "Bacon's Rebellion" was a rising against "special privilege." The fundamental cause was not discontent at the inefficiency of the government toward the Indians, but social discontent. 

Berkeley was deserted. During much of the struggle, he could hardly muster a corporal's guard. The aristocracy of the tide water region, however, did not join Bacon. They were too much opposed to rebellion, and too jealous toward the democratic features of the movement; so they held aloof from either

BACON'S REBELLION, 1676 

side. Bacon was supported, however, by the great body of small planters, especially in the western counties.¹ 

When the rebellion began, popular clamor forced the governor to call a new Assembly. This body was controlled by the reform party, and is known as Bacon's Assembly (Source Book, No. 106). Manhood suffrage was restored; a representative Board was established in each county to act with the Justices in all matters of taxation and local " by laws "; the exemptions of the privileged families were abolished; fees were strictly regulated; and various minor abuses were corrected. 

Bacon himself stood for an even more democratic program. 

Soon after the meeting of the Assembly he held a convention of his party at "the Middle Plantation," and there issued a proclamation in the name of " the Commons of Virginia,” signing it "Nath Bacon, Gen'l By the Consent of the People." 

This document (Source Book, No. 107) denounced Berkeley's favorites as sponges " that had sucked up the public treasure, and declared all who sheltered them " traitors to the people." 

But while Bacon was still in full tide of success, a sudden fever carried him off and the Rebellion collapsed for want of a leader. Then a new Assembly declared all " Bacon's laws" void. 66 

After the failure of Bacon's Rebellion, the common freeholder had only one political power: once in two years he could vote for a member of the Assembly. Elections took place at the county courts, which became social gatherings also, with feasting and sports-wrestling, running, shooting at the mark - and sometimes with brutal rough-and-tumble fights. The speechmaking by rival candidates at these gatherings furnished no mean political training. 

1 These sturdy, honest people were vilified, especially after the failure of the rebellion, by aristocratic contemporaries. One Virginian gentleman refers to them as "Tag, rag, and bobtail." Another declared that Bacon "seduced the Vulgar and most ignorant People (two thirds of each county being of that Sorte) Soe that theire whole hearts and hopes were set upon him." Another describes the rebels as "a Rabble of the basest sorte of

VIRGINIA COUNTY AND NEW ENGLAND TOWN 

As large a part of the free White population came out to vote as in New England. But the common Virginia farmer voted on a much smaller range of matters, and much less often, than the common New England farmer. He had no voice in the many questions of local government such as were discussed and settled in the New England town meeting. Nor had he any hand even in choosing local officials.

Geography, we have seen, caused the New Englanders to group themselves in villages or towns. In Virginia, soil, climate, and products made it profitable to cultivate large plantations by cheap labor. Hardly any New England farm contained 500 acres: the usual Virginia plantation (after the year 1700) contained at least 5000.¹ So, in Virginia, the county became the smallest political unit, and control fell to wealthy planters in appointed Boards.

After 1691 the central governments of Massachusetts and Virginia grew more and more alike (page 85), but the local governments grew farther and farther apart; and the influence of local government upon society is so great that Virginia as a whole grew more aristocratic, and Massachusetts more democratic. The New England town meeting trained a whole people to democracy: the Virginia County Courts developed the most remarkable group of leaders the world has ever seen. 

IV. NEW COLONIES, 1660–1690 

England now quietly extended her claims to territory on the south, and in 1663 Charles II granted a vast Carolina province to certain English lords. Soon after, part of the unoccupied territory conquered from the Dutch (page 82) was given to another group of English proprietors, under the name New Jersey. In both these districts, sturdy settlers were soon wresting homes from the wilderness and winning self-government from distant proprietors. That interesting story cannot be told here; but two other new colonies, New York and Pennsylvania, must have some attention.

NEW YORK, TO 1690 

1. The people of Dutch New Netherland had had no selfgovernment. They were ruled arbitrarily by a "Director 

General," who (with his council) was responsible only to the Dutch proprietary company or to the government in Holland. 

There were a number of great landlords (patroons) in the colony who each had great authority over the settlers on his lands. 

Settlers from Connecticut had established four English towns on Long Island which afterwards passed under the rule of New Netherland. In 1653 a meeting of representatives from various parts of the colony was held, to demand some self-government. This meeting was inspired by those English towns, and their delegates controlled it. The Dutch governor, Stuyvesant, in explaining the matter to the authorities in Holland, wrote: "It ought to be remembered that the Englishmen, who are the leaders in these innovations, enjoy more privileges than the Exemptions of New Netherland grant to any Hollander." 

Before true representative government grew out of this agitation, came the English conquest of New Amsterdam in 1664. 

King Charles gave most of the conquered province to his brother James, Duke of York, for whom it was renamed. The inhabitants, as a conquered people, had no constitutional claim to political rights. Accordingly, the charter to James said nothing of any share by the people in the government. James, however, found himself obliged to satisfy the Long Island towns by promising them privileges "equal to those in the New England colonies," and, in 1682, it proved necessary to introduce a representative Assembly for the colony. 91 2. Pennsylvania's history really begins with the founding of the Colony of New Sweden. One Willem Usseliux, a native of 

Antwerp, failing to get backing in the Netherlands for a trading company with Africa, Asia, and America, appealed to Gustavus II of Sweden for funds. With the King's help the Australian Company was formed. A few years later this company, by union with the Ship Company, became the South Company. The advantages of trading, however, were less than had been expected, and the company changed its plans to colonizing in South

COLONY OF NEW SWEDEN 

America. These plans were again changed to founding a colony in America after consultation with Peter Minuit, who knew about America through his connection with New Netherland. 

So it was that Minuit set out on August 9, 1637, in the Swedish ships Kalmar Nyckel and Fogel Grip, manned by Dutch sailors. 

The colonists landed in March, 1638, on the west side of Delaware Bay, and on the 29th, Minuit bought a tract of land from the Indians on the west shore of the Delaware from Bombay Hook to the River Schuylkill. He called the land New 

Sweden. 

Twenty-three men remained behind when the two ships sailed back to the mother land. Lieutenant Måns Kling was in command and directed the military activities. Hendrick

Huygen was in charge of civil and economic matters. 

There followed several "return" trips of the Kalmar Nyckel with more Swedish, Dutch, and Finnish colonists, including the second governor, Peter Hollander. In 1642, the South and 

Ship Company was reorganized into the West India or New Sweden Company and a third governor was sent to the colony Johan Printz. Upon his arrival he built a home and fort on 

Tinicum Island (near Chester), and twenty emigrants and their families settled there with him. This was the first permanent seat of government in what is now Pennsylvania. 

Until 1655 the New Sweden Colony existed under the sporadic interest of the Swedish government. Then the Dutch of New Netherland invaded the colony and overthrew it, only to be, in turn, overcome by the English. 

Pennsylvania belongs with Rhode Island and Maryland in the group of colonies that stood especially for religious freedom. The Quakers, or Friends, of all the new religious sects of the seventeenth century, were most offensive to church and government in European lands. They "swore not at all," not even to take the oath of allegiance to a king. As pacifists, they would not serve in the army. Believing all men equal "in the sight of God," they refused to doff their broad-brimmed hats even to royalty.

Now the great God hath been pleased to make me concerned in your part of the world, and the king of the country where I live hath given me a great province therein. But I desire to enjoy it with your love and consent, that we may always live together as neighbors and friends, - else what would the great God do to us, who hath made us (not to devour and destroy one another but) to live soberly and kindly together in the world. WILLIAM PENN'S "HOLY EXPERIMENT" 

93 Many Quakers had sought to find homes in English America; but, except in Rhode Island, they had met with treatment at least as harsh as they were seeking to escape. Finally some leaders among them decided to set up a colony of their own. 

For that purpose they bought part of New Jersey from the English proprietors. One of those leaders was William Penn, son of a wealthy English admiral who had become famous some years before by conquering Jamaica from Holland. While a student at Oxford, Penn had risked his prospects by joining the despised Quakers, but, happily, his father did not disinherit him.

Penn had in mind to try out what he called "a Holy Experiment." This, he decided, called for a larger and freer field than little New Jersey. Accordingly (in consideration of a large debt due his father from the king) he secured a large grant of wild territory stretching westward from the Swedish settlements on the Delaware which were also included in the grant but under a separate government. King Charles pleasantly insisted on naming the wild district "Penn's Woods," or Pennsylvania. 

The boundaries of the grant were vague, overlapping those of Massachusetts and Connecticut and, still more, of New York and of Maryland. 

Early Pennsylvania owes more to Penn than any other colony does to a proprietor. It had few of the hardships that had made so large a part of the history of earlier colonies. Thanks to 

Penn's wise and just policy with the natives, there were no Indian troubles. Rich Quakers in England and Wales helped the enterprise cordially, and the Mennonites (a German sect much like the English Quakers) poured in a large and industrious immigration. By the year 1700, when the colony was only twenty years old, it ranked next to Virginia and Massachusetts in wealth and numbers! Unlike the other colonies (except conquered New 

York), the population was at least half non-English from the first - Welsh, German, Swedes, Dutch, French, Danes, and Finns.

The Charter of 1680 from the king gave Penn authority over his colony much like that at first given to Baltimore for Maryland. But Penn wrote, "The people must rule. I propose.

"THE PEOPLE MUST RULE" 

to leave myself and my successors no power of doing mischief· that the will of one man may not hinder the good of a whole country." 

So he surrendered most of his own powers to the colonists themselves in the famous Charter of 1701. This grant remained the constitution of the colony until 1776. 

The people chose a one-house legislature each year, to meet at a date fixed by the charter. This Assembly (like those in 

Connecticut and Rhode Island) could be dissolved or adjourned only by its own vote; but the governor (appointed by the proprietor) could veto its acts. Freedom of conscience was guaranteed to all who believed in "one Almighty God"; and the right to vote was given to all who accepted Christ as "the 

Savior of the World" and who owned 50 acres of land or £50 of personal property. (During the eighteenth century, Pennsylvania was the only English colony where Catholics could vote. Even Rhode Island disfranchised them in 1719.)

CHAPTER IX "COLONIAL AMERICANS," 1690-1760 

The thirty years which we have just studied were a period of transition, marked by two special characteristics: (1) swift expansion of territory; and (2) an “irrepressible conflict" between the natural 

English demand for imperial unity and the more essential American demand for self-government. 

This conflict, too, had brought about a mighty change in the colonists. 

Until 1660 they had been English frontiersmen. After 1690 they were, more and more, Americans. True, they were still colonial Americans, dependent on England partly from custom and affection and partly from need of her protection against the French. 

During the next seventy years the two marks of the 1660-1690 period grow ever stronger, and one new element is added · incessant war with the French and Indians. 

I. GROWTH IN NUMBERS AND TERRITORY 

Despite almost constant war, the seventy years between the English Revolution and the American Revolution were a period of marvelous prosperity for the colonies. 

The older districts grew from straggling frontiers into rich and powerful communities, with intense local pride and with no small degree of luxurious living. The wealthy merchants of the few coast towns, and the large planters of the South, used . gold plate on their tables and gold lace on their imported velvets and silks. "There is no fashion in London," wrote an English visitor in 1720, "but is to be seen in three or four months in Boston."

But this luxury concerned only the older districts, and only a small class even there. The frontier was moving steadily toward the west, and in 1732 the new colony of Georgia was added 95

COLONIAL AMERICANS, 1690–1760 

on the south. Settlers in such new districts were always repeating the hard and dangerous experiences of the first comers to America. 

Growth was not so exclusively from immigration as before, but it was largely so still. The 250,000 colonists of 1690 (page 77) had half of them been born in Europe. In the next seventy years the population increased sixfold — to 1,600,000 in 1760. 

Only a third of these had been born in the Old World. 

Non-English elements appeared in large numbers. The largest one element came from unhappy South Germany. The rulers there were driving out their Protestant subjects, and in the wars of Louis XIV the victorious French armies completed the ruin.

The survivors of persecution by their rulers and of devastation by invaders began to arrive in America about 1690. They settled mainly in New York and the Carolinas and especially in Pennsylvania - where many of their quaint Old World customs survive, almost unchanged, among the "Pennsylvania Dutch of to-day. To this colony alone came more than 

100,000 German Protestants between 1700 and 1775.¹

A small but highly valuable contribution to American blood, due likewise to religious persecution, was made by the Huguenots (French Protestants), driven from their homes by the persecution of Louis XIV. They came mainly to the Carolinas; but some settled in New England, New York, and Virginia. 

The names Paul Revere, Peter Faneuil, and James Bowdoin suggest the services of their sons in Massachusetts. 

More important even than the German immigration, and next to it in numbers, was the coming of the Scotch-Irish during these same seventy years. These men were really neither Scotch nor Irish, but Saxon English, though there. had been some mixture with Celtic blood both in Scotland and 1 ¹It is easy to be misled by these impressive figures. Before 1700 the original 25,000 Puritan settlers of 1640 had multiplied to some 150,000 or 175,000, and by 1760 to at least 750,000. So, too, of the 40,000 Virginia settlers of 1670. Moreover, New England and Virginia, before 1700, had already shaped in large measure the course of future colonial growth.

NEW KINDS OF IMMIGRANTS 

97 Ireland. For centuries their fathers had lived in the Lowlands of Scotland as frontiersmen against the Celtic Scots of the Highlands. In the reigns of Elizabeth and James they had colonized northeastern Ireland, - frontiersmen against the 

Catholic and Celtic Irish. 

But after 1690 English navigation laws (page 101) crushed their linen manufactures, the chief basis of their prosperity. English laws against the Irish 

Catholics bore heavily also upon these Presbyterian "dissenters" in Ireland. So, about 1700, with hearts embittered toward England, they began once more to seek new homes, this time in America. 

To understand the importance of the Scotch- 

Irish in American history, we must turn to the appearance of a new "West" in this same period. The colonies had always had a frontier, but now first the frontier became a distinct section in American life.

OLD HUGUENOT CHURCH in Charleston, South Carolina-one of the most beautiful and interesting buildings in that beautiful and interesting city.

Our first frontier was the tide-water region, reaching fifty miles, perhaps, up navigable streams. But by 1660, in places, settlement was growing fairly dense, and towns had arisen at the mouths of rivers and on good harbors-Boston, Portsmouth, Providence, New Haven, New York, and Baltimore.¹ 

¹ Philadelphia and Charleston, similarly situated, grew up later, of course, because of the later founding of Pennsylvania and Carolina.

By that time, however, a second thin frontier had pushed farther up the streams, about a hundred miles, to the foothills of the Appalachians. Water-power was abundant there, and during the second half-century (or by about 1700), a new line of towns grew up at the "fall line"-Pittsfield, Trenton, Richmond, Raleigh, Columbia. (Identify all these on your maps.) 

So far, the moving frontier had always kept in touch with settled areas, but just beyond this “fall line" rose rugged, forest-clad mountains. By 1770, hunters and pioneer farmers were pushing over the first range of these into the long, narrow, north-and-south valleys that lay between the Alleghenies and the Blue Ridge. Here appeared our third frontier — with a hundred miles of tangled wilderness between it and the nearest outposts of the settled areas. For these pioneers to bring supplies from the East, or to send back products in trade, was as hard as for the first settlers on the coast to trade with England.

Here, then, began our first true "West"; and the dominant element among its settlers was this new American type, the Scotch-Irish. They came to America mainly through the ports of Philadelphia in the north and Charleston in the south. 

Many stopped in the settled areas; but a steady stream passed on directly to the mountains and over them. Reaching the 

Appalachian valleys in the far north and south, the two currents drifted toward each other, until they met in the Shenandoah Valley in western Virginia. Thence, just before the American 

Revolution, under leaders like Boone and Robertson (whose stories we shall read soon), they began to break through the western wall, to make a fourth frontier at the western foothills and even farther west, in what we now call Kentucky and Tennessee.

They were hard, dogged farmers and reckless fighters and hunters tall and sinewy of frame, saturnine, restless, dauntless of temper. Other immigrants to the New World had forced themselves into the wilderness, for high reasons, with gallant

THE SCOTCH-IRISH AND THE WEST 

99 resolution, against natural inclination. But these men loved the wild, and its independent life, for itself. Unorganized and uncaptained, armed only with ax and rifle (in the use of which weapons they have never been equaled), they rejoiced grimly in their task of subduing a continent. First of American colonists, too, did they face away from the Old World in their thought, and begin to look west toward the glorious destiny of the new continent.

These "Scotch-Irish" English of the West rank, in our early nationmaking, alongside the Cavaliers of Virginia and the Puritans of New England. Until about 1850 they were the typical American frontiersmen, especially in the middle West and Southwest. They have furnished, too, many leaders to our national life, — Andrew Jackson and "Stonewall" Jackson, Horace Greeley, Jefferson Davis, Patrick Henry, William McKinley, and Woodrow Wilson. 

II. THE CONQUEST OF NEW FRANCE 

From 1689 to 1763, with only short pauses to take breath,

France and England wrestled for the splendid prize of the Mississippi valley. This struggle with the French and their dreaded 

Red allies made a somber background for all other movements in the English colonies. It was not for a moment to be forgotten by the daring frontiersman shifting his home for better and cheaper land, or by the Assemblyman wrangling with a royal governor for larger self-government. 

For the most part the campaigns were fought in Europe; but at bottom the conflict was not settled on the battlefield. Two kinds of colonization were at war; and the English system had not only made more populous colonies but had also made them more interested in defending themselves (pages 6, 7). True, the despotic French governor could wield all the resources of New France (though this advantage was offset in part by the official corruption that always threatens such a system), while, among the English, dissensions between colony and colony many times cost dear. But in the long run the despotic governor proved no match for a self-governing people. Had the French ever succeeded in seizing Boston (as they hoped to do), they could never

have held it against the New England militia - not even as long as King George did a few years later. On the other hand, the 

English needed only one decisive victory. The mass of French colonists had had so little to do with government that they cared little whether they were ruled by King Louis or by King George, provided only they were treated decently. 

The closing chapter of the struggle was "the Great French War" of 1754-1763, sometimes called "the French and Indian War." All grade students are told that story. The interest centers around two heroic antagonists, Montcalm and Wolfe; and 

Wolfe's victory at Quebec thrust France forever out of the continent. By the treaties of 1763, England received Florida from 

Spain, and Canada and the eastern half of the Mississippi valley from France. The rest of that valley France ceded to her ally 

Spain, and, except for some West India islands, she ceased to be an American power. North America was left to the vigorous 

English Empire and to decaying Spain, with a dividing line, temporarily, at the great central river.¹

III. AMERICAN FREEDOM VS. ENGLISH CONTROL 

The Attempts of England to Extend her Control Concerned sometimes Colonial Trade, sometimes Colonial Government. 66 1. Several new Navigation Acts extended England's old commercial policy. To the enumerated articles to be exported only through the home country (page 79), rice was added in 1706, and copper, beaver skins, and naval stores (pitch, tar, flax, hemp, cordage, and masts) in 1722. England, however, offered bounties on all copper and naval stores sent to her; and this legislation (so far) had little effect on American industries. 99 But a new sort of interference was more serious. In 1696 parliament forbade any colony to export (even to England or to ¹England left the French settlers undisturbed in their religion and customs. VICIOUS "NAVIGATION" LAWS 

another colony) any cloth manufacture, and in 1732 the exportation of hats was forbidden. 

Cotton cloth was little known anywhere, its place being taken by linen or hemp. The cloth most used in the colonies was a coarse serge or linsey-woolsey (a mixture of hemp and wool). This was "homespun." It was spun and woven in the home, almost always only for the family use. After 1700, however, manufacturing shops began to appear - several looms under one roof, with weavers giving time regularly to the work. An English governor of New York warned English manufacturers that such shops in the Long Island towns were turning out "excellent serge that any man may wear.' 

The fashionable hats worn by Englishmen and Americans were made from beaver skins- -so that "a beaver" became slang for "a hat." 

Since the skins all came from America, the manufacture of hats had become an important industry in the northern colonies. 

These two laws were not really "navigation" laws. They were not meant to regulate commerce but to restrict manufactures. 

Bad as this was, the restriction, so far, was indirect. No colony was forbidden to make any article for its own people to use or buy. But just this was to follow. In 1750 the building or use of iron mills was prohibited altogether and the few iron mills in the colonies had to shut down. IOI 

99 The colonist continued to extract iron from the ore and to "cast" it into "pigs" and "bars." England was glad to buy it in these crude forms (to work up into manufactures), and she even encouraged its production by arrangements equivalent to paying bounties. The law, therefore, did not forbid “casting" the molten ore. So colonial iron furnaces still cast kettles and pans. And the farmers and blacksmiths still bought from the furnaces iron rods, out of which to shape, on their own forges, their spikes, nails, hoops, wagon-tires, hoes, horseshoes, and other simple implements.

But when every allowance has been made, these English laws of 1696, 1732, and 1750 were selfish and sinister. There was not even such excuse for them as for the earlier navigation acts. The motive now was plain jealousy and greed on the part of English manufacturers colonists to buy their products. who wanted to compel the Such policy would have be-

come crushingly harmful, had the colonists continued much longer under English rule. 

2. Attempts by the English government at closer political control first took the form of efforts to make colonies into royal provinces. For sixty years Virginia had been the only royal province. In 1685 New York was added to this class, when its proprietor became king. William III, at the opening of his reign, made Massachusetts practically a royal government (page 85). By a stretch of authority, too, he cut off New Hampshire from Massachusetts and made it a royal government. 

In the remaining colonies the Board of Trade found some just grounds for complaint. In particular, it was annoyed by 

Rhode Island's stubborn persistence in a shameful trade with pirates; by the refusal of Connecticut to let royal officers command her militia in war against the French; and by the absence of any militia in New Jersey and Pennsylvania. So, in 

1701, the Board recommended that parliament "reunite" the eight charter and proprietary colonies to the crown. 

Parliament, however, had great respect for charters, and failed to pass any one of the bills that the Board of Trade asked for. So the Board finally fell back upon the early policy of William III, and attacked colonial grants one by one, as occasion offered. Before 1730, by taking advantage of a serious disorder, a flaw in title, or the willingness of a proprietor to sell, it added New Jersey and North and South Carolina to the list of royal provinces. Out of the last named, Georgia was carved for a proprietary province, but it, too, soon came under a royal government. Down to the Revolution Maryland and 

Pennsylvania remained proprietary, and Connecticut and Rhode 

Island remained "corporate" (charter) colonies.

The common distinction between royal, proprietary, and charter colonies is not of great consequence. Connecticut and Rhode Island kept the right to elect all branches of their government, while everywhere else the governor was appointed by king or proprietor. Pennsylvania is not classed as a

SELF-GOVERNMENT IN ALL THE COLONIES 103 

charter colony because it had no royal charter, but it possessed, through its grant from Penn, the next freest constitution (page 94). Massachusetts, with a charter, was a royal province in all practical respects. 

The really important thing about the colonial governments was not these trivial differences: it was their resemblances. All had representative Assemblies, with much control over their governors; and all had the private rights of Englishmen, — jury trial, free speech, freedom from arbitrary imprisonment, which were not then found in the colonies of any other nation. 

Even in a royal province, the governor often showed little desire to carry out English instructions that conflicted with colonial views. Partly, this was because the governor, living in close touch with the colonists, was likely to see their side of the case; but more commonly it was because his salary depended upon his keeping up a good understanding with the colonial legislature. 

Every governor, in the words of a colonist, had "two Masters, one who gives him his commission, and one who gives him his Pay." If the Assembly passed a bill distasteful to the home government, the governor could veto it; but the Assembly might then cut down his salary, or leave it altogether out of the vote of supply, which was always the last business of the session. 

During the long contests of these seventy years the colonial Assemblies made larger gains than the English government. 

After James II, no monarch attempted to suppress a colonial Assembly. Everywhere the elected branches won complete control over both raising and spending money. After stubborn struggles they shut out the appointed councils (the "upper" houses) from any authority over money bills - just as in England the House of Lords was no longer permitted to amend or reject. "bills of supply." In each colony, too, the Assembly came to elect a Colonial Treasurer, wholly independent of the governor's control. Many other matters, too, formerly managed by officials appointed by the governor, were turned over to committees or officials elected by the Assemblies.

Private rights, also, were more clearly defined. With the approval of the crown lawyers, the doctrine was established that the Common Law of England, with all its emphasis on personal liberty, was also the common law of the colonies. And at least one advance was made in the colonies over English custom in the matter of personal liberty- namely, a greater safety for a free press.

In 1735 a tyrannical governor of New York removed the chief justice of the colony from office for personal reasons. John 

Zenger in his Weekly Journal criticised this action, declaring that it threatened slavery to the people. Zenger was prosecuted for libel, and the new chief justice, who presided at the trial, was plainly bent on seeing Zenger punished severely. He tried to limit the jury to deciding only whether Zenger was responsible for the publication (a matter not denied), reserving to himself the decision how far the words were punishable. 

This was an evil custom of English courts in such cases to a much later period. But Zenger's lawyer argued convincingly that public criticism is a necessary safeguard for free government, and that the jury must have the right to acquit Zenger if it found that his charges were true. "Men who injure and oppress the people," said the lawyer bluntly, " provoke them to cry out and complain, and then make that very complaint the foundation for new persecution." This cause is "not the Cause of a poor Printer alone, nor of New York alone," but of "every free Man on the Main of America." He called upon the jury to guard the liberty "to which Nature and the Laws of our Country have given us the Right, the Liberty of exposing and opposing arbitrary Power (in these parts of the World at least) by speaking and writing the Truth. A free people are not obliged by any Law to support a Governor who goes about to destroy a Province." 

The jury declared Zenger "Not guilty." This victory for free speech was celebrated joyously throughout the colonies.

Gouverneur Morris afterward styled it "the morning star of that liberty which subsequently revolutionized America." 1

A FLINTLOCK PISTOL OF EARLY COLONIAL DAYS.

CHAPTER X LIFE IN THE COLONIES 

1. The name "Blue Laws" is often given to much colonial legislation. This term means either that the laws punished ordinary crimes too severely, or that they interfered unreasonably with personal liberty.

In the first sense, the colonists certainly could not be blamed by Europeans of their own day. Everywhere life was still harsh and cruel; but American legislation was far more humane, and less bloody, than French or English. When the colonies were young, there were fifty offenses punishable with death in England; and this number was increased to two hundred before the "sanguinary chaos" was reformed. New England never had more than eighteen capital offenses. 

True, many barbarities did survive. It was a common thing to mark a criminal by cutting off part of his ears. Pillory and whipping post were used everywhere. As late as 1748 a law of 

Virginia (Source Book, No. 115) required every county to keep the instruments ready for such punishments — and suggested also a ducking stool for "brabbling women." Many other punishments of the time seem to us ingeniously repulsive, such as branding for robbery. New England sometimes used a softened form of this penalty for an habitual drunkard, compelling him to wear a large red D sewn upon his coat. 

In the second meaning of Blue Laws, New England, especially, does come in for some just criticism. Not that she was much worse than the rest of the world. To-day, as a rule, law aims to correct a man's conduct only where it directly affects 106

The Pillory. 

The Ducking-Stool 

The pillory was much the lighter of these punishments, but it was cruel enough. After "respectable" observers had satisfied their gloating and had departed, the pilloried unfortunate was left in his painful position for hours. during which rude boys or rougher men might make him a target for rotten eggs or for more dangerous missiles.

THE "WITCH HOUSE" IN SALEM, built in 1635, and the oldest house now standing there. It was the home (and office) of Judge Jonathan Corwin, who presided at the witchcraft trials.

other people; but in that day, all over Christendom, the state tried to regulate conduct purely personal. This was because state and church were so closely connected. In Virginia, the colonial law compelled attendance at church and forbade traveling on Sunday (Source Book, No. 33). In the Puritan colonies such legislation was more minutely vexing - and more rigorously enforced.

THE WITCHCRAFT MADNESS 

66 At the same time, the most common specific charges against New England are wholly false. It is still widely believed that in 

Connecticut the law forbade a woman to kiss her child on Sunday; that it prohibited playing on any instrument of music except the drum, trumpet, and jewsharp "; and that it required all males" to have their hair" cut round according to a cap." 

These "laws" are merely the ingenious vengeance of a fugitive Tory clergyman (S. A. Peters), who during the Revolution published in England a slanderous History of Connecticut. 

2. The deplorable surviving superstition of the age showed in the "Salem witchcraft madness" of 1692. Throughout the seventeenth century, all but the rarest men believed that the devil walked the earth in bodily form and worked his will sometimes through men and women who had sold themselves to him. 

These suspected "witches usually lonely, scolding, old women were feared and hated. In Switzerland, Germany,

France, and Great Britain, great numbers of such wretches were put to death, not merely by ignorant mobs, but by judicial trials before the most enlightened courts. In England, in 1603, parliament' sanctioned this Common Law practice by a statute decreeing death for those who should have "Dealinges with evill Spirits," and as late as 1711 a certain Jane Wenham was convicted, under this law, of "conversing with the Devil in the shape of a cat." In Virginia, Grace Sherwood was swum for a witch" in 1705, and the jury declared her guilty-though she escaped punishment through the enlightened doubts of the gentry Justices. In more progressive Pennsylvania the most that could be secured from a jury was a verdict against an accused woman of "guilty of haveing the Common fame of a 66

witch, but not guilty as Shee stands Indicted." In Maryland a woman was executed on the charge of witchcraft. But most of the American persecutions occurred in New England. 

Connecticut executed eleven witches, and about as many more suffered death in Massachusetts before 1690. Then came the frenzy at Salem; and within a few months twenty were executed, while the prisons were crammed with many scores more of the accused. The clergy took a leading part in the prosecutions, and the hideous follies of the trials are almost incredible. 

While the madness lasted, the flimsiest accusations were equivalent to proof. One neat woman had walked some miles over bad roads without getting herself muddy: "I scorn to be drabbled," she said. Plainly she must have been carried by the Devil! 

And so "she was hanged for her cleanliness."

Finally the common sense of the people awoke, and the craze passed as suddenly as it had come. With it, closed all legal prosecution for witchcraft in New England, rather earlier than in the rest of the world. The atrocious judicial murders crowded into those few months, however, must always make a shameful chapter of history. 

3. Education was making far more rapid advance among the common people than was being made in the Old World. Of the original immigrants below the gentry class, to be sure, a large proportion could not write their names; and for many years in most colonies there were few schools. Parents were sometimes exhorted by the laws to teach their children themselves; but all lacked time, and many lacked knowledge. 

Mary Williams, wife of Roger Williams, signed deeds by her "mark"! (Source Book, No. 89.) So did Priscilla Alden in

Plymouth; and in 1636 the authorities of that colony (sixteen years after its founding) excused themselves for having as yet no school, on the plea of poverty. In Virginia, in 1671, Governor 

Berkeley had made his famous boast, "I thank God there are no free schools here nor printing," and had "hoped" that for a hundred years more the colony might remain unvexed by those causes of "disobedience and heresy."

SCHOOLS 

109 Massachusetts and Connecticut from the first had a remarkable system of public education, and the other New England colonies gradually followed in their footsteps. The Dutch churches had begun free schools early in New York; but, because of that connection with the church, these afterward disappeared. Even in Massachusetts, it is true, illiteracy increased for a time after 1650 (see illustrations in the Watertown Records in Source Book, No. 83); and throughout the colonies the closing years of that century were a period of deplorable ignorance.

But that period was the low-water mark of education in America. With the dawn of the eighteenth century, and its greater prosperity, conditions began to improve. A generation later, to be sure, one of Berkeley's successors complained bitterly that chairmen of committees of the Virginia Assembly could not write or spell intelligibly. But by 1724 twelve free schools had at last been established in that colony by endowments from wealthy planters, and twenty more private schools were flourishing. South of Virginia the churches did something for elementary education, though no public schools were yet found there. At the opening of the Revolutionary period, though the actual years of schooling for a child were still usually few, an astonishingly large part of the population could read many times as large as in any other country of the world at that time.

In 1698 the South Carolina Assembly founded at Charleston the first public library in America; and, half a century later, Franklin started a subscription library in Philadelphia.

In 1700 there was no American newspaper. The Boston 

News Letter appeared in 1704; and, by 1725, eight or nine weeklies were being published in the colonies. Ten years later, Boston alone had five. All these publications were extremely small and they had only a limited circulation. There were no agencies, such as we have now, for

collecting news. Still these papers spread some information about world-doings; and (more important still) they gave active-minded and leading men a chance to express opinions to their fellow citizens (page 104). In New England such education as there was, was open to all on fairly equal terms, while south of Pennsylvania, education, high or low, was practically only for the few. But on the other hand the planters of the 

South were by all odds the best educated men in America. Many of them were acquainted with literature, history, politics, law, and such science as the age had; and they kept in touch with European culture and habits of thought, through private libraries stocked with the best English books of the age.

BENJAMIN FRANKLIN as an apprentice at his brother's printing press.

The schools of early Massachusetts and Connecticut demand a longer treatment. Here was the glory of Puritanism, — for the public school system of America to-day, in its essential features, is their gift. 

In Massachusetts, private schools were found in some villages from the building of the first rude cabins. In 1635, five years after Winthrop's landing, a Boston town meeting adopted one of these private schools as a town school, appointing a schoolmaster and voting from the poor town treasury fifty pounds (over a thousand dollars to-day) for its support. So Salem in 1637, and Cambridge in 1642. Such schools were a new

THE PURITAN SCHOOL SYSTEM 

III growth in this New World, suggested, no doubt, by the parish schools of England, but more generously planned for the whole public, by public authority. They were free in the sense of being open to all. Commonly they were supported in part by taxation, but tuition was charged also to help cover the cost.¹ 

So far, the movement and control had been local. Next, the commonwealth stepped in to adopt these town schools and to weld them into a state system. This step, too, was taken by the men of the first generation, - pioneers still struggling for existence on the fringe of a strange and savage continent. houses to keep up a grammar school (Latin school). This great law of 1647 (written with solemn eloquence, as if, in some dim way, the pioneers felt the grandeur of their deed) remains one of the mighty factors that have influenced the destiny of the world. 

James Russell Lowell, after a delightful reminiscence of the New England crossroads schoolhouse, continues:- "This little building, and others like it, were an original kind of fortification invented by the founders of New England. They were the first lawgivers who saw clearly, and enforced practically, the simple moral and political truth, that knowledge was not an alms, to be dependent on the chance charity of private men or the precarious pittance of a trust-fund, but a sacred debt which the commonwealth owed to every one of its children. The opening of the first grammar-school was the opening of the first trench against monopoly in state and church; the first row of pot-hooks and trammels which the little 

Shearjashubs and Elkanahs blotted and blubbered across their copybooks was the preamble to the Declaration of Independence." 

The Puritan plan embraced a complete state system from primary school to "university." In 1636, a year after Boston established the first town school, Massachusetts established her " state university" (as Harvard truly was in the seventeenth century, though it was named for the good clergyman who afterward endowed it with his library). Then the law of 1647 joined primary school and university in one whole by a clause providing that with each grammar school there should be “a teacher able to instruct youth so as they may be fitted for the University" (Source Book, No. 82). 

True, this attempt was too ambitious. Grinding poverty made it impossible for frontier villages of four or five hundred people to maintain a Latin school; and, despite heavy fines upon the towns that failed to do so, such schools gradually gave way, except in one or two large places, to a few private academies, which came to represent the later New England idea in secondary education. Thus, the state system was broken at the middle, and both extremities suffered. The universities ceased to be state institutions; and the primary schools ran down sadly, especially toward 1700. Between 1696 and 1770 several other small colleges were set up: William and Mary in Virginia, Yale in Connecticut, Princeton in New Jersey, King's (now Columbia) in New York, the University of Pennsylvania (through the efforts of Benjamin Franklin), and Brown in Rhode Island. None of these institutions, however, then equaled a good high school of to-day in curriculum or faculty. Indeed they were far excelled by the learned institutions of the 

Spaniards in Mexico. The planters of the South often sent their sons to the great English Universities (after preparing at home by the aid of private tutors); but on the whole, in spite of all the advance in its elementary schools, America was still sadly lacking in higher culture.

state system of public instruction was never wholly lost sight of in America.

THE PEOPLE AND THEIR WORK 

4. Population had risen to 1,600,000 by 1760. (See page 96.)

Fifteen years later, when the " embattled farmers" of Concord and Lexington "fired the shot heard round the world," this number had grown to 2,500,000. The main element in every colony was still English. All the way from New York to 

Georgia the western districts were held by Scotch-Irish. The largest non-English elements were found in the Middle Colonies; but in South Carolina also, between the western counties and the coast region, lay a solid strip of German settlements. That 

Colony, too, was beginning to receive some Highland Scots. 

In 1619, while Virginia was still the only English colony on the continent, she received the first importation of Negro slaves, twenty in number. In 1770, nearly half Virginia's population was Black, and much more than half of South Carolina's. In 

Maryland the proportion was about a fourth, and in New York a seventh. Negroes, indeed, made half the population south of 

Mason and Dixon's Line, and about a fifth of the total population of the colonies. 

5. Labor was supplied, in the main, in New England by free men working for wages, or for themselves; in the South by Negro slaves; and in the Middle colonies by indentured White servants and by slaves. (The cut facing page 114 shows that some White bond servants were still found in New England.) 66 The White bond servants were of several classes. The man who sold himself into service for a term of years, in return for passage money for himself or his family, was known as a redemptioner," or "free-willer." The German immigrants of the eighteenth century, like many of the English settlers (page 18), came largely in this way. Many White convicts were transported from England and condemned to a term of service, fourteen years. After 1717, this class averaged 1000 a year.

Classed with these convicts in law, but very different from them in character, were the political" convicts," - prisoners sold into service by the victorious parties, each in turn, during the seven or 

---

English civil wars of the seventeenth century. Often the true convicts were not hardened criminals, but rather the victims of the atrocious laws in England at the time. Some of them (like a much larger part of the redemptioners), after their term of service, became prosperous citizens. Charles Thomson, Secretary of the Continental Congress, was a "redemptioner."

So, too, was Zenger (page 104). Many members of colonial legislatures came to America as " bond servants."

Still the condition of White servants was often a deplorable servitude. Colonial newspapers teem with advertisements offering rewards for runaway servants. More than seventy such notices are contained in the "Newspaper Extracts " published in the New Jersey Archives for that little colony, for only the two years, 1771, 1772. This must have meant one runaway servant to each 1000 of the population; and probably not half the runaways are in those advertisements. One is described as "born in the colony," about 50 years old, and as having "served in the last war [French War], and a carpenter by trade." 

6. Communication was improving slightly in the later colonial period. Some roads were built between the principal settlements in the North (dirt roads only, dusty or muddy in summer and piled high with snow in winter), and some inns appeared. 

In 1732 the first stage line in America was started between New York and Boston. Soon there was another from New 

York to Philadelphia; and in 1766 the enterprising owner of the "Flying Machine " advertised that his stages would carry passengers over that route in the amazingly short time of two days! In another broadside, he informs the public that one of his stages has adopted the more comfortable coach form, previously used only for private vehicles. Soon the old stagewagon had wholly disappeared, in favor of the stage-coach. 

South of Philadelphia, all travel was by horseback along narrow trails, or by boat, and everywhere goods were still carried on pack horses or by water. Travel even by coach was not always pleasant: often the passengers had to help lift the conveyance out of the mud. The many streams had to be forded

TRAVEL BEFORE RAILWAY DAYS. 

The men in the stage-coach above are probably wondering whether this is one of the times when they must get out in the mud and put shoulder to wheel. (See page 114.)

The ferry was the only way a horse and a wagon could cross deep streams until they were bridged. Note the ropes from the ends of the boat to the strong "cable." By lengthening or shortening one of these ropes, the ferryman could make the current carry him across. (Do you see why?) But he was sometimes away from home, and sometimes on the wrong side of the river for the impatient traveler. Nor was it always easy to control skittish horses when crossing.

or crossed by ferries. When possible, without waiting too long for a boat, people preferred to travel from one coast town to another by water, although they had to provide their own bedding and food for the trip. 

7. Occupations, for the most part, changed very slowly. 

Nineteen twentieths of the people were farmers. The South had little other industry since its slaves were not fitted for the work of skilled artisans. Tobacco raising was the chief employment in the tidewater districts of Maryland, Virginia, and North Carolina, and rice cultivation in South Carolina and Georgia. 

These tidewater staples were grown mainly on large plantations. The Virginia planter in particular sought to add estate to estate, and to keep land in his family by rigid laws of entail.¹ 

Still, there was always a considerable number of small farmers in Virginia; and in North Carolina this element was the main one. The western counties of all the colonies were occupied wholly in small farming. 

In the Middle colonies, foodstuffs were raised on a large scale. 

These colonies exported to the West Indies (both English and 

French) most of the bread, flour, beer, beef, and pork used there.

In these colonies, too, immigrant artisans from Germany early introduced simple manufactures, cloth, pottery, glassware, hats, shoes, furniture, not by the factory system yet, of course, but by the "Domestic system," in their households or in small shops (page 101). 

ROADS AND TRAVEL 

In New England, occupations were yet more varied. The majority of the people lived still in agricultural villages and tilled small farms, but they could not wring all their living from the scanty soil. Each farmer was a "Jack-of-all-trades." In the winter days, he hewed out clapboards, staves, and shingles; and in the long evenings, at a little forge in the fireplace, he hammered out nails and tacks from a bar of iron. Manufactures were on a smaller scale than in the Middle colonies 1 "Entail" is a legal arrangement to prevent land from being sold or willed away out of a fixed line of inheritance. Entail is found only where primogeniture (inheritance by the oldest son) is the rule.

except for shipbuilding for both American and English markets (page 78). With her splendid timber at the water's edge, Massachusetts could launch an oak ship at about half the cost of a like vessel in an English shipyard. Another leading industry of New England was the fisheries, cod, mackerel, and finally, as these bred an unrivaled race of seamen, the whale fisheries of both polar oceans. 

New England, too, was preeminently the commercial section. Her schooners, often from villages like Gloucester, carried almost all the trade between colony and colony for the whole seaboard. Much of this business was like a tin peddler's on land. 

A sharp Yankee shipmaster loaded his schooner with a miscellaneous mass of small wares of New England make - kitchen utensils, simple tools, and so on- and stopped to trade at port after port along the coast southward until his stock was sold out. 

But in centers like Boston and Newport (as also in New York and Philadelphia in the Middle colonies) there grew up an aristocracy of great merchants (in the old English meaning of the word), with warehouses, offices, wharves, and fleets of tallmasted ships on every sea and with agents in all parts of the world. One favorite "circle of exchange' (6 was the three cornered route": (1) New England merchants carried rum to 

Africa, to exchange for Negro slaves; (2) these they sold largely in the West Indies for sugar; (3) this they brought home, to make into more rum, - with which to buy more slaves. 

All the colonies imported their better grades of clothing and furniture and metal ware from England. Southern planters consigned their tobacco to agents in England and purchased these imports there through the same agents. The Northern and Middle colonies usually imported from England more than they sold there. But they sold to the West Indies more than they bought, receiving the balance in money, mainly French and Spanish coins, with which they settled the balances against them in England. 

8. A serious lack of coin greatly hindered business.

"Hard money" was being drained constantly to England — as we have 

---

TRADE BY BARTER 

117 just explained. No coins were struck in the colonies, except for the" Pine-Tree Shilling" of Massachusetts (page 81); and there were no banks, to issue currency. Trade was largely carried on not by money, but by barter; and in all colonies, especially in the first century, debts were settled and taxes were paid in produce ("pay ") at a rate for each kind fixed by law. 66 Wages and salaries were paid in the same way. Toward the end of the colonial period the accounts of Harvard show that a student, afterward president of the college, paid his tuition with an old cow - which had to be accepted at the same value as a young and good cow. The following record of a vote by a Plymouth town meeting in 1667 hints, too, at the difficulty of getting "good pay " in such a method: 99 

"That the sume of fifty pounds shalbee alowed to Mr. Cotton [the minister] for this present yeare (and his wood). To be raised by way of Rate [assessed as a tax] to be payed in such as god gives, ever onely to be minded that a considerable parte of it shalbee payed in the best pay." 

In the need of a "circulating medium" (especially during the French and Indian Wars, when the governments needed funds), nearly all the colonies at some time after 1690 issued paper money. The matter was always badly handled, and great depreciation followed, with serious confusion to business. In consequence, the English government finally forbade any more such issues, to the great vexation of many debtors in America. 

9. The deep-lying differences between the three great sections of colonial America were mirrored in certain external features of their homes.

The South had few towns. Ordinary planters lived in white frame houses, each with its long porch in front, often in parklike grounds, set at intervals of a mile or more apart. The small class of wealthy planters lived on vaster estates, separated from neighbors by grander distances. In any case, a true "plantation," like a medieval manor, was a unit, apart from the rest of the world. The planter's importations from Europe were unloaded at his own wharf, and his tobacco (with that

of the neighboring small farmers) was taken aboard. Leather was tanned; clothing for the hundreds of slaves was made; blacksmithing, woodworking, and other simple industries needful to the little community were carried on, usually under the direction of White foremen. The mistress supervised weaving and spinning; the master rode over his fields to supervise cultivation. The two usually cared for the slaves, looked after them in sickness, allotted their daily rations, arranged "marriages." The central point in the plantation was the imposing mansion of brick or wood, with broad verandas, surrounded by houses for foremen and other assistants and by a number of offices. At a distance was a little village of Negro cabins. The chief bond with the outer world was the lavish hospitality between the planter's family and neighbors of like position scattered over many miles of territory. 

A wholly different society was symbolized by the exterior of New England. Farms were small, and the little fields were fenced by stone walls gathered from the soil. Hamlets dotted the landscape-each marked by the spire of a white church, and, seen closer, each made up of elm-shaded streets with rows of small but decent houses in roomy yards. 

The symbol of the West was neither the country mansion with its broad verandas nor the town clustering about a white spire. It was a stockaded fort (page 174) with scattered log cabins in stump-dotted clearings, spotting the forest for miles about it.

As early as 1660, in Virginia, there was a difference noticeable between eastern and western counties. The great planters were not much attracted to the rude frontier, and so the western districts were left to a democratic society of small farmers. 

99 So too in New England. By 1700, good land was scarce in the settled districts, and the town freeholders were less and less willing to admit "cottagers" (page 64) to rights of wood and pasture. So the more enterprising of the landless men began to strike out for themselves in new settlements far up

NORTH, SOUTH, AND WEST 

the rivers, usually at some point where there was good water power for a mill site and where land could be taken at will. 

Long before the Revolution, a more democratic New England had begun in the pine woods up the Kennebec and Androscoggin in Maine, along the upper course of the Merrimac in New Hampshire, in the Green Mountains of what was one day to be Vermont, and in the Berkshires of Massachusetts - as about Pittsfield on the upper Housatonic. 

119 Meanwhile, farther west, beyond the first mountain range, in the long valleys from Georgia to New York, the Scotch-Irish and the Germans were building the true West, cut off from the older settlements by the bristling Blue Ridge. 

But in all the western regions, English or German or Irish, east or west of the Blue Ridge, there was little aristocracy. 

There were few large proprietors, few gentry, few servants, almost no slaves. The gold lace and powdered wigs of the older sections were rarely seen, and only on some official from the eastern counties. Nearly every male settler was a free proprietor working his own land with his own hands, and eating and wearing the products of his own labor. There were fewer schools and fewer clergy than in the older region; and the hard conditions of life and the constant touch with savage enemies developed a rudeness of manner and a ruthless temper. 

Both for good and bad, this frontier had already begun to Americanize more completely the older tidewater districts.

PART III SEPARATION FROM ENGLAND 

America warred victoriously for the right, in a struggle whose outcome has vitally affected the whole human race. THEODORE ROOSEVELT. 

CHAPTER XI THE UNDERLYING CAUSES 

The American Revolution was more than a war against England. It was an economic, social, and intellectual transformation. CHARLES A. BEARD. 

The colonists in English America had come to feel that their economic interests were different from those of England - and sometimes opposed to them. The English government itself had forced them to see this by enacting navigation laws to restrict colonial markets and to hinder colonial manufactures. 

Then the Peace of 1763 removed the danger of conquest by France; and the colonies (now grown into a compact group of thirteen powerful peoples) began to feel quite able to take care of themselves. They no longer needed English protection: why should they put up longer with English interference in their industries or in their government?

The English colonial system had usually been well-meaning; but usually, too, it had been short-sighted or ill-informed, and sometimes it had been selfish. And it always carried the possibility of more serious interference. But any interference was vexatious to a proud people who now felt safe enough and strong enough to manage their own affairs. America had grown up. 

It was time for her to set up for herself. 

In growing up, America had also grown away from England, in ways of living and thinking. Indeed from the start, there had been a great difference. Not all England had been trans- 121

UNDERLYING CAUSES OF THE REVOLUTION 

planted to America: only certain selected people and selected institutions, upon the whole, the more democratic elements. 

No hereditary nobility was established in America, and neither monarch nor bishop appeared in colonial society. No wonder that after 150 years European English and American English did not always understand each other. 

The colonies had been held to England not only by the external bond of foreign peril but also by kinship and filial affection. These internal ties, however, had been sapped, insensibly, after 1700 (1) by this divergence in habits of living, (2) by a large immigration that had never known England as a mother country, and (3) by the incessant friction over trade restrictions, paper money, and royal vetoes. Now that the external bond had been cast away at the Peace of 1763, a shock might easily jar the two halves of the empire asunder. 

The French wars prepared for the Revolution in three ways. 

1. The common danger during the long wars had done something to bring the colonies together. In 1698, at the opening of the period, William Penn drew up a scheme for colonial federation; and in 1754 Benjamin Franklin presented his famous plan for union (Source Book, No. 114) to a congress" of colonial governors at Albany. Between these dates seven other like plans appeared. True, the majority of colonists everywhere ignored or rejected all such proposals, but the discussion prepared men for union when a stronger motive should arise. 66 2. The conquest of Canada, as has just been said, removed the pressing need of English protection against France. Farsighted men had long seen that the colonies might be less obedient to the mother country if the dreaded French should cease to threaten them from the north. In 1748 Peter Kalm, a shrewd 

Swedish traveler, wrote, " It is of great advantage to the crown of England that the colonies are near a country under the government of the French. . . . These dangerous neighbors are the reason why the love of the colonies for their metropolis does not utterly decline." And at the Peace of 1763, the French states.

WRITS OF ASSISTANCE 

123 man Vergennes prophesied: "England will soon repent of having removed the only check that could keep her colonies in awe. 

They no longer need her protection. She will call upon them to contribute toward the support of burdens they have helped bring upon her, and they will answer by striking off all dependence." 

3. The wars left England with an enormous war debt. As 

Vergennes prophesied, this debt led her to try to tax America which jarred the parts of her empire asunder. 

This new English policy had two main phases. 

The government used "Writs of Assistance" to enforce old Navigation

Acts with new energy; and it imposed new taxation, by the 

Sugar Act of 1764 and the Stamp Act. 

1. "Writs of Assistance" were used in America first during the last French War at the demand of William Pitt, who was then at the head of the English ministry. Pitt's purpose, however, was not to raise revenue, but to stop what he indignantly called "an illegal and most pernicious Trade. . . by which the Enemy is supplied with Provisions and other Necessaries, whereby they are principally, if not alone, enabled to sustain and protract this long and expensive War." And it is quite true that some New Englanders, for the sake of a shameful gain, were feeding French armies in Canada and French fleets in the West Indies at the very time that England was fighting desperately to protect New England against those armies and fleets. 

But the remedy was worse than the evil. A "writ of assistance" was essentially a general search warrant a kind of writ that had grown up in England under the despotic Stuart kings. Unlike ordinary search warrants, it did not name a particular thing to be searched for, nor a particular place to be searched, nor did it state the name of the witness on whose testimony it was issued. It authorized any officer to enter any house upon any suspicion, and so was "directed against a whole people." (It took its name from the fact that it authorized the officer to call upon any bystander for assistance.) Such writs ran counter to the ancient English principle that an Englishman's house was 

---

UNDERLYING CAUSES OF THE REVOLUTION 

"his castle," into which not even the officer of the law might enter without the owner's consent, except upon definite cause shown.

When George III came to the throne, in 1760, all writs of the past reign expired. Accordingly, in 1761, a revenue officer at 

Boston asked a Massachusetts court to issue new "Writs of

Assistance." It then became the place of James Otis, the brilliant young Advocate General, to argue for them. Instead, he resigned his office, and took the case against them. 66 Otis was a flame of fire.

Then and there the child Inde- "the pendence was born." 1 He called the general warrants 

Worst instrument of arbitrary power, the most destructive of

English liberty and of the fundamental principles of law, that ever was found in an English law book." He contended, he said, against "a kind of power, the exercise of which had cost one king of England his crown, and another his head."

The judges upheld the writs. But almost at once came the peace, which removed the particular need for such warrants; and for a brief time Americans forgot all past irritations in their enthusiastic gratitude for the conquest of Canada. 

2. Soon, however, a new English ministry under George Grenville, reopened the old wounds by new attempts to raise revenue in America. Grenville was an earnest plodder, wholly without tact, but he put forward some plausible arguments. The Intercolonial wars had made England the greatest world power, but they left her, too, staggering under a debt such as no country to that time had dreamed of. Eight million Englishmen owed a war debt of ninety dollars a head — incurred in defending two million colonials, whose debt counted less than two dollars a head. The struggles in America, too, had been little more than skirmishes, compared with the Titanic conflicts in Europe. 

Even in America, England had furnished nearly all the troops and most of the money. Further, Grenville did not ask the colonies to pay any part of the debt already incurred by Eng- 

¹ So wrote John Adams some years afterward. The other quotations in the paragraph are from notes taken at the time by Adams, then a law student.

GRENVILLE'S TAXATION PLANS 

125 land; they were only to bear a part of the cost of their own defense for the future. (The English government thought that ten thousand troops should be kept in America to guard against reconquest by France.)

It was plain, however, that the colonial Assemblies would vote no money to support a regular army in time of peace. Indeed, many leading Americans muttered that the proposed troops were really "designed as a rod and check over us." So, to get the money for a garrison, Grenville turned to the authority of parliament. (1) He would make the Navigation Acts a source of government revenue, instead of merely a means of benefiting English trade-as both English and Americans had always thought of them; and (2) he would have parliament impose internal taxes in America - a thing never before attempted. 

The first part of Grenville's plan resulted in the Sugar Act of 1764. This law (1) revised the Navigation Acts so as to make them promise more revenue; (2) set up more efficient machinery to prevent smuggling and to collect tariff duties; and (3) forbade all trade with the French and Dutch West Indies. 

But these islands had become the chief customers for the food products of the Middle colonies, and the British West Indies alone could not supply the molasses and sugar wanted by New England (page 116). The law ruined much of the industry of several colonies. Smuggling lightened the disaster somewhat; but zealous revenue officers soon seized many ships, and nearly half the rest of the colonial shipping was held rotting at the wharves for lack of business.2 

1 The Navigation Acts had placed small duties on goods imported into America (page 79); but these had hardly covered the cost of collection. 

They had been designed mainly as a convenient way of seeing that the trade laws were obeyed. 

2 Part of this loss of trade was due to a general industrial depression in Europe and America after the great wars. This "panic" of 1764-1769 was the first in our history, and the colonists attributed all the depression to the Sugar Act to which their particular troubles were largely due. "Hard times " in America have always produced political unrest; and those of the next few years made one factor in preparing men for the Revolution. 

---

UNDERLYING CAUSES OF THE REVOLUTION 

With every mail from America the commercial colonies poured storms of protest against the Sugar Act upon the ministry. But that law did not directly harm the Southern colonies; and so it was not possible to rouse against it a united America. Moreover, though it did aim at revenue, in its form it was like those earlier acts to regulate trade to which the colonists had long been accustomed. Leaders in America needed a better rallying cry to stir the people to action against English rule. 

The Stamp Act (the second part of Grenville's plan) furnished that needed war cry. Early in 1764 Grenville published this proposed law; but before introducing the bill into parliament, he gave the colonies a year to provide some other means for supporting a garrison, if they should prefer. The colonies suggested no substitute plan (for they wanted no garrison), but they made vehement protests against this one. 

In the fall of 1764, the Sugar Act fell into the background; and colonial town meetings and Assemblies hailed petitions upon the ministry against the proposed Stamp Act. These communications 

Grenville never made known to parliament, and in March of 1765 the bill became law almost without discussion. 

The law was modeled upon one in England, and it resembled laws that we have had in this country on various occasions since. It required the use of stamps for newspapers, pamphlets, cards, dice, and for all legal documents (wills, deeds, contracts, promissory notes, and so on). In a few instances (where a document transferred valuable property), the cost rose to several pounds, but as a rule it ranged from a shilling to a penny. Not one penny was to go to England. The whole revenue was appropriated to the future support of a garrison in America.

The American protests, from the first, showed a new attitude. 

In opposing the Sugar Act, the colonists opposed an injury to their pockets and to their material prosperity. They did not deny the right of parliament to regulate their trade: they objected only to the ruinous way in which parliament had exercised

"NO TAXATION WITHOUT REPRESENTATION " 127 

that power. But in protesting against the Stamp Act they did not complain of the financial burden: they insisted that parliament had no right to tax them at all. They styled the law unconstitutional (in the same sense in which Otis had called the Writs of Assistance unconstitutional). 

Separate colonies, or groups of colonies, had been more stirred by other measures than by the Stamp Act. John Adams tells us that an earlier English law forbidding a "Land Bank" in 

Massachusetts (to issue paper money) "raised a greater ferment" in that colony. 

Franklin makes a like remark about Pennsylvania. Other shrewd American observers believed that a chief cause of the Revolution, in some colonies was the English plan to establish bishops in America. (See cut facing page 143.) 

None of these grievances, however, made a universal appeal.

But now astute leaders, more or less hostile to English rule (like Samuel Adams in Massachusetts), seized the chance to rally a general dissatisfaction against England by appeals to the old English cry, - "No taxation without representation."

But that phrase meant in America a very different thing from what the same words meant in England. Since 1688, representative institutions in England had been shrinking, while in America they had been expanding. The English system, as 

Macaulay said, had become "a monstrous system of represented ruins and unrepresented cities." Populous cities had grown up without gaining any voice in parliament, while decayed cities (perhaps without any resident voters) kept their ancient "representation" - their delegates being now appointed 

SAMUEL ADAMS in old age. portrait by Copley.

From a
