PART IV THE MAKING OF THE SECOND WEST 

The West is the most American part of America. What Europe is to 

Asia, what England is to the rest of Europe, what America is to England, that the western States and Territories are to the eastern States. — James Bryce. 

CHAPTER XV THE SOUTHWEST: SELF-ORGANIZED 

I. WHEN SETTLEMENT BEGAN AND HOW 

In 1763 France had ceded to England all her lands between the Appalachians and the Mississippi. Six thousand French settlers had remained in the district, in three groups: (1) about 

Detroit; (2) near Vincennes on the Wabash; (3) at the "Mississippi towns," Kaskaskia and Cahokia (map facing page 181). These were the only White settlements west of the mountains. They all lay north of the Ohio; and so were in the district that parliament annexed to Quebec in 1774 (page 143). 

A little before that, a royal proclamation (map facing page 121) forbade English colonists to settle anywhere west of the mountains. The English government dreaded Indian wars which were sure to follow the advance of the frontiersman and it was influenced also by rich commercial companies that wished to keep the vast Mississippi valley as a fur-trade preserve. 

But even had England remained the owner, this attempt to shut out settlers was doomed to failure. The restless border farmers in the Appalachian valleys had begun to feel crowded in their narrow homes. For some years, stray hunters, who had ventured as far west as the great river, stirred the frontier with romantic stories of the vast central basin: and just before the 

169

Revolution a few hardy families pushed the line of American settlement across the mountains. 

This migration into a new "West" went on steadily through the Revolutionary War. It is natural for us to think of those years as given wholly to patriotic war for political independence from England. But during just those years thousands of earnest Americans turned away from that struggle, in order to win better homes and economic independence beyond the mountains from the Indian and the wilderness. 

Until some years after the Revolution, this movement concerned only " the dark and bloody ground" between the Ohio and the Tennessee rivers. This region had long been a famous hunting ground where Indians from north and south slew the bison and one another. Frequent war parties moved along its trails, but no tribe claimed it as a home. So here lay the "line of least resistance " to the on-pushing wave of settlement. 

II. THREE GROUPS OF SETTLEMENTS 

1. Watauga. — In 1769 a few Virginian frontiersmen moved their families into the valley of the Watauga, one of the headwaters of the Tennessee. Two leaders stand foremost in this migration - James Robertson and John Sevier. Robertson was a mighty hunter who had spied out the land to find a better home for his family. A backwoodsman born, he had learned "letters and to spell " after marriage, from his wife; but he was a natural leader, with splendid qualities of heart and head. Sevier was a "gentleman" of old Huguenot family and of some culture, the most dashing figure of the early frontier. 

The essential thing about Watauga was, however, not its leaders, but the individuality and democracy of the whole population. No wagon roads pointed west; and it was a generation more before the white, canvas-covered wagon (afterward familiar as the "prairie schooner ") became the sign of the immigrant.

At best, the early Southwest had only dim and rugged trails through the forests (" traces " blazed by the hatchet on trees).

Along such trails, men, rifle always in hand, led pack horses loaded with young children and a few necessary supplies; while the women and older children drove the few lean cattle. WATAUGA 66 

One side was

By 1772 the Watauga settlers were grouped about thirteen stations." A " station was a stockaded fort. formed usually by a close row of log huts, facing in. The remaining sides, with a log "blockhouse " at each corner, were a close fence of hewn “pickets," considerably higher than a man's head, driven firmly into the ground and bound together. Within were supply sheds for a short siege, and sometimes a central and larger blockhouse, a sort of inner "keep." a sort of inner "keep." Stockade and blockhouses were loopholed at convenient intervals for rifles. (See cuts on page 174 and facing page 187.)

The fort, however, was only for times of extraordinary danger. 

Ordinarily, the families lived each in its log cabin upon its own farm — in the center of its four hundred or its thousand acres. 

For many years these "farms" remained forest-covered, except for a small stump-dotted "clearing" about each cabin. The clearings nearest one another were often separated by miles of dense primitive forest. At an alarm of Indians, all families of a" station "abandoned these scattered homes and sought refuge within the stockade. In more peaceful times, "neighbors," from many miles around, gathered now and then to a "house- raising" for a newcomer for to roll up into place the mighty logs that made the walls was no job for one or two men. The two qualities that especially characterized this new West, says Theodore Roosevelt, were capacity for self-help and capacity for combination." 

66 In the spring of 1771 the Watauga settlers had been reinforced by fugitive" Regulators " from North Carolina (page 132), who, like the first comers, thought that the settlement lay in southwestern Virginia. That same summer, however, a surveyor " ran out " the southern boundary of Virginia — and found that 

Watauga lay in territory claimed by North Carolina. That colony, in the disorders of that time, could not well have cared for so inaccessible a section (the Carolina fugitives had come 

---

by a long detour through Virginia); nor would Watauga submit to more injustice from the Eastern counties. Instead, it decided to set up for itself as an independent community without reference either to mother colony or to England. 

So in 1772 the men of the thirteen forts gathered at Robertson's station in mass meeting, and organized a government by adopting" Articles of Association." This was the first written constitution ever adopted by a community of American-born men, (Connecticut's "Fundamental Orders" had been the work of men reared in England.) The new constitution provided for manhood suffrage and for absolute religious freedomin amazing advance of the Revolutionary constitutions adopted a little later by the thirteen States (page 157). 

For six years Watauga remained an independent government. 

Then, in 1778, when the Revolution had reformed North Carolina, the group of Watauga settlements recognized the authority of that State and became Washington County. 

Communication with Virginia was not exceedingly difficult because the long valleys trending to the northeast ran near together as they entered that colony. But a hundred miles of forest-clad mountains, without a trail fit even for a pack horse, separated Watauga from the nearest settlements in Carolina. Watauga had mountains on its west as well as on the east; but its water communication with the Mississippi justifies us in looking upon it as part of the land "west of the mountains." 

2. Kentucky. Among the many daring hunters and Indian fighters, who, preceding settlement, had ventured from time to time into the bloody Indian hunting grounds south of the Ohio, Daniel Boone was the most famous. As early as 1760, Boone hunted west of the mountains; and in 1769 (the year Watauga was founded) he went on a "long hunt" there with six ions. After five weeks' progress through the forest stretching continuously from the Atlantic, this little party broke through compan- 

---

BOONE AND KENTUCKY 

173 its western fringe and stood upon the verge of the vast prairies of America the famous "blue-grass " district of Kentucky. 

Hitherto (except for petty Indian clearings) American colonists had had to win homes slowly with the ax from the stubborn forest. Now before the eyes of these explorers there spread away a lovely land, where stately groves and running waters intermingled with rich open prairies and grassy meadows, inviting the husbandman to easy possession and teeming with game for the hunter, - herds of bison, elk, and deer, as well as bear and wolves and wild turkey, in abundance unguessed before by 

English-speaking men.

The prairies, even when reached, did not at first attract settlers. The lack of wood and water (until the presence everywhere of underground streams was learned) seemed to more than offset the hardship of clearing forest land. But in Kentucky 

Boone had found a happy mixture. And on his return to his 

Carolina home from this two-year "hunt," he declared that he felt himself "ordained of God to settle this wilderness."

Small expeditions of would-be settlers and backwoods surveyors (to locate lands) were soon following the trail of the hunters into "Kain-tuck-ee," in spite of frequent deaths by the scalping knife or at the stake. (The Woods Indian of the West, armed now almost as well as the Whites, was a far more formidable foe than the feeble tribes of the coast had ever been.) 

Boone himself led several of these parties. But in 1773 his first attempt to establish his own home in that land of promise was repulsed by an Indian raid, in which one of his sons was killed and the next year every settler fled from Kentucky at the breaking out of a great Indian war along the Virginia and 

Pennsylvania border. 

This was "Lord Dunmore's War." A dastard White trader had murdered the helpless family of Logan, a friendly Iroquois chieftain. In horrible but natural retaliation, a mighty Indian confederacy was soon busied with torch and tomahawk on the frontiers. Pennsylvania suffered most, and its conservative government (page 131) did little to protect its western citizens.

Virginia, however, acted promptly. To crush the confederacy she sent an army far beyond her settlements, into the distant Northwest, which she still claimed as her own though parliament had just annexed the territory to Quebec. This Virginian force was composed chiefly of hardy frontier riflemen, with deerskin hunting shirts for uniform, led by an English earl, the royal governor, Lord Dunmore. - I The rear division of the army, when about to cross the Ohio at the mouth of the Kanawha, was surprised by the whole force of the natives, through the generalship of the Indian leader 

Cornstalk; but, after a stubborn fight, the frontiersmen won a decisive victory. Of this Battle of the Great Kanawha Theodore 

Roosevelt has said: "It so cowed the northern Indians that for two or three years they made no organized attempt to check the White advance. . . . [It] gave opportunity for Boone to settle in Kentucky, and therefore for Robertson to settle Middle 

Tennessee, and for Clark to conquer Illinois and the 

Northwest. It was the first link in the chain of causes that gave us for our western boundary in 1783 the Mississippi, and not the Alleghenies." Mi Permanent settlement in 

Kentucky began the next spring (1775). In March and April (while Massachusetts Minute Men were chasing wearied Red Coats back from Concord), a strong expedition marked out the Wilderness Road¹ and began to build Boonesboro. This was soon the center of a group of smaller

In 1777 Kentucky (with its present bounds) was formed into a county of Virginia. Before the close of the Revolution, 25,000 people had settled there; and when the peace made Indian hostility less likely, a still larger immigration crowded through the Wilderness Road and down the Ohio. 175 3. The Cumberland Settlements. - Meanwhile Watauga had become the mother of a more western colony. Its population had increased rapidly, and its "stations" were growing into straggling villages. In ten years it had become no longer a place for real frontiersmen. And so, in 1779, Robertson, with some of his more restless neighbors, migrated once more, to a new wilderness home (a rich and fertile one) in west-central Tennessee, on the bend of the Cumberland. 

Many immigrants followed with the usual proportion of rough and lawless frontier characters; and those settlers who wanted order and decency decided that it was necessary at once to set up a firm government. So, on May 1, 1780, a convention of representatives at Nashboro adopted a constitution, — which, however, styled itself merely "a temporary method of restraining the licentious." It provided for a court of “judges,” one to be chosen by manhood suffrage in each of the twelve stations. 

This court" held all the powers of a government; but, if a "judge" gave dissatisfaction, his "station " might at any time hold a new election (an early instance of the modern "recall"). This Cumberland constitution recognized the right of North Carolina to rule the district whenever she should be ready to do so; and in 1783 that State organized it into a county. 

III. FROM THE REVOLUTION TO 1800 

In 1784, North Carolina ceded her lands beyond the mountains to the Congress of the Confederation, but that dilatory body never got around to accept the grant. Accordingly,

the Westerners complained bitterly that Carolina had cast them off, and (August, 1784) a convention of forty delegates declared that district an independent State with the name Frankland, "the Land of the Free." A constitution was adopted, and soon a complete State government was set up, with Sevier for governor. But now North Carolina "repealed" her cession; and, after some years of struggle and even of petty warfare, she succeeded in reëstablishing her authority. 

Tennessee remained a true frontier longer even than Kentucky did. It was farther from the coast settlements, and much less accessible. The population, therefore, grew more slowly and remained poor longer. The Frankland legislature had even been compelled to fix a currency "in kind": a pound of sugar to pass as one shilling; a raccoon skin as two shillings; a gallon of peach brandy as three. (Scornful Easterners were fond of jesting about this "money which cannot be counterfeited," -forgetting that their own fathers had used a like currency.)

Indian peril lessened in Kentucky after the Revolutionary War, though occasional raids from the Illinois tribes across the Ohio continued for a long time. But the Tennessee settlements had been thrust into the special hunting grounds of the neighboring Creeks and Cherokees (page 10); and after 1783 those warlike confederacies were especially incited and armed to raid the American frontier by the unfriendly Spanish governors in

New Orleans and Florida. It is estimated that as late as the middle nineties, the average death rate from Indians in Tennessee was a man, woman, or child, every ten days. Sevier, Andrew Jackson, and Sam Houston, each won his early fame in repelling and punishing these raids. (The government of the 

United States had had nothing to do, of course, with the settlement of the district, and for a long time it took little or no part in its defense.) A striking passage of Professor McMaster's makes clear some phases of this frontier life. 

HARDSHIP AND DANGER 

“The pioneer cabins stood in the midst of an almost unbroken wilderness, and the people dwelling in them lived in never-ending dread of the bullets and arrows of the savages. The dense forests of hardwood trees, the matted under-brush, the tall cane that covered the face of the earth for miles and miles in every direction, turned the whole country into a lurking-place and ambush for the most crafty and implacable of foes. No man dared to fell a tree, to plant an acre of corn, to pick a berry from a bush, to go to the nearest spring for water, or even to sit in the shade of his own cabin, but his gun and his powder-horn were ready beside him."

For some years, only feeble ties held any of the Western settlements to the Atlantic States. In all of them there were attempts at independent Statehood. These natural and praiseworthy efforts were opposed both by Virginia and North Carolina, and also by Congress. Then these legitimate Western attempts merged obscurely in less justifiable plots for complete separation from the Union. 

For even this extreme phase of the movement, there was great provocation in the gross neglect shown by the East toward pressing needs in the West. The older States had just rebelled against the colonial policy of Great Britain; but they were strongly inclined to use a selfish policy toward their own "colonies" in the West. Even in the matter of protection against 

Indians, they hampered the frontier without giving aid. The 

Westerners made many petitions (1) to control directly their own militia; (2) to be divided into smaller counties with courts more accessible; and (3) to have a court of appeal established on their side of the mountains. (Many a poor man found legal redress for wrong impossible because a richer oppo- 66 

---

nent could appeal to a seaboard supreme court.) These reasonable requests were refused contemptuously by North Carolina, and granted only grudgingly by Virginia. 

Congress, too, was jealous or neglectful: in particular, for a long time, it made no effort to secure for Westerners the right to use the lower Mississippi. For nearly all its course, one bank of the Mississippi was American; but, toward the mouth, both banks were Spain's, and so (according to the custom of past ages) Spain could close this outlet for our Western commerce.¹ 

But the surplus farm produce of the new West could not be carried to the East over bridle paths. It was worthless, unless the Westerners could use the huge system of natural waterways to the Gulf and so on to the outside world. 

So, from the first, the backwoodsmen floated their grain and stock in flatboats down their smaller streams to the Ohio, and then on down that river and the Mississippi to New Orleans whence they hoped to ship it to the West Indies or to our own Eastern cities. (Even from western Pennsylvania, farm produce could be sent by this round-about way to Philadelphia cheaper than by the short overland route.) On the long river voyages, perils were constantly encountered from shifting shoals, hidden snags, treacherous currents, and savage ambuscades to say nothing of the hardship and danger of the wearisome return on foot through the Indian-haunted forest. 

FLATBOAT ON THE TENNESSEE. 

These natural perils, however, the hardy frontiersman accepted light-heartedly; but he was moved to bitter wrath when 

1 In 1763 Spain had granted England the right to navigate the river to its mouth, and in 1783 England had passed on her right to us — so far as she could. But Spain denied her power to transfer it; and anyway, as we shall see at once, our people needed another privilege along with that one.

- his river voyage accomplished - fatal and malicious harm befell him at the port. He had to have "right of deposit" at 

New Orleans the right, that is, to unload his goods and perhaps to store them awhile so as to re-ship to ocean vessels. 

That essential privilege the Spanish governors granted only in return for outrageous tolls; and at times they capriciously refused it altogether and confiscated the American cargoes. 

Since our government showed little eagerness in this life-ordeath matter,¹ the West finally began to seethe with furious demands for possession of the mouth of the Mississippi. How to get it, mattered little. The Westerners would help Congress win it from Spain; or they were ready to try to win it by themselves, setting up, if need be, as a separate nation; or some of them were ready even to buy the essential commercial privilege by putting their settlements under the Spanish flag. 

The last measure was never discussed publicly; but (strange as it seems to us now) some of the noblest of the Western leaders, at one time or another, were secretly mixed up in such negotiations with Spanish agents. American nationality and patriotism, we must remember, were just in the making; and it was still natural for even good men to look almost altogether to the welfare of their own section. Those leaders must not be charged with shameful conduct 2as men of a later day would be for such action. But it is fortunate for America that, soon after 

1790, they were pushed aside by a new generation of broaderminded immigrants, who were not so much bound up in any one section but were able (in the phrase of the time) to "think con- tinentally." Thus all "separatist " movements died. 

Moreover, about that same time, Virginia and Carolina began to take a broader and more generous view of the West; and, 1 In 1795 (at almost the end of this period) Washington's administration did secure the privilege nominally for a brief and uncertain period (page 246).

CHAPTER XVI THE NORTHWEST: A NATIONAL DOMAIN 

I doubt whether one single law of any law-giver, ancient or modern, has produced effects of more distinct, marked, and lasting character than the Ordinance of 1787.- DANIEL WEBSTER. 

The Southwest had been won, piece by piece, by little bands of backwoodsmen, acting, each, on its own account and organizing its settlement in its own way. But in the Northwest the first English-speaking settlers found the government ahead of them. It had surveyed the lands; it had marked off territorial divisions for their local organizations; and it gave military protection. The Northwest, therefore, child of the nation as it was, never showed those tendencies toward separatism that we have seen in the Southwest. 

I. HOW THE NATION CAME TO OWN IT 

Six States could make no claim to any part of the West, Maryland, Pennsylvania, Delaware, New Jersey, New Hampshire, and Rhode Island; and the title of South Carolina applied only to a strip of land some twenty miles wide. But, as soon as the Revolution began, the other six States reasserted loudly old colonial claims to all the vast region between the mountains and the Mississippi (map opposite). They planned to use these lands, too, in paying their Revolutionary soldiers, while the small States taxed themselves in hard cash for the war which was to win the territory from England. 

Virginia, North Carolina, and Georgia each claimed to the Mississippi. So far, there was at least little conflict of title between the States. North of the Ohio, claims did overlap. Virginia claimed all the Northwest, under her old charter; and she had given life to this title by Dunmore's War and by Clark's conquest of Illinois, and, after 181

1779, by governing the conquered district as the County of Illinois. New York also claimed all the Northwest, by the slightest of all titles. The middle third was claimed by both 

Massachusetts and Connecticut on the basis of old charters, which had made their grants reach "from sea to sea."

While opposing these "large State" claims, Maryland invented a new and glorious colonial policy for America, and, standing alone through a stubborn four-year struggle, she forced the Union to adopt it. As early as November, 1776, her Convention set forth this resolution: "That the back lands, claimed by the British crown, if secured by the blood and treasure of all, ought, in reason, justice, and policy, to be considered a common stock, to be parcelled out by Congress into free, convenient, and independent Governments, as the wisdom of that body shall hereafter direct." and Virginia 

With clear A year later, since Congress had failed to adopt this policy, Maryland made it a condition without which she would not ratify the Articles of Confederation. By its own terms, that constitution was not to bind any State until all ratified it. By 

February, 1779, every other State had ratified. Further delay was in many ways perilous to the new Union; charged Maryland bitterly with lack of patriotism. eyed purpose, however, the little State held out, and public opinion gradually shifted to her side. October 10, 1780, Congress formally pledged the Union to the new policy, urging the States to cede the western lands to the central government, to be disposed of "for the common good of the United States." It guaranteed that all lands so ceded would be “formed into separate republican States, which shall become members of the federal union and have the same rights of freedom, sovereignty, and independence as the other States."

This completed the American plan of colonization. Previously, the world had known only two plans: Greek and

Phoenician colonies became free by separating at once from the mother cities; the seventeenth and eighteenth century colonies

of European countries had remained united to the mother countries, but in a condition of humiliating dependence. For the United States Maryland had devised a plan combining permanent union with freedom.

New York had already agreed to give up her western claims, and now Connecticut promised to do likewise. In January, 1781, Virginia's promise followed, for her lands north of the Ohio.¹ 

The formal deeds of cession were delayed by long negotiations over precise terms, but it was now certain that Maryland had won. Accordingly (March 1, 1781), she ratified the Articles.

That constitution at last went into operation, and the new confederacy possessed a 66 national domain."

ORGANIZATION BY THE NATION II. ORGANIZATION BY THE NATION 

It was now up to Congress to make good its promise in the resolution of October, 1780. So when Thomas Jefferson in Congress announced Virginia's cession, he also proposed a plan of government for all territory "ceded or to be ceded." This plan was enacted into the Ordinance of 1784.

Jefferson supposed that all States would complete their cessions promptly. Accordingly, the Ordinance cut up all the western territory (north and south) into fifteen proposed States-bounded, so far as possible, by meridians and parallels of latitude (map facing page 186) and endowed with names, such as Michigania, Metropotamia, and Polypotamia. Certain provisions were to be a matter of compact between each new State and the United States: the State was forever to remain part of the United States, to preserve a republican form of government, and not to tax United States lands within its ¹ Kentucky remained part of Virginia until 1792 (page 180). The cessions are given on the map facing page 181. Virginia kept title to the "Military Reserve," a triangular tract of several million acres just north of the Ohio, so as to pay her Revolutionary soldiers with land grants there. 

Connecticut kept 3,250,000 acres south of Lake Erie, as a basis for a public school fund. This "Western Reserve was soon settled by New Englanders. 

---

borders, nor to tax non-residents more heavily than its own citizens. A remarkable attempt was made also to exclude slavery from all the Western territory after the year 1800. This provision, however, failed of adoption by one vote.

In 1787 this Ordinance of 1784 was replaced by the great Northwest Ordinance — which, however, in important matters was modeled closely upon its predecessor. During the three intervening years no district had secured population enough to organize a territorial government under the law. Meantime, some parts of the East had begun to look jealously at the prospect of so many new States, which might soon outvote the Atlantic section in Congress. Congress, therefore, had appointed a committee to prepare a new ordinance, with view particularly to reducing the number of future States. 

Now in 1786 some New England Revolutionary soldiers had organized a "company " to establish themselves in new homes on the Ohio; and early in 1787 this Ohio Company sent the shrewd Manasseh Cutler (one of their directors) to buy a tract of western land from Congress. Cutler found the proposed

Territorial Ordinance under discussion. Negotiations for the land deal and for the new Territorial law (under which the settlers would have to place themselves) became intermingled. 

Cutler proved an adroit lobbyist, and finally both measures were passed. The ordinance, with a number of new provisions to satisfy the New Englanders, became law on July 13; and a few days later the land sale was completed. The Ohio Company bought for its settlement one and a half million acres at twothirds of a dollar an acre," but was allowed to pay in the depreciated "certificates" with which Congress had paid off the army (page 166) and which had now fallen to twelve cents on the dollar. 66 Since the new Territorial Ordinance applied only to the district north of the Ohio, it is usually known as "The Northwest Ordinance." The American type of "colony" was first established under it; and during the next century its principles

THE NORTHWEST ORDINANCE OF 1787 185 

became so fixed in our practice that many intelligent people think of them as part of the Constitution itself.¹ 

The region northwest of the Ohio was to be divided by Congress, from time to time, into suitable districts for States -of which there were not to be in all more than five. For any given district, there were to be three stages of government. 

1. Until it should contain five thousand free male inhabitants, there was no self-government. Congress appointed a "governor " and three "judges." (After the United States adopted the new Constitution the next year, many powers given to Congress by this Ordinance were transferred by new laws to the President.) The governor created and filled all local offices; and governor and judges together selected laws suitable for Territorial needs from the codes of older States, subject, however, to the absolute veto of Congress. 

2. In the second stage the governor was still to be appointed; but there was now to be also a two-House legislature, House of Representatives elected by landowners, and a Legislative Council of five men selected by Congress from ten nominated by the Territorial lower House. This legislature was to send a 

Territorial delegate to Congress, with right to debate but not to vote. The appointed governor had an absolute veto upon all acts of the legislature and also controlled its sittings, calling and dissolving sessions at will. Thus, in this stage, the inhabitants had about the same amount of self-government as in a royal province before the Revolution. 

3. The third stage was provided for in the following words: 

66 Whenever any of the said States shall have sixty thousand free inhabitants [a population about equal to that of the smaller States of the Union then], such State shall be admitted into the Congress of the United States, on an equal footing with the original States in all respects whatever, and shall be at liberty to form a permanent constitution and State government." 

1 See again the quotation at the head of the chapter. The document is among the five-cent Old South Leaflets, and also in West's Source Book. 

The class should verify the statements in this chapter about it.

Then followed six articles "for extending the fundamental principles of civil and religious liberty. . . [and] to . . . establish those principles as the basis of all . . . governments which forever hereafter shall be formed in the said territory." These were declared to be "articles of compact between the original States and the people . . . in the said Territory . . . forever [to] remain unalterable, unless by common consent." These six articles form a noble bill of rights. To like provisions in the previous ordinance they now added freedom of religion, habeas corpus privileges, exemption from cruel or unusual punishments, and jury trial. The Third Article declared that "schools and the means of education shall forever be encouraged "; and the 

Sixth Article prohibited slavery. 

More specific provision for supporting schools in the Northwest is due, not to the same Ordinance of 1787, as is sometimes said, but to two other laws of this same period. 

1. In 1785 Congress had passed the Survey Ordinance (originating with Jefferson). That law (1) provided for our present rectangular system for surveying land in advance of settlement, too and (2) gave one thirty-sixth of the national domain (section 16 in each township) for the support of public schools. 

At first each township had control of its section 16. 

Happily, however, it was soon decided to give control of all school lands to State officials, rather than to local officers, and to turn all proceeds into a permanent State fund of which only the interest is divided each year among various localities of the State. The States admitted since 

1842 have received also section 36 of each township for school purposes, besides lavish grants for internal improvements. 

¹ The rectangular survey is described, with diagrams, in West and West's Our Country. Its simplicity proved a tremendous help to rapid settlement; and it has also influenced Western life in other more indirect ways. 

County boards run roads on section lines and on the subdividing lines of the sections. The counties, made up of square townships, take on a rectangular shape, and the States themselves tend to a like form, as compared with the States in the older parts of the country (see map facing page 479).

COMMON SCHOOLS AND UNIVERSITIES 

2. The other great act of the dying Congress of the Confederation which deserves grateful remembrance was passed a few days after the Northwest Ordinance. Cutler was not content even with the generous terms he had secured for the Ohio Company until he obtained a further free grant of forty-six thousand acres "of good land" in the proposed Territory "for the support of an institution of higher learning," the land to be located, and funds used, "as the future legislature of the proposed settlement may direct." Here begins the policy of national land grants to "State universities." When the Territory of Indiana was set off on the West, a like grant was made for it; and so on, for each new Territory since. After 1873, such grants to new 

Territories were doubled in amount. 187 

III. EARLY SETTLEMENT 

The Ohio Company pressed its preparations eagerly, and in the winter of 1787-1788, fifty New Englanders under General Putnam made the western journey as far as Fort Pitt (Pittsburgh). Here they built a huge boat, with sides protected by bullet-proof bulwarks, naming it the Mayflower in memory of their forefathers' migration to a new world. As soon as the ice broke up, they floated down the Ohio to the mouth of the 

Muskingum, and there founded Marietta.

Various hamlets soon clustered about this first settlement, each, as a rule, centered about a mill, — and within two years the colony contained a thousand people. Thousands more floated past Marietta during its first season.

The United States government opened no land to settlement until it secured title from the Indian owners though many White "squatters" settled ahead of government permission. 

In 1785 Congress had obtained a large cession of land in southern Ohio from Indian tribes there- and so the way had been prepared for the Marietta settlement. But the treaty did not prevent Ohio Indians from raiding even this district repeatedly, and finally it had to be won again for settlement - along with much more territory - by United States "regulars." In 1790 

---

and 1791 two expeditions to punish hostile Indians were repulsed, with the loss of a large part of our small army. But in 1794 a crushing defeat of the natives by General Anthony Wayne induced them to sue for peace by ceding much of the rest of Ohio. There was no more serious Indian trouble in the 

Northwest until just before the War of 1812. 

The second stage of Territorial government (with a representative legislature) began in 1799. The next year Congress divided the whole district into two "Territories." In 1803 the eastern one was admitted to the Union as the State of Ohio. 

The western had become the "Territory of Indiana." 

The Western settlements lived over again the hardships of the Atlantic coast settlements of a century and a half before; but they did not merely copy that earlier development. The first frontiers had had to work upon European-born men. This "fourth frontier," North and 

South, worked upon men already Americans - whom it swiftly made 66 more American." The frontier, as Dr. Turner has so well said, had become "the line of most effective Americanization.” 

FOR FURTHER READING. Frederic J. Turner was the first true interpreter of the West in our history. His Frontier in American History remains the best presentation of the meaning of the West; but any student with a taste for books should read also the delightful essay by Samuel Crothers, "The Land of the Large and Charitable Air in The Pardoner's Wallet, and Woodrow Wilson's "Course of American 

History" in his Mere Literature. For the story, Roosevelt's Winning of the West, Paxson's American Frontier, and Sparks' Expansion continue admirable. The story is given also in Ogg's Old Northwest; in the closing chapters of Channing, III, and in the opening chapters of IV; or in McLaughlin's and Bassett's volumes in the American Nation.

PART V FROM LEAGUE TO NATION 

CHAPTER XVII THE “LEAGUE OF FRIENDSHIP ” 

I predict the worst consequences from a half-starved, limping government, tottering at every step. GEORGE WASHINGTON, in 1786.

I. BEFORE THE ARTICLES WERE ADOPTED (1776-1781) 

Richard Henry Lee's motion for Independence (page 153) contained also a resolution that " a plan of confederation be submitted to the States." Congress at once appointed a committee to draw up a plan; but it did not approve the "Articles of Confederation" until November of 1777. Ratification by the States was delayed four years more (page 182). Almost until the capture of Yorktown, the Continental Congress¹ acted as a central government without any express authorization. 

During those years were the States one nation or thirteen ? 

No one at the time thought the Declaration of Independence binding upon any State because of the action at Philadelphia, but only because of action by the State itself. Congress had not even advised the States on Independence. It waited for the States to instruct their delegates, and the delegates of no State voted for the Declaration until authorized by their own State. The action at Philadelphia on July 4, 1776, amounted to a joint announcement, in order, in Franklin's phrase, that they might all "hang together," so as not to "hang separately." Twenty years 1 ¹ In March, 1781, Congress became "The Congress of the Confederation.

" 189

afterward, in a decision of our Supreme Court, Justice Chase said: "I regard this [the Declaration of July 4, 1776] a declaration not that the united colonies in a collective capacity were independent States, but that each of them was a sovereign and independent State" (3 Dallas, 224). 

On the other hand, it will not do merely to assert bluntly that the States were older than the Union. States and Union grew up together. The States took form fastest; but, from the beginning, there was a general expectation that they would soon be united. Except for some such expectation, they would hardly have been born at all, and except for the creation of a union, they certainly could not have lived. The Union did not create the States;¹ but it did preserve them. 

Just after July 4, 1776, there was nothing but common sense to keep any State from acting as an independent nation. Some of them did act so, even in foreign relations. (Virginia negotiated with Spain about protecting their common trading interests in the West; and her legislature "confirmed " the treaty made by 

Congress with France in 1778.) But, on the whole, with great good sense, the States allowed their possible independence to lapse by disuse. Congress managed the war and other foreign relations; and this practice was soon made the constitutional rule by the Articles of Confederation. 

II. UNDER THE ARTICLES, 1781-1788 

The ratification of the Articles failed to make a strong union. 

When the war was over, the States felt less need of union; and the Congress of the Confederation found that it had less power even than the Continental Congress had had. The

Declaration of the thirteen United States."

29 99 Yet the people were suffering grievously from the lack of a strong central government. The year 1783 saw the beginning such a 66 of "bad times" 'panic as often follows war (cf. page 125). While the war was going on, the disorder in industry was partly covered up by the streams of gold and silver coin that trickled steadily into the pockets of farmers and storekeepers who were selling supplies at high prices to the English and French armies. Coast towns, too, throve on privateering in which ugly business the shipowners made many a huge fortune.

But when peace came, the demoralization of regular business could no longer be concealed. Men could not find work. Farmers could get no coin for their produce, and only low prices even

in the doubtful paper money. Commerce languished, and ships rotted at the wharves, because the old trade with the West Indies was closed to us. Numbers of old soldiers, who had mortgages coming due, lost their homes because the "government money" which they had laid aside to pay with had no Re- longer any value. covery from these distressing conditions was needlessly slow because of the weakness of Congress. 

That body (1) could not negotiate to advantage with European powers for treaties of commerce, nor (2) could it raise funds to restore the value of its paper." 

1. British navigation laws now shut our ships from trade with the British West Indies just as they shut out all other foreign nations. That trade, however, from old custom, was particularly necessary to us. Congress tried to get a treaty with England to secure it again; but the English government (irritated by the inability of Congress to make our States keep the treaty promise regarding pre-war debts) asked contemptuously whether it was expected to negotiate with one nation or with thirteen. Nor did we succeed any better in obtaining commercial arrangements with France or Holland. 

2. Congress had "paid off" its soldiers (page 166), and some other obligations, by printing interest-bearing "certificates" to the amount of $26,000,000; but by 1788 a dollar of such paper was passing for twelve cents of gold. (The $240,000,000 of paper currency had long before been practically repudiated.) Abroad, Congress was in like disgrace. For a

STRIFE AND ANARCHY 

193 

time it had paid interest on the six million dollars borrowed from France during the Revolution - but only by borrowing two million more from Holland. And the time had come when Yankee ingenuity could wheedle no penny more from friendly Frenchman or Dutchman.

The evils just considered (especially that about our foreign trade) concerned matters belonging directly to the care of a central government. Two other serious evils were due indirectly to the weakness of Congress: (1) strife between State and State and (2) anarchy within a given State. I. 

Strife between the States. Each State had its line of custom houses against all the others, with all sorts of discriminations, fruitful of discord. Connecticut taxed goods from Massachusetts more than the same articles from England, in hope of drawing away British trade from the older colony, and, on another frontier, she waged a small war with Pennsylvania over the ownership of the Wyoming valley, while she seemed on the verge of war, for similar reasons, with New York and New Hampshire. New York taxed ruinously the garden produce of the New Jersey farmers, who supplied her and who had no other market; and New Jersey retaliated with a confiscatory tax of a thousand dollars upon a spot of sandy coast which New York had bought from her for the site of a lighthouse. South Carolina and Georgia were coming to blows over the navigation of the 

Savannah. Kentucky, Tennessee, Vermont, and Maine were all demanding independence of the older States of which they were still legally a part. In all ages the two fruitful causes of war between neighboring nations have been disputes over trade and over boundaries; and just such disputes were now threatening to turn the Atlantic coast into a stage for bloody wars. 

2. Anarchy within a State. The struggle against English control of the colonies had led some of the intelligent patriots (men like Samuel Adams and Richard Henry Lee) to object to any control over the States even by Congress. So perhaps it is not strange that it had made many ignorant men hostile to any government central or State. For years, even before open war, they had associated service to liberty with anti- 

---

THE CRITICAL PERIOD, 1783–1788 

social acts boycotts, breaking up courts, terrorizing officers of the law. Many of them had won easy reputation as patriots by refusing to pay honest debts due in England; and they now felt it a hardship to pay debts to their neighbors. 

Demagogues declaimed, to applauding crowds, that all debts ought to be wiped out (Source Book, No. 151 b).

The worst of it was, too, that these semi-criminal forces were reinforced by the bitter discontent of multitudes of wellmeaning men who were suffering real hardships. Many an old soldier, who had lost his home by mortgage foreclosure, felt that the loss was due to his having received insufficient pay in worthless money, while the law of the time drained his slender resources by extortionate court fees, and threatened him with hopeless imprisonment for undeserved debt.¹ 

Two disorders of the time had special importance. 

1. The Ignorant Craze for Cheap Money. Many people thought that the lack of money could be supplied, and trade started up, if the State governments would only print an unlimited amount of paper money, even though no real wealth were pledged to redeem such paper. Under our Constitution to-day, the States are forbidden to make any paper legal tender" (to compel people to take it as money, that is); but under the Confederation there was no such safeguard, and so some ruinous laws of that sort were enacted. In New Hampshire an armed mob besieged the legislature until it was terrified into passing the desired law. 

In Rhode Island that same result came without violence. 

There, in the election of 1783, the "cheap money" party won. 

Then creditors fled from the State, to escape being forced to take pay in the new "legal tender" for old loans of good money; and storekeepers closed their shops rather then sell goods for the worthless stuff. The legislature decreed it a penal offense, punishable without jury trial, to refuse the paper in trade. A certain butcher (Weeden, by name) did refuse to 

1 The Source Book (No. 151 a) gives one statement of real grievances.

sell meat for such money to one Trevett, and was brought to trial the famous Trevett vs. Weeden case. Weeden's lawyer pleaded that the refusal of jury trial was contrary to the " constitution" and therefore void. The judges took this view and decided against the law. The legislature summoned them to defend their decision, voted that their explanation was "unsatisfactory," and, when their terms expired soon after, refused to reappoint them. But their decision stood, and they had laid an important foundation for the tremendous power of later American courts. 

SHAYS' REBELLION 

2. Shays' Rebellion. For six months in 1786-1787, parts of western Massachusetts were in armed rebellion against the State government. Rioters broke up the courts, to stop proceedings against debtors; and Daniel Shays (a captain of the Revolutionary War), leading two thousand men, was barely repulsed from the Federal arsenal at Springfield. Says Francis A. Walker (Making of the Nation, 17):-"The insurgents were largely, at least in the first instance, sober, decent, industrious men, wrought to madness by what they deemed their wrongs; but they were joined by the idle, the dissipated, the discontented, the destructive classes, as the insurrection grew."

Congress talked about raising troops to restore order. It was too slow and timid, however, to help. But the State governor (James Bowdoin) acted promptly and decisively. He called out the militia (collecting subscriptions for its support from Boston capitalists), and the rebels were dispersed in a sharp mid-winter campaign. Still, a few months later, Bowdoin was defeated for reëlection by John Hancock, who was supposed to sympathize with the rebels and who did then pardon Shays and other imprisoned leaders.

This rebellion was one of the chief events leading to the new 1 The word "constitution" in this decision was used in the English sense, as in Henry's Stamp Act Resolutions and by Americans commonly in those years. See pages 127, 135, 138, and elsewhere. The Rhode Island charter did not expressly mention jury trial. (The court, of course, did not deny the right of the legislature in that day to make paper money legal tender.)

Federal Constitution. Men could look calmly at Rhode Island vagaries, and even at New Hampshire anarchy; but riot and rebellion in the staid, powerful Bay State was another matter. 

It seemed to prophesy the dissolution of society, unless there could be formed at once a central government strong enough "to ensure domestic tranquillity." When Henry Lee in Congress spoke of using influence to abate the Rebellion, Washington wrote him in sharp rebuke: "You talk, my good Sir, of using influence. . . . Influence is no government. Let us have one [a government] by which our lives, liberties, and properties may be secured, or let us know the worst." 

III. THE CONFEDERATION BREAKS DOWN 

(Because It Could Not Be Amended) 1 The Confederation called itself a "firm league of friendship." 

No one would have claimed it to be a national government. The 

Congress was made up of delegates appointed annually by the State legislatures and paid by them. Each State had one vote in Congress; and, on certain important kinds of business, nine 

States had to agree. The States were forbidden to make any treaties with foreign powers or with each other, or to make any laws or tariffs in conflict with any treaty that had been made by Congress. Congress was to have sole control over foreign affairs; and at home it was to regulate the postal service, weights and measures, and the coinage.

The final Article read: "Every State shall abide by the de termination of the United States, in Congress assembled, on all questions which by this Confederation are submitted to them. 

And the Articles of this Confederation shall be inviolably observed by every State, and the Union shall be perpetual." But an earlier Article had provided that each State keep its "sovereignty" and every power not expressly delegated. 

¹ If a State had an odd number of delegates, the majority of them cast the one vote. If the number of delegates was evenly divided, the vote was lost. For the rule for one vote, see Source Book, No. 130 and No. 146.

THE ARTICLES OF CONFEDERATION 

The Articles of Confederation was much the best constitution for a confederacy of states that the world had ever seen. It had many improvements over the ancient Greek confederations and over the Swiss and Dutch unions of its own day. The trouble was that the American people had outgrown any mere confederacy. They needed some closer approach to a national government. 197 The faults of the Articles had been found (many of them in a higher degree) in all the confederacies of the past. They may be classed under four heads: poor machinery of government; insufficient powers; impossibility of amendment; and the fact that the government dealt, not with individual citizens, but only with the States.. 

1. The requirement that nine States in Congress must agree for important business hindered action unduly, especially when for long periods not more than nine or ten States were represented. Moreover, the union had no executive and only a feeble germ of a judiciary. ____ 2. No federal government had ever had a longer list of important matters committed to its control, but the list should have contained at least two more powers: power to regulate interstate commerce would have prevented much strife between the States; and authority to levy a low tariff for revenue would have done away with the chief financial difficulties. 

3. But these defects (1 and 2) were the least important ones.

They might have been remedied, and probably would have been, in part at least, had it not been for the third evil. The amending clause (in the Thirteenth Article) demanded the unanimous consent of the thirteen State legislatures for any change in the Articles. In practice, this prevented any amendment. 

In February, 1781, Congress submitted to the States an amendment to give it authority to put a five per cent tariff on imports the proceeds to be used in paying the Continental debt and the interest on it. This modest request for an indispensable power roused frantic opposition.

*If taxes can thus be levied by any power outside the States," cried misguided patriots, "why did we oppose the tea duties!" And Richard Henry Lee affirmed that if the amendment were adopted, Liberty would "become an empty name." After a year's discussion, twelve States voted Yes, but little Rhode Island defeated the project. 

Congress at once made a second request for the same power for only twenty-five years. Four States voted No. 

Congress made them a solemn appeal not to ruin the only hope of redeeming the faith of the Union; and, after three years of negotiation, three of them did change their vote. 

But New York, jealous of her growing commerce, still refused and far-seeing men gave up hope of efficient amendment by constitutional means. Revolution (peaceful or violent) or anarchy were the only alternatives. 

4. That difficulty in amending the Articles followed from the fact that the Confederation was "a league of sovereign states." (No "sovereign" can be bound by a change in a bargain except by his own consent.) The fourth evil, too (the failure of the government to reach individual men), came from the same cause; and it was even more fundamental. It could be changed only by changing the confederation of sovereign States into some kind of national union. For three millions of weak subjects Congress might have passed laws. On thirteen powerful partners it could merely make requisitions. John Smith or Henry Jones would hardly think of refusing obedience to a command from a central government; but New York or Virginia felt as strong as Congress itself, and would do as it pleased. 

In the final outcome it was fortunate that amendment was impossible. Otherwise, the Articles might have been patched up, and the "limping government" so kept alive. But no ordinary amendment could have cured the fundamental evil. The 

Constitutional Convention of 1787, when it came, perceived this clearly and so gave us not an amendment but a wholly new Constitution. For several years, from 1781 to 1787, thinkers

THE CONFEDERATION BREAKS DOWN 

199 had been groping towards the idea that we must have a new kind of federation, such that the Central government could act directly upon individual citizens.

The fundamental defect of the Confederation had been found in every federal union in earlier history. All had been confederations of states. The American Constitution of 1787 was to give to the world a new type of government, a federal state. 

In the old type the states remained sovereign states confederated. In the new type they are fused, for certain purposes, into one sovereign unit. 66 Tocqueville (page 65) called this kind of federal government a great discovery in political science." It was adopted by 

Switzerland in 1848, by the Dominion of Canada in 1867, by the German Empire in 1871, by Australia in 1900, by South Africa in 1909, and by the new German Republic in 1919.

CHAPTER XVIII MAKING THE CONSTITUTION 

Since the creation of the world, America now presents the first instance of a people assembling to weigh deliberately and calmly, and to decide leisurely and peacefully, upon the form of government by which they will bind themselves and their posterity. - JAMES WILSON whom Fiske calls "perhaps the most farsighted man in the Convention." 

This example of changing a constitution by assembling the wise men of the state, instead of assembling armies, will be worth as much to the world as the former examples we have given it. - THOMAS JEFFERSON, writing from Paris. 

I. GETTING A CONVENTION 

When the second revenue amendment failed, in 1786 (page 198), a Continental convention had already been called to consider more radical changes.

Suggestions for a convention to form a stronger government had been made from time to time by individuals for several years. No concrete result followed, however, until these proposals became connected with a commercial undertaking. 

Washington had long been interested in Western lands, and at the close of the Revolution he owned some thirty thousand acres in Kentucky and in the Virginia Military Reserve (page 183). A visit to the West impressed him powerfully with the need of better communication with that region, for business prosperity and even for continued political union; ¹ and he urged 

Virginia to build roads to her Western possessions. In pursuance of this idea he became president of a company to improve 1 1 Referring to the danger that the Westerners might join Spain, he wrote: "They . . . stand, as it were, upon a pivot. The touch of a feather would turn them either way." But, unlike Jefferson and Franklin, Washington felt no very deep interest in opening the Mississippi. Instead, he hoped to improve communication across the mountains. 200

THE ANNAPOLIS CONVENTION 

201 the navigation of the upper Potomac. This matter required assent from both Virginia and Maryland. These States were in dispute also over tariffs levied by Maryland at the mouth of Chesapeake Bay. Washington invited commissioners from the two States to meet at Mount Vernon. That gathering decided there ought to be another meeting in which Pennsylvania should be represented since she, too, was interested in Chesapeake commerce. And finally Virginia invited all the 

States to send representatives to Annapolis to consider the matter of uniform tariffs on all foreign commerce. 

Only five States appeared at this Annapolis Convention (September 1, 1786). But New Jersey had instructed her delegates there to secure, not only uniform duties, but also other measures which might render the Confederation adequate to the needs of the times. The meeting made this idea the basis of a new call to all the States urging them to send Commissioners to Philadelphia the following May, - 66 "to devise such further provisions as shall appear to them necessary to render the constitution of the federal government adequate to the exigencies of the Union," and to report to Congress such an act as when agreed to by them [Congress], and confirmed by the legislatures of every State, will effectually provide for" those exigencies. 

Then the sudden increase of anarchy that same fall (page 195) brought men to recognize that something must be done at once. 

James Madison persuaded the Virginia legislature to appoint delegates (in spite of vehement opposition by Patrick Henry and 

Richard Henry Lee) and to head the list with the name of Washington. Other States followed promptly; and the Philadelphia 

Convention became a fact. 

II. CHARACTER OF THE CONVENTION 

The famous Philadelphia Convention lasted four months from May 25, 1787, to September 17. The debates were guarded by solemn pledges of secrecy. Most that we know about them comes from Madison's notes. Madison had been disappointed in the meager information regarding the establishment of earlier 

---

confederacies, and he believed that upon the success of the federation now to be formed "would be staked possibly the cause of liberty throughout the world." Accordingly, he determined to preserve full records of it. 

Missing no session, he kept careful notes of each day's proceedings and of each speaker's arguments; and each evening he wrote up these notes more fully, submitting them sometimes to the speakers for correction. In 1837, when every member of the Convention had passed away, Congress bought this manuscript from Mrs. Madison, and published it as "Madison's Journal of the Constitutional Convention." 1 (From it come all quotations in this chapter not otherwise credited.)

203 the Declaration of Independence eleven years before; seven had served as governors; and twenty-eight, as members of the

Virginia and New Jersey were to give their names to the two schemes that contended for mastery in the Convention. 

Their delegations, therefore, are of special interest. Virginia sent seven members. Among them were Washington, George 

Mason (who eleven years before had drawn the first State constitution), Edmund Randolph (her brilliant young Governor), and Madison, who was to earn the title "Father of the Constitution." New Jersey sent four delegates, all tried statesmen: Livingston, eleven times her Governor; Patterson, ten times her Attorney-General; Brearly, her Chief Justice, who had taken the greatest step in America so far toward increasing the dignity and power of the judiciary (page 214); and Houston, many times Congressman.

The illustrious company were of course men of the eighteenth century, and their ideas were more like John Winthrop's than Abraham Lincoln's. They wished a government for the people, but by what they were fond of calling "the wealth and intelligence of the country." It seemed an axiom to them that the unhappy conditions of their country were due (as Gerry of 

Massachusetts phrased it) to "an excess of democracy."

In the early years of the Revolution, the patriot leaders had been forced to throw themselves into the arms of democracy (page 133) for protection. So those years had been marked by a burst of enthusiasm for popular government. But, when that struggle was over, the "leaders of society " began to look coldly upon further partnership with distasteful allies no longer needed; and this tendency was magnified by the turbulence of the times. 

By 1785, especially among the merchants and lawyers, a conservative reaction had set in; and this expressed itself emphatically in the Philadelphia Convention. Says Woodrow Wilson (Division and Reunion, 12): "The Federal government was not by intention a democratic government. In plan and in structure it had been meant to check the sweep and power of popular majori-

1 ties. . . . [It] had in fact been originated and organized upon the initiative, and primarily in the interest, of the mercantile and wealthy classes." 

May 31, Gerry declared that he " abhorred " pure democracy as "the worst of all political evils." The same day Roger Sherman of Connecticut objected to the popular election of the members even of the lower House of Congress, because "the people, immediately, should have as little to do as may be about the government"; and Randolph explained that in the Virginia plan, the 

Senate was designed as a check against "the turbulence and follies of democracy." Two days later, Dickinson declared a "limited monarchy . . . one of the best governments in the world. It was not certain that equal blessings were derivable from any other form. A limited monarchy, however, was out of the question. The spirit of the times forbade the experiment. . . . But though a form the most perfect perhaps in itself be unattainable, we must not despair." June 6, he returned to this theme, urging that the Senate should be "carried through such a refining process [viz., indirect elections and property qualifications] as will assimilate it, as nearly as may be, to the House of Lords in England"—in order that it might safeguard property against democracy.¹

Gouverneur Morris of Pennsylvania, one of the most brilliant and effective men in the Convention, also believed it essential ¹ Hamilton held the most extreme ground against democracy. He "acknowledged himself not to think favorably of republican government. 

In his private opinion, he had no scruple in declaring that the British government was the best in the world [he is speaking, of course, of the unreformed oligarchic government of his day] and he doubted much whether anything short of it would do in America." The House of Lords he especially commended as a permanent barrier against every pernicious innovation." 66 

Hamilton then presented a plan, which, he said, represented his own views of what was desirable: an Executive for life, with an absolute veto over the national legislature and also indirectly over all State legislatures through its appointments of State governors; a Senate for life, chosen, like the Executive, by indirect election; and an Assembly chosen by freeholders only. ____

The Convention had many conflicting interests. It contained

No praise is too high for the patience and "sweet reasonableness" (failing only with a few individuals and on rare occasions) 

---

with which on all these matters the great statesmen of that memorable assembly strove first to convince one another, and, failing that, to find a rational compromise. 

High praise, too, is due their profound dislike for mere theory, their political habit of seeking out that which had been proven good. Mr. Gladstone once said: "As the British constitution is the most subtle organism which has proceeded from progressive history, so the American constitution is the most wonderful work ever struck off at a given moment by the hand and purpose of man." This sentence has helped to spread the idea that the 

Philadelphia Convention invented a whole set of new institutions. 

Such an impression is mistaken. Practically every piece of political machinery in the Constitution was taken from the familiar workings of State constitutions. 

III. HOW THE CONVENTION WORKED 

Some months before the meeting, Madison had drawn up several propositions concerning a new government, in letters to Jefferson and Washington. The Virginia delegates were the first to arrive at Philadelphia. While waiting, they formulated these suggestions of Madison's into a rough plan. 

May 29, Randolph presented this Virginia Plan to the convention in a brilliant speech. It provided for a two-House legislature. The lower House was to be chosen by the people and was to be apportioned among the States in proportion to population or wealth (so that Virginia, Pennsylvania, and Massachusetts each would have sixteen or seventeen delegates to one from Delaware or Rhode Island). The upper House was to be chosen by the lower and there was no security that a small State would have any representation in it. As to power, this central legislature was to fix its own limits; and (to prevent conflict between State and Nation) it was to have an absolute veto upon State legislation. This would have created a government more like that of modern France than like that of the present 

United States.¹

HOW THE WORK WAS DONE 

207 The further procedure had seven periods.¹ 

I. For two weeks, in committee of the whole, the Randolph resolutions were debated, clause by clause. Then came an interruption. So far, the large States, in favor of real national union, had had things their own way; but at last the small-State delegates had united upon the New Jersey Plan, which was now presented to the Convention by Patterson. The Virginia 

Plan substituted a new constitution for the old one. The New Jersey Plan would merely have amended the old Confederation in some particulars. It would have given Congress power to impose tariffs and to use force against a delinquent State; and it designed a true executive and an imposing federal judiciary (the latter, very vague in the Virginia Plan). 

2. The committee of the whole gave another week to comparing the two plans. Then it set aside the new proposals and returned to the Virginia 

Plan, on the basis of which it agreed upon nineteen great resolutions. 

3. From June 19 to July 26 those resolutions were considered again, in formal Convention, clause by clause. Midway in this period came the great crisis, when day by day the Convention tottered on the brink of disruption in the contest between large and small States. That calamity was finally averted by the Connecticut Compromise (page 209). 

4. The Convention then adjourned for eleven days, while its conclusions were put into Articles and Sections, by a Committee of Detail. 

5. From August 6 to September 10, the Convention considered this draft of a constitution, section by section. 

6. A Committee of Revision ("Committee on Style") redrafted the

Constitution according to the latest conclusions of the Convention. To 

Gouverneur Morris, chairman of this committee, we owe in large degree the admirable arrangement and clear wording of the document. 

7. From September 12th to the 17th, the Convention reviewed its work in this form, making a few more changes. September 17 the Constitution in its final form was signed by thirty-nine delegates, representing twelve States.

Thirteen of the fifty-five delegates had left; and three of those present (Randolph, Mason, and Gerry) refused to sign. Randolph afterwards urged ratification in Virginia, but Mason and Gerry remained earnest opponents of ratification. In July, Mason had said that it could not be more inconvenient for any gentleman to remain absent from his private affairs than it was for him; but he would "bury his bones in this city rather than expose his country to the consequences of a dissolution without anything being done." On August 31, however, he claimed that he "would sooner chop off his right hand than put it to the Constitution as it now stands." (His “Objections” are in the Source Book, Nos. 162, 163.)
