It proved an admirable campaign document - for Jackson. 

In the election of 1832 the foremost question was Jackson or the Bank. The President was a novice in politics, but he had outplayed the politicians and selected the one issue that could keep his old following united. The West and Southwest hated the 

Bank and loved Jackson; the old South at least hated the Bank;

AND NULLIFICATION 

373 and once more the workingmen of the Eastern cities declared vehemently against all monopolies. The Bank went into politics with all its resources, open and secret. In particular it made loans on easy terms to fifty members of Congress, amounting in all to nearly half a million dollars; it secured the support of the leading papers; ¹ and it paid lavish sums to political writers all over the country to attack Jackson. 

Jackson was reëlected by 219 electoral votes, to 49 for Clay, and he received a larger popular vote, in proportion to population, than any President had ever had. For the first time, a President had appealed to the Nation over the head of Congress. In this campaign the National Republicans (page 334), complaining of Jackson's attempts to dominate Congress, took the name Whig - which in England had long indicated opposition to royal control over parliament.

C. AN INTERRUPTION: NULLIFICATION 

Meantime the question of nullification was pressing to the front, and it drew the tariff question along with it. In the summer of 1828, while the South was seething with talk of secession, Calhoun had brought forward what he thought a milder remedy for the injustice of the tariff. This was the theory of nullification in his famous Exposition, which was approved by the legislature of South Carolina.

That paper argued (1) that the tariff was ruinous to the South; (2) that "protection " was unconstitutional; (3) that any 

State had a constitutional right peacefully to nullify within her borders a law so injurious and unconstitutional, until Congress should appeal to the States and be sustained by three fourths of them the number necessary to amend the Constitution. 

The South hoped for easier relief, however, through Jackson's favor for tariff reform, and was willing to defer action. But, unexpectedly, the question of nullification was argued in "the great debate" in the Senate (January 19-29, 1830). 

¹ One opponent became a supporter on receiving a loan of $50,000. 

---

THE (6 REIGN OF JACKSON " 

Senator Foote of Connecticut had voiced Eastern jealousy of

Western growth by a resolution to limit the sale of public lands. 

The Westerners resented this attack on their development vigorously. Benton gladly seized the chance once more to set forth his plans for preëmption laws and other schemes to make easier the way for the pioneer. But soon the debate ranged far from the original matter. Senator Hayne of South Carolina denounced warmly the East's selfishness, pledged to the West the continued support of the South, and at the same time sought to draw the West to the doctrine of Calhoun's Exposition. Webster replied to Hayne's argument for nullification in two magnificent orations, stripping bare the practical absurdity of the doctrine, and portraying in vivid colors the glory of American Nationality.

Webster argued that the Constitution made us a Nation. To strengthen this position, he maintained that as one nation " we the people of the United States " had made the Constitution. (See Appendix II.) But this historical part of his plea was really immaterial. The vital thing was not the theory of union held by a departed generation, but the will and needs of the throbbing present. And when he argued that the United States was now one Nation, and must so continue, he gave deathless form to a truth which, inarticulate before, had yet been growing in the consciousness of the progressive North and Northwest. 

A brilliant picture of the manifold benefits of the Union closed with the splendid flight of eloquence which was to count in years to come for more than argument and more than armies. 

Professor MacDonald (Jacksonian Democracy, III) sums up an admirable discussion of the debate as follows: "Hayne argued for a theory, which, however once widely held, had been outgrown, and which could not under any circumstances be made to work. Webster argued for a theory, which, though unhistorical in the form in which he presented it, nevertheless gave the Federal government ground on which to stand. The one . . . looked to the past, the other to the present and future. Both were statesmen; both loved their country: but Hayne would call a halt, while Webster would march on."

WEBSTER REPLYING TO HAYNE. 

While the Union lasts, we have high, exciting, gratifying prospects spread out for us and our children. Beyond that, I seek not to penetrate the veil. When my eyes shall be turned to behold, for the last time, the sun in heaven, may I not see him shining on the broken and dishonored fragments of a once glorious Union; on States dissevered, discordant, belligerent; on a land rent with civil feuds, or drenched, it may be, in fraternal blood! 

Let their last feeble and lingering glance rather behold the gorgeous ensign of the republic, now known and honored throughout the earth, still full high advanced, its arms and trophies streaming in their original luster, not a stripe erased or polluted, not a single star obscured-bearing for its motto no such miserable interrogatory as, What is all this worth? Nor those other words of delusion and folly, Liberty first and Union afterwards - but everywhere, spread all over in characters of living light, blazing on all its ample folds, as they float over the sea and over the land, and in every wind under the whole heavens, that other sentiment, dear to every true American heart - Liberty and Union, now and forever, one and inseparable! 

- Webster's closing words in the "Great Debate."

The Ladies Hermitage Association.

AND NULLIFICATION 

375 The Southern leaders now arranged a Jefferson Day banquet at Washington (April 13, 1830), at which most of the toasts were saturated with State sovereignty. But Jackson, the guest of honor, startled the gathering by proposing the toast 66 Our Federal Union: it must be preserved." Soon he took advantage of other opportunities to declare that he would meet nullification with force. True, he did now recommend a reduction of the tariff. But Clay, master still in Congress, thought he could defy both Jackson and Calhoun; and the new "tariff of 1832" removed only the absurd atrocities of 1828, returning to about the basis of 1824. This merely strengthened the principle of protection, and did not in any way satisfy the South. 

South Carolina now called a State Convention; and on November 19, 1832, after five days of debate, that body adopted an Ordinance of Nullification, declaring the tariff laws void within the State, and threatening war if the Federal government should attempt to enforce them.

December 10, Jackson replied by an admirable proclamation to the people of South Carolina, warning them of the peril into which they were running, and affirming his determination to enforce the laws - by the bayonet if necessary. But to Congress, a few days before, he had once more recommended further revision of the tariff. The legislature of Virginia, at the suggestion of members of the Cabinet, urged compromise. Clay, too, was alarmed now at the prospect of disunion, and he joined hands with Calhoun to draw a tariff bill acceptable to South Carolina, providing for a reduction of the duties in the tariff of 1832, to be made gradually, so that by 1842 no rate should exceed 20 per cent a lower rate than in 1816. 

March 1, 1833, Congress passed both this compromise tariff and a Force bill giving the President forces to bring rebellious South Carolina to obedience, and the President took what satisfaction he could by signing the Force bill a few minutes before the Tariff bill. March 11, the South Carolina convention rescinded the nullification ordinance. Both sides claimed victory. South Carolina certainly had got all she had asked.

D. THE BANK AGAIN AT THE FRONT 

66 Jackson took his reëlection in 1832 as a verdict from the people against the Bank. Its charter had three years still to run; still in 1833 Jackson insisted that the Secretary of the 

Treasury should thereafter deposit government funds, as they came in, with certain "pet" State banks instead of with the 

National Bank. But the "dying monster," as Jackson men called the Bank, fought savagely. Indeed it did not believe it was dying. Biddle was confident he could force a new charter through Congress over Jackson's veto. August 1, 1833, he ordered the twenty-six branch banks to call in loans and reduce their bank-note circulation, so as to make “ hard times," claiming, of course, that such contraction was necessary because of the loss of the government deposits. In the midst of a prosperous year, a short, sharp panic followed, manufactured heartlessly by the money power. The harvest was abundant; but the lack of the usual credit was felt cruelly in the South and West where large amounts of money were always needed at that time of year to move cotton and grain to Eastern markets. Interest rose from six and eight per cent to fifteen and even to twenty-four per cent; and farms and crops went for a song under the auctioneer's hammer. Delegations of business men rushed to 

Washington to urge Jackson to surrender. (6 

Jackson, however, could not be moved; and soon both Congress and public opinion deserted the Bank. In 1834 Biddle gave up the struggle. The Bank applied to Pennsylvania for a charter as a State Bank, and meantime returned to its old policy in loans and circulation. Business became normal at once. 

E. THE PANIC OF 1837 

Three years after this artificial panic, natural causes brought on a real panic like that of 1819.

Since the War of 1812, State banks had doubled in numbers. 

Many of them, especially in the South and West, were "wildcat" banks, weak and recklessly managed. Other lines of

INFLATION AND PANIC 

377 business were equally reckless. The people, especially in the 

South and West, bought their daily supplies " on credit" from the store; the storekeepers had bought the goods on long time from Eastern wholesalers; and these in turn had bought on credit from the factory or the foreign merchant. All this was perhaps necessary; but it encouraged extravagance. Less excusable was the rage to invest in land and to speculate in stocks on credit, loaned largely by unreliable State banks. (After 1834 the "pet "banks, in which the government deposited funds, felt able to loan more freely than before.) 1 

The orgy of building roads and canals, too, was in full swing (page 319). The West had failed to get much in the way of internal improvements from the Federal government; ¹ but, confident in its future, it was pushing canals and even railroads into the wilderness. Often this was done wastefully; and in any case such money was sunk " where it could pay no interest for many years. Illinois, with half a million people and a quarter of a million dollars for its yearly revenue, bonded itself for roads and canals to the amount of $14,000,000. In 

1820 State debts all together were under $13,000,000; in 1840 they were $200,000,000, mainly owed to European capitalists who drew $12,000,000 interest yearly from America. 

Then in the final year of his administration, Jackson became alarmed at the rapid sale of public lands, paid for in paper only ;. and his famous "Specie Circular " ordered United States land offices thereafter to accept only gold and silver in payment for public lands (July, 1836). This was notice to the country that the vast bulk of its currency was dubious in value, and no doubt it hastened the "panic " that was due anyway because of overinvestment on borrowed capital. 

Martin Van Buren, of New York, Jackson's faithful counselor, was elected to the presidency, in time to reap the whirlwind. In 

¹ Jackson did not think such aid constitutional, and vetoed a number of bills. Still, in one way or another, more money was appropriated for such improvements during his administration than under any preceding President. Cf. also page 334.

VAN BUREN, 1837-1841 

May, 1837, every bank in the country suspended specie payment, and great numbers closed their doors. Gold and silver went into hiding, and bank paper depreciated in fantastic and varying degrees in different parts of the country, but everywhere ruinously. Merchants failed; factories closed down; farm and city homes were lost on mortgages; unemployed thousands faced starvation. The Labor movement was crushed out (page 

344). Normal conditions were not restored for five years. 

F. VAN BUREN'S FOUR 

YEARS, 1837-1841 

Van Buren saw his chance for a successful administration ruined by the disaster; but he met the situation with calm good sense. His message to

Congress pointed out the real causes of the panic and the slow road back to prosperity. Meantime, for the government funds, he recommended an Independent Treasury (independent of all banks). In 1840 this plan was adopted, though for some years the Whigs fought desperately to revive their pet scheme of a National Bank. The government built itself great vaults at Washington and other leading cities; and for many years the 

Treasury Department handled the National funds solely in these. 

The two other great measures of Van Buren's four years were the ten-hour order (page 346) and a preemption law. 

By 1830 the sale of public lands was bringing in as much revenue as the tariff. The money was not then needed. Hence arose the Eastern proposal to stop sales for a time (page 374). 

But soon the Democratic party in the West started a more formidable movement to give each State all the public domain within its borders - to dispose of in its own way. 

MARTIN VAN BUREN.

THE PREËMPTION ACT OF 1841 

379 To steal this Democratic thunder, and to preserve a very desirable uniformity in dealing with the public lands, Clay had countered with a proposition for distributing among the States merely the proceeds of the sales of the public lands. His first bills to this end failed; but, with the return of prosperity in 

1841, a compromise measure with three main features became law. 

1. Ninety per cent of proceeds of land sales were to be distributed (for a limited time) among the States in proportion to their representation in Congress. 

2. The policy (ever afterward maintained) was inaugurated of giving to each new State a liberal amount of the government lands within its borders to form a State fund for internal improvements.¹ 

3. The preemption provision, so long urged by Benton and the 

West, was incorporated in the bill, so that the whole law is usually referred to as the Preëmption Act of 1841. 

III. THE WHIG FIASCO OF 1841 

The campaign of 1840 marks the final disappearance from American politics of all open belief in aristocracy. The two parties rivaled each other in avowals of devotion to the will of the people; and the Whigs won because their clamor was the loudest and because the Democrats were discredited by the panic of '37. 

The Whig candidate was William Henry Harrison, the victor of Tippecanoe. An opponent referred to him contemptuously as a rude frontiersman fit only to live in a log cabin and drink hard cider. The Whigs turned this slur into effective ammunition. They had no official platform, and their candidate for 

Vice President, Tyler, was a States-rights Democrat who hap- 1 The second provision was extended so as to provide similar internalimprovement land grants for those of the older States which had not already had a liberal control over the lands within their borders. This grant was in addition to the customary grant of school lands, and followed out the principle of the original grant to Ohio for internal improvements (page 279).

TIPPECANOE AND TYLER, TOO 

pened to be hostile to Van Buren. But they swept the country in a "Hurrah Boys" campaign for "Tippecanoe and Tyler, too," the chief features being immense mass meetings in the country and torchlight processions in the cities, both sorts of entertainment centering round log cabins and barrels of cider. 

The Whigs secured also a working majority in both Houses of Congress; but the victory was futile. Harrison died within a month of the inauguration; and Tyler opposed his veto to the 

Whig measures. In 1841 he killed two bills to restore a United 

States Bank, in place of the Independent Treasury. Whig papers raised a bitter cry of "Judas Iscariot," and every member of the Cabinet resigned except Daniel Webster.

Webster kept his unpleasant position as Secretary of State in order to complete an important negotiation with England. 

Soon after the settlement of the dispute regarding the St. Croix 

River (page 245), another difference of opinion had arisen regarding the northern boundary of Maine farther to the west. 

England claimed one line, and the United States another, from different interpretations of the words of the Treaty of 1783. 

The King of the Netherlands, to whom as arbiter the contention was submitted, exceeded his province by drawing a compromise line without reference to the merits of the question; so the United 

States refused to accept the award. In 1842 the question was settled by the Webster-Ashburton Treaty, which gave each country about half the disputed territory. 

Tyler likewise killed two bills for an extreme protective tariff, but finally approved the more moderate tariff of 1842. This law undid the Compromise of 1833 — which had just taken full effect and restored rates to the level of 1832, or 1824. 

The panic had left the Treasury empty, and the general cry for revenue reinforced the manufacturers' cry for protection. The Whigs certainly had a "mandate" from the country for the change. "Protection" was the one principle that they had stood for in the campaign. Curiously enough, the ground on which they had demanded "protection" was altogether new. 

The old demand (1816–1832) had been aristocratic — in the interest of wealth. "Protect the manufacturers," it said, "because they have to pay

THE TARIFF AGAIN 

381 such high wages." The new demand, formulated by Horace Greeley and advocated by him with religious fervor in his New York Tribune, stood for social and democratic reform — in the interest of the workers. "Protect manufacturers,” it said, “in order that the workmen may continue to get high wages."

Tariff history, down to the Civil War, is conveniently disposed of here in a few words. The Democrats came back to power at the next election (page 392), and enacted the " Walker revenue tariff" of 1846. Imports such as coffees and teas and other articles of common use, not produced in the United States, were taxed high, while manufactures previously protected (iron, wool, etc.) were taxed only thirty per cent. The measure was called a free-trade tariff, but it afforded a moderate protection, besides nearly doubling the revenue. In 1857 rates were reduced for a time, to a real "tariff for revenue 

basis.

PART IX SLAVERY 

The whole commerce between master and slave is a perpetual exercise of the most unremitting despotism on the one part and degrading submission on the other. Our children see this, and learn to imitate it. .. Can the liberties of a nation be thought secure when we have removed their only firm basis -a conviction in the minds of the people that these liberties are the gift of God! ... 

I tremble for my country when I reflect that God is just. THOMAS JEFFERSON, in 1784, after the failure of his plan for emancipation in Virginia. 

CHAPTER XXXIII 

A SURVEY TO 1840 

In 1837-1840 the slave power began to demand more territory, and for twenty years slavery was the dominant question in politics. This chapter is an introduction to that story. 

I. THE SLAVE POWER APOLOGETIC-TO 1820 

The Revolution, with its emphasis upon the rights of man, created the first anti-slavery movement in America. (So, too, Revolutionary France abolished slavery in her colonies in 1794, as did all the Spanish-American states as they won their independence after 1815.) This movement was moral and religious, rather than political, and it belonged to the South quite as much as to the North. It was considerate of the slaveholder's difficulties; and the slaveholders during this period apologized for slavery as an evil they would be glad to get rid of safely. 

For thirty years after the Declaration of Independence, slavery seemed dying out. Every State north of Delaware had freed its slaves or had at least decreed freedom for all children thereafter born of slave parents. In the Southern States, too, many leaders, like Washington and Jefferson, were urging gradual emancipation - with some provision for removing the Negroes. 382

(The American Colonization Society set up the Negro Republic of Liberia, but found it impossible to send Negroes there as rapidly as they were born in America.) 

The South made no serious opposition to the exclusion of slavery from the Northwest Territory in 1787. To be sure, the new Constitution of 1788 sanctioned slavery and made it the duty of Congress to provide legal machinery for capturing and returning any slaves that might escape into the free States. 

Accordingly, in 1793, during Washington's first administration, Congress passed our first Fugitive Slave law. 

ON THE DEFENSIVE TO 1820 

That law ought to have given the benefit of any doubt to a man claimed as an escaped slave, until the claim was proved. Such had been the practice of the old Roman law (West's Early Progress, 328). This American law followed rather the medieval maxim that a masterless man must belong to some master. It assumed that the claim of a pretended master was good until disproved. A free Negro, seized in a strange locality (or kidnapped from his home and carried to a distant place), might easily find it impossible to prove his freedom · especially as the law made no provision for summoning witnesses or for jury trial.

The law provided that a man claimed as a fugitive slave might be taken before any State judicial officer, who must then act as the judge in the case. 

This was an attempt to impose Federal duties on State officials without consulting them. Fifty years later (in the Prigg v. Pennsylvania case of 1842) the Supreme Court decided that this clause was unconstitutional. The Court upheld the rest of the law! But this one leak was ruin for it. The officials in the North generally refused to act thereafter, and the law became practically a dead letter. Hence the new Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 (pages 

400, 404) which had much to do with bringing on the Civil War. 

If slavery was to die, two things were needful: new slaves must not be imported, and slavery must not spread. 

1. While the Revolutionary War was still going on, every 

State except Georgia and South Carolina prohibited the foreign slave trade. A little later, at the demand of those two States, the Constitution forbade the Federal government to put a stop to it before 1808 (page 213). But as the end of that period drew near, on the recommendation of President Jefferson, Congress did order that such trade should cease at the earliest possible moment.

SLAVERY TO 1840 

After 1807, England kept a naval patrol on the African coast to intercept "slavers," who were regarded as pirates by most European nations. Unhappily, England's invitations to the 

United States to join in this good work, in 1817 and 1824, were rejected by our Government. The War of 1812 had made us exceedingly sensitive regarding the "right of search,” and we now refused to permit an English ship (in time of peace) to search a vessel flying the American flag, even to ascertain whether that flag covered an American ship. Consequently our flag was used by slavers of all nations (especially, it must be confessed, of our own), engaged in stealing Negroes in Africa to sell in Brazil or Cuba, or in the cities of our own Lower South. In 1842, in the Ashburton Treaty, the United 

States did join England in agreeing to keep a joint squadron off the coast of Africa to suppress the illegal trade; but we took no proper share in the work until the opening of the Civil War. 

2. Three great attempts of the Federal government to prevent slavery from spreading have been treated in earlier chapters. 

To be sure, we did add slave territory in 1803, but the extension of slavery was in no way the motive for acquiring "Louisiana." 

The slave power had not yet begun to seek new territory for the sake of strengthening slavery. It is true, too, that Congress recognized slavery in the District of Columbia. That district had been ceded to the Federal government by Virginia and Maryland; and, as a matter of course, Congress reenacted for it the slave codes of those States. But during this same period Congress resisted firmly many attempts by the early settlers of Indiana and Illinois Territories (mostly from the South as we have seen) for the repeal of the antislavery clause in the Northwest Ordinance.¹ 

1 Then, to supply the labor so much needed in all new countries, the people of early Indiana and Illinois tried evasion of the Federal law. Thousands of slaves were brought into the two Territories under forms of "labor contracts," and Territorial "Black laws" were enacted to enforce this slavery. 

Says McMaster (History, V, 188): "To all intents and purposes, slavery was as much a domestic institution of Illinois in 1820 as of Kentucky." 

But soon after 1825 a new immigration into those States (page 320) put an end to this practical extension of slavery.

THE ABOLITIONISTS II. THE SLAVE POWER BECOMES AGGRESSIVE 

1. The ten years from the Missouri Compromise to the administration of Jackson form a transition period. In the struggle over Missouri (page 331), the North had shown a more aggressive determination than ever before to limit the area of slavery. Only fifteen Northern Congressmen voted against the antislavery provision - and twelve of these were defeated for reëlection. Southerners, on the other hand, were becoming less apologetic regarding the evil, and now spoke of slavery usually as inevitable and permanent. Not one Southern Congressman voted for a "free" Missouri. 

385 This new attitude of the South was due to money interests. 

Slavery was growing more profitable. After the invention of the cotton gin, the value of each field hand in the Black Belt rose swiftly from $200 in 1790 to $1000 in 1840. The Border 

States, too, where slave labor was not particularly profitable, found that they could raise and sell slaves to more Southern districts at huge profits. 

2. Then by 1830 the South had begun to advocate slavery as a positive good, economic and moral, for both master and slave, and as the only possible corner stone" for the highest type of civilization. Calhoun gave the remaining twenty years of his life mainly to urging this view. 66 

III. THE ABOLITIONISTS 

This aggressive attitude of the Slave Power was caused in part by the appearance of new aggressive antislavery workers, known as Abolitionists, who cried out for immediate and complete destruction of slavery. Foremost among these stands William 

Lloyd Garrison. Young, poor, friendless, Garrison began to publish the Liberator in Boston in 1831. The first number (printed on paper secured with difficulty on credit, and set up wholly by his own hand) carried at its head a declaration of war: "Let Southern oppressors tremble I shall strenuously contend for immediate enfranchisement . . . I will be as harsh as truth and as uncom-

SLAVERY TO 1840 

promising as justice . . . I do not wish to think, or speak, or write, with moderation . . . I am in earnest — I will not equivocate - I will not retreat a single inch- 

AND I WILL BE HEARD.' 

99 To the end, this remained the keynote of the Garrisonian Abolitionists. Their vehemence made them social outcasts, even when they were not in danger of physical violence. Among the group were Wendell Phillips, a youth of high social position, who forsook his career to become the despised orator of the Abolition cause; Whittier, the gentle Quaker poet, whose verse rang like a bugle call; Theodore Parker, a Unitarian minister of Boston, "the terrible pastor of Abolition"; and, at a later time, James Russell Lowell, whose scathing satire in the Biglow Papers struck effective blows for freedom, and whose established position helped to make Abolitionism "respectable." 66 This group had no direct influence upon political action against slavery. Many of them disclaimed desire for any such influence. 

Garrison once burned in public a copy of the Constitution, defaming it as a Covenant with Death and an agreement with Hell"; and the only political action advocated by him for 

Northern men was secession by the free States. So, too, Lowell's "Hosea Biglow" exclaimed: "Ef I'd my way, I hed ruther

We should go to work an' part, They take one way, we take t'other, Guess it wouldn't break my heart. 

Men hed ought to put asunder 

Them that God has noways jined; 

An' I shouldn't gretly wonder 

Ef there's thousands of my mind." 

A more moderate group of Abolitionists contained such men as 

William Ellery Channing, James Freeman Clark, Thomas Wentworth Higginson, and Samuel J. May (Unitarian ministers), Emerson, Longfellow, Gerrit Smith, William Jay, and the aged

Gallatin. (Emerson at first condemned the Garrisonian extremists with a harshness unnatural to his gentle spirit, but later he said that "they might be wrong-headed, but they were wrongheaded in the right direction.”)

Other foes of slavery, like Lincoln, rejected the name Abolitionist altogether, and believed that the Garrisonian group harmed more than they helped. Garrison and his friends did rouse bitter antagonism and made their opponents more aggressive. Still they achieved their purpose by being "heard." 

The nation would have been glad to forget the wrongs of slavery: these men made that impossible -sometimes by exaggerating and misrepresenting those wrongs - and they trusted to the moral sense of the people to do the rest. They made slavery a topic of discussion at every Northern fireside, and slavery could not stand discussion. 

ATTACKS UPON FREE SPEECH IV. THE SLAVE POWER ATTACKS FREE SPEECH 

After 1831 the former freedom of discussion about slavery vanished south of Mason and Dixon's Line. Antislavery societies dissolved; antislavery meetings could no longer find halls or audiences; antislavery publications were forced out. 

In many cases these ends were secured by mob violence. 

In 1835 James G. Birney, a Kentuckian who had long worked valiantly against slavery in Alabama and in his native State, was driven to move his antislavery paper across the Ohio to Cincinnati. Even there, his office was sacked, and his life sought, by a bloodthirsty mob, largely from Kentucky, while respectable Cincinnati citizens merely advised him to seek safety in silence.

This was in 1836. The year before, a Boston mob, “ in broadcloth and silk hats," had broken up one of Garrison's meetings, gutted his printing office, and dragged Garrison himself through the streets by a rope around his body until he was rescued and protected by the mayor by being jailed! And in Alton, Illinois, the year after (1837), mobs twice sacked the office of Elijah Lovejoy, an Abolitionist editor, and finally murdered Lovejoy, when he tried to defend his property from a third assault. 

Respectable Northern people and large property interests often showed a curious cowardice in these conflicts. Alton, in a measure, was dependent upon trade from the Missouri side of the Mississippi.

SLAVERY TO 1840 

Cincinnati's prosperity, in like fashion, was supposed to depend upon Kentucky trade. In both towns the cry arose that antislavery publications alienated the Slave State visitors and customers, and "hurt business." Before this direful threat, mayors, ministers, bankers, and all the newspapers in both cities were whipped into submission. 

Southern opinion demanded, too, that the Northern States (within their own borders) or the Federal government (for the whole nation) should stifle discussion by law. 

In 1835, in response to vehement appeals from Southern legislatures, President Jackson recommended

Congress to pass laws that would exclude "incendiary publications" from the mails. "But," cried antislavery men - and many others never before so counted "Who is to judge what is incendiary?

On such a charge, the Bible or the 

Constitution might be excluded."

And after a sharp struggle, the bill failed to pass. 

Thus while Garrisonian Abolitionists were trying to persuade the North that slavery was a moral wrong against the Negro, the folly of the Slave Power called into being a new Abolitionist party which thought of slavery first and foremost as dangerous to Northern rights. 

This party went into politics to limit slavery by all constitutional means. Among the leaders of these "political Abolitionists" were Birney and the young lawyer, Salmon P. Chase. 

Says Professor Hart in his Life of Chase: 

Candle and Tinder Box (with flint and steel for lighting). This necessity of every colonial home was still a chief convenience in Jackson's presidency. Friction matches were costly; and kerosene lamps were still thirty years away. 

"Like thousands of other antislavery men . . . Chase was aroused, not by the wrongs of the slave, but by the dangers to free White men. 

He did not hear the cries of the Covington whipping post across the river [the Ohio], but he could not mistake the shouts of the mob which destroyed Birney's property and sought his life; and his earliest act as an antislavery man was to stand for the everyday right of a fellow resident of Cincinnati to express his mind."

The Aggressive Slave Power had come to feel keenly the Need of More Territory from which to form New Slave States.

I. WE DOUBLE OUR TERRITORY AGAIN, 1837-1853 A. TEXAS 

In 1821 Spanish Mexico became an independent federated republic, and, a few years later (1829), abolished slavery. Texas was then one of the States of Mexico. It had been settled mainly from our Southwest, and the American settlers were commonly slave-owners. Mexico did finally exempt their province from the emancipation edict, but not until that measure had aroused great unrest among them. 

These Texans, too, had gone into Texas at the invitation of the Spanish government, with promises of a large amount of self-government. But in 1835 the new Republic of Mexico fell under the control of Santa Anna, a military dictator, who planned to do away with this privilege of Texas. So, early in 

1836, the Texans seceded, organized an independent state (with slavery), and elected as their first president "Sam" Houston, a famous Indian fighter and an old friend of Andrew Jackson. (The declaration of Independence was signed by fifty-six men, of whom fifty-three were from our South.) 

A Mexican army "invaded " Texas, captured a small Texan garrison in the Alamo (see cut facing page 397) after a gallant resistance, and massacred every prisoner. Then, April 21, it 389

met the main body of Texan frontiersmen under Houston at San Jacinto. The Texans charged six times their number with the vengeful cry, "Remember the Alamo," and won a complete victory. The independence of Texas was promptly recognized by the United States and by England and France. Mexico, however, did not give up her claims. 

The Texans hoped to be annexed to the United States. Indeed, many of them had gone to the country years before with that express plan as other Americans still earlier had gone into West Florida (page 288). But war between the United 

States and the proud and sensitive Mexicans would almost certainly have followed annexation; and both Jackson and Van 

Buren refused to recommend that measure to Congress. 

Still, here was a chance, seemingly the only chance, to get more slave territory, to balance the free Northwest. (Texas, it was argued, was large enough to make at least five States.) 

So the South soon began to demand the annexation, some fiery leaders even shouting "Texas or Disunion!" In 1844 

President Tyler arranged an annexation treaty; but our Whig

Senate refused to ratify it, and John Quincy Adams and twentyone other Northern Congressmen matched the Southern "fireeaters "by joining in a public letter advising secession if Tyler's "nefarious" scheme went through.

The balance of power was held by the free States of the Northwest. The majority of the people there disliked extending the area of slavery as they had shown but they were eager for more territory for the Union, and they had few scruples about fighting Mexico (or England) to get it. The South finally won the Northwest to its side by playing skillfully on this sentiment for expansion-combining with the demand for Texas a demand for "all of Oregon." (See map facing page 396.) 

Regarding Oregon (page 303) a new situation had come to pass. In the Florida treaty of 1819, Adams, our Secretary of 

State, had induced Spain to waive any claim to the Pacific coast north of the 42nd parallel. Many Americans felt that

THE OREGON QUESTION 

391 this "quitclaim" from Spain made our title to Oregon good; but England held that Spain had had no title to surrender. 

The ten-year period of joint occupation had expired in 1828, but the arrangement had been renewed, subject to a year's notice by either England or the United States. The debates on the matter in Congress showed that body as a whole rather indifferent. Indeed, the predominant feeling was that we could never occupy a region so inaccessible and “ barren,” and ought not even if we could. Still, some enthusiastic Western members of robust faith had urged (even then-without a railroad yet in America) that in a few years Oregon would be nearer Washington than St. Louis had been a generation earlier, and that it would inake our indispensable gateway to the West- "the long-sought road to India.” ¹ ern ocean When the second ten years of joint occupation expired, Americans were making farming settlements in Southern " Oregon." 

Missionaries to the Indians had followed the fur-traders along the "Oregon Trail" across the two thousand miles of wilderness from the Mississippi; and their glowing reports of the 

Western country drew adventurous colonists. In 1842 Dr. 

Elija White and Dr. Marcus Whitman guided considerable bands into the rich river valleys of that region. 

All earlier White men in the Oregon Country had been explorers, fur-traders, trappers, or missionaries. These actual settlements of American farmers made an American claim to the country that even our indifferent East could not ignore. 

At the time of the Ashburton Treaty, England had proposed a division of the disputed district along the line of the Columbia; but the United States insisted that it must have at least the north half also of the Columbia basin, and had offered only to accept the 49th parallel as the line of partition. (John 

Quincy Adams, when Secretary of State twenty years earlier, had suggested that division.) 

¹ In passionate reproach of Eastern indifference, Senator Benton exclaimed, "It is time that Western men had some share in the destinies of this Republic." On these debates, read at least Turner's New West, 128–133.

Van Buren (who at first had seemed their strongest man) because of his anti-slavery and anti-expansion stand, and nominated 

James K. Polk on a platform calling for "the Reoccupation of Oregon" and "the Reannexation of Texas." Their jubilant orators at once began to shout the slogan "Fifty-four forty, or fight," and some of them even promised that their party would get also California and Canada for the United

States - with hints, too, regarding Mexico and Central America!

war.

Polk's inaugural indicated an intention to redeem his campaign pledges and to take all of Oregon also, even at the cost of England now renewed the sensible proposal to divide the region offering to accept our old suggestion of the 49th parallel for the dividing line. This line was already the international boundary east of the Rockies. It was practically identical with the northern watershed of the Columbia, and it gave us all we could claim on the basis of "occupation." 

Polk wisely referred the matter to the Senate, and, with its approval, negotiated in 1846 a treaty of partition along the proposed line. The Northwest, however, claimed bitterly that its interests had been betrayed and that Polk had surrendered to mighty England in order better to prey on weak Mexico. 

C. WAR WITH MEXICO Wins More TERRITORY 

The acquisition of Oregon left Polk still far from content as to our front on the Pacific. He wanted California, for its splendid harbors at San Diego and San Francisco. Since we had no claim to the country, he tried to buy it, but could not wheedle or scare Mexico into selling. No way remained but war and for this a pretext was found in a boundary dispute between Mexico and our new State of Texas. 

Texas extended without question to the Nueces River. Not content with that boundary, she claimed as far as the Rio Grande- on grounds at least questionable. For the United 

States to back up this claim was to make war with Mexico certain. But Mexico had shown great arrogance in all attempts by the United States to negotiate on the matter. So 

General Zachary Taylor, in command of American troops in Texas, was now ordered to move his little army to the Rio Grande, where his position threatened a Mexican city across

the river. The Mexicans demanded a withdrawal. Taylor refused, was attacked, won a victory, and crossed the river. 

Polk announced to Congress (May 11, 1846), "War exists, and, notwithstanding all our efforts to avoid it, exists by the act of Mexico!" Congress accepted the pretext and adopted the war. 

Abolitionists talked secession, but, outside New England, the war was popular.¹ Certainly it was waged brilliantly. General 

Zachary Taylor invaded from the north, and General Winfield 

Scott advanced from the Gulf. 

The Mexicans were brave and subtle; but American armies won amazing victories over larger entrenched forces, and the contest closed with the spectacular storming of the heights of Chapultepec and the capture of the City of Mexico (September 15, 1847). At the outbreak of the war 

American troops had been dispatched to seize California and 

New Mexico territory which included, besides the modern 

States of those names, most of the present Arizona, Nevada, Utah, and parts of Colorado and

Wyoming (map facing page 396). In the treaty of peace, after ceding Texas as far as the Rio Grande, Mexico was forced to accept $15,000,000 for this other territory (losing in all nearly half her area). Members of the President's Cabinet wanted to take all of Mexico, and the press boasted confidently that the

Almost at once, however, it was discovered that the best route from Texas to California (the old Spanish Trail from Santa Fe to San Diego) lay south of the American acquisitions. 

So in 1853 James Gadsden, representing the United States, bought from Mexico for ten million dollars another small cession south of the Gila.

This Gadsden Purchase was our last expansion before the overthrow of slavery; but it was not the last attempt by the Slave Power. Proslavery men had long looked covetously at Cuba. Polk offered Spain a hundred million dollars for the island, but the Spanish government declared bluntly that it would rather see the island sunk in the sea. Then, Southern leaders began to advocate forcible seizure.¹ This piratical doctrine was set forth with particular emphasis in 1854 in the famous Ostend Manifesto, a document published in Europe by a group of leading American diplomats there. Among these was James Buchanan, who became President in 1857 and at once renewed attempts to buy Cuba and also to secure slave territory in Central America.

II. FREEDOM OR SLAVERY FOR NEW TERRITORY 

Population increased in the decade 1840-1850 from seventeen to twenty-three millions. Immigration from Europe had now begun in earnest. Until 1845, no one year had brought

100,000 immigrants (page 307). That year brought 114,000; 

1847 (during the Irish famine ¹) brought 235,000; and 1849 (after the European "year of revolution " 2) brought almost 300,000. This tremendous current, once started, continued unabated to the Civil War. It still came almost wholly from the northern European countries, and most of the immigrants were sturdy laboring men. In the main they avoided the South with its slave labor; but Southern railroads were built largely by Irish immigrants, and some of these finally settled in Southern cities.

Florida became a State in 1845; but Slavery's gain in the 

Senate through the addition of that State and. of Texas was balanced by the admission of Iowa (1846) and Wisconsin (1848). 

In the lower House of Congress the fifteen free States now had nearly a half more members than the fifteen Slave States. 

This situation gave especial importance to the question whether slavery or freedom should control the new territory acquired from Mexico. As soon as the war with Mexico began, the President had asked Congress for a grant of two million dollars to enable him to negotiate to advantage. To this "Two-Million-Dollar 

Bill" in the House of Representatives, David Wilmot, a Pennsylvania Democrat, secured an amendment providing that slavery should never exist in any territory (outside Texas) to be so acquired. Northwestern Democrats voted almost solidly for this Wilmot Proviso, partly from real reluctance to see slavery extended, partly to punish Polk and the Slave Power for "betraying" the Northwest in the Oregon matter. The session expired (August, 1846) before a vote was reached in the Senate. 

In the next session the Proviso again passed the lower House, but was voted down in the Senate, where the Slave Power had now rallied. THE ELECTION OF 1848 

397 Congress had no constitutional power to forbid the people of any part of the Union, with their property, from seeking homes in that domain. This meant a right for Southerners to carry their slaves and slave law into any "Territory." Then, said the South, when the time for Statehood arrives, let the inhabitants of each Territory decide the matter of slavery or freedom for themselves. - - There were now three distinct doctrines regarding slavery in the 

Territories: 

(1) the old idea that Congress could permit or exclude; (2) Calhoun's new claim that slavery could not be excluded by any power until Statehood was attained; (3) the middle position (soon adopted by Douglas) that Territorial settlers (without waiting for Statehood) ought to be allowed to settle the matter in their Territorial legislatures. 

The third was "squatter sovereignty" — which appealed powerfully to the democratic instincts of the West. It was not inconsistent with belief in the legality of the first doctrine, but it was inconsistent with the other "proslavery" claim.

Finally, the country went into the presidential election of 1848 without having any settled civil government for the vast area recently acquired. This neglect was serious. New Mexico and California were seats of ancient Spanish settlement at such centers as Santa Fe and the various Missions near San Francisco; and the sensitive and highly civilized population resented military government by the American conquerors. Moreover, in 

January, 1848, just before the cession by Mexico, gold was discovered in California at Sutter's Fort, near Sacramento. Then followed a vast and varied immigration, which needed imperatively a settled government. 

The Whigs, who had won their one success in 1840 with a military hero, now repeated their tactics of that year. They adopted no platform whatever, and nominated Zachary Taylor of Louisiana, a slaveholder, a straightforward soldier, and the hero of the war. The cautious Democratic platform warily evaded all mention of slavery and of the burning Territorial

question; but the presidential candidate was Lewis Cass of 

Michigan, the originator of the "popular sovereignty" plan for Territories.

The antislavery Democrats had hoped again to nominate Van Buren, who for a time had the strongest vote in the Convention,¹ and some of them finally held a convention of their own and made him their candidate. A few weeks later, he was nominated also by a new Free Soil party, which had absorbed the Liberty party (page 392). The Free Soilers recognized frankly that 

Congress could not interfere with slavery in the States, but they insisted on its prohibition in the Territories, with the cry, Free Speech, Free Labor, Free Soil, and Free Men." They cast 

300,000 votes (five times as many as the Liberty party four years before), and in New York their allies, the Van Buren Democrats, drew from Cass just enough to give that State (and the election) to the Whigs. 66 66 Meantime, California, lacking even a Territorial government, grew to the stature of Statehood. Thousands of Fortyniners," from all quarters of the globe (but mainly from the Northern States of the Union), rushed to the rich gold fields some around Cape Horn by ship (too often, in their haste, in schooners barely fit for short coast-trips); some across the feverstricken Isthmus of Panama (where thousands found themselves stranded for months from lack of shipping up the Pacific coast); but more by wagon train across the Plains, defying Indians and the more terrible Desert, along trails marked chiefly by the bleaching skeletons of their forerunners. And on the Pacific coast itself, whenever rumor reported that some prospector had "struck it rich," distant camps and towns were depopulated to swell the new, roaring settlement, toward which, over mountain paths, streamed multitudes of reckless men, laden with spade, pickax, and camp utensils. In a few months, the mining region contained some eighty thousand adventurers. 

1 Democratic National Conventions used a "two-thirds rule," in making nominations until June, 1937, when it voted to use a majority vote like other parties.

To maintain rude order and restrain rampant crime, the better spirits among the settlers adopted regulations and organized Vigilance Committees to enforce them, with power of life and death. 

On taking office, President Taylor at once advised New

Mexico and California to organize their own State governments and apply for admission to the Union. The Californians acted promptly on this suggestion, and (November, 1849) a convention unanimously adopted a "free 

State" constitution. 

Taylor sought to keep faith, and urged Congress to admit the new State.

The country was aflame. 

Every Northern legislature but one passed resolutions declaring that 

Congress ought to shut out slavery from all the new territory. The South, on the other hand, raged at the prospect of losing the richest fruits of the 

Mexican War, and public meetings and legislatures urged secession if such action were taken. Said Toombs of Georgia on the floor of Congress, if 

THE COMPROMISE OF 1850

Taylor died suddenly in July, 1850, to be succeeded by Millard Fillmore, the Vice President. This gave a breathing spell, and 

Clay came forward once more with a compromise, aiming to reconcile the South to the loss of California by giving them their will on other disputed points. Proud of his title of " the Great

Pacificator," he pleaded for "a union of hearts" between North and South through mutual concession: otherwise, he feared there was little chance for the survival of the political Union which he loved.

Clay's "Omnibus measures were supported by the new President, and finally passed in separate bills after a strenuous eight months' debate. They provided for: (1) the admission 

of the "free" California; (2) organization of the rest of the Mexican cession as the Territories of New 

Mexico and Utah, both on squatter-sovereignty principles; (3) prohibition of the slave trade (not slavery itself) in the District of Columbia; and (4) a new Fugitive Slave

Law, with all the abominations of the old one (page 383) and with provision for new Federal officials to make it effective. 99 66 

THE HENRY CLAY OF 1850. See page 372. 

This was the "Compromise of 1850," the last compromise on slavery. Many Southern Representatives voted No, in order that the measure, if passed at all, should be passed by Northern votes. At the moment it seemed a huge concession to Southern demands. A vast domain had been won, apparently, for future slave States - though the actual course of events was to prevent any such state from being formed. The only immediate gain for the North was a free California, which could not have been long refused in any case. This made sixteen free States to fifteen slave states, and put a final end to the old balance in the Senate.

THE COMPROMISE OF 1850 

It was Webster who really secured the passage of the compromise. 

He had opposed the annexation of Texas and the war, but now he urged that the North owed concession to the weaker South. 

Moreover, slave labor, he was sure, could never be profitable in sterile New Mexico. It was not necessary to exclude it by law of Congress: it was already excluded "by the law of nature.” 

He "would not take pains to reënact the will of God." 

To-day most students of history agree that in this famous "Seventh of March" speech

Webster was moved by deep love of America. He was now an old man, with failing powers, and he had begun to despair of the Union's being saved unless the South was pacified. 

Mr. Rhodes, however (History, I, 153), speaks in solemn judgment, referring especially to the acceptance by Webster of the Fugitive Slave Law:- "Webster could see the will of God' written on the mountains and plateaus of New Mexico, but he failed to see [it] implanted in the hearts of freemen." And at the time nearly all antislavery men thought him a traitor to his old beliefs, sometimes charging bitterly that he was basely bidding for Southern support in the hope of winning the presidency. This stern condemnation was voiced in the gentle Whittier's Ichabod:-- "From those great eyes 

The soul has fled.

To his dead fame. 

Walk backward, with averted gaze, And hide the shame."

SLAVERY AND EXPANSION, 1850-1860 

Calhoun, dying and despairing, opposed the compromise as insufficient. If the North wished to preserve the Union, he urged, it must concede some kind of political equilibrium between itself and the weaker South. His papers show that he meant to propose an amendment to the Constitution providing for two Presidents, one from each section, with a mutual veto. But like his great rivals, Clay and Webster, he passed from political life with this debate. 

More significant than the attitude of these statesmen of a passing day was the appearance of a new group of antislavery men. Their leader, William H. Seward, opposed the compromise as Calhoun did, but for opposite reasons. He insisted that peace could come only with the extinction of slavery. As to the Territories, said he "The Constitution devotes the Domain to . . liberty. . . . But there is a higher law than the Constitution, which devotes it to the same noble purpose."

CHAPTER XXXV 

It has been fitly said that from 1789 to 1820 the Union was maintained by the compromises in the Constitution, and from 1820 to 1861 by Congressional compromises. Most compromises of both sorts had to do with slavery. After 1850 it was never possible to agree upon another; nor did either party abide long by the Compromise of that year. 

North and South had come to have two types of civilization one based on free labor, one on slave labor. In the sixty years since the adoption of the Constitution, the North had moved steadily toward a new system of industry and new ideas about society: the South had remained stationary. As a 

Southern writer said: "The whirl and rush of progress encompassed the South on every side. . . . Yet alone in all the world she stood unmoved by it." The North had adopted the new 

Websterian views of the Constitution, in accord with modern needs: the South clung to the old views expressed by Calhoun. 

The great Protestant denominations - Baptists, Methodists, Presbyterians were each splitting apart into distinct churches, North and South, on the slavery issue. Southern associations were forming, pledged to import manufactures from England rather than from the North. 

Neither section had any understanding of the other's good side. Unity was already gone in hearts, in industry, in religious organizations. It was going in commercial intercourse. 

It could not long endure, on such terms, in government—unless one section could impose its type of civilization upon the other. 403

COMPROMISE BREAKS DOWN, 1850-1860 

Many Southern leaders had become convinced of this fact before 1850. An attempt at secession was headed off then only by the Compromise of that year. If it had come then, it would quite likely have been successful; for the North then would hardly have waged a great war to preserve the Union. This is Webster's justification. The Compromise preserved the 

Union ten precious years longer.

I. THE WEAK POINT IN THE COMPROMISE 

All the old leaders deprecated any further discussion about slavery; but the Fugitive Slave Law kept Northerners thinking about that subject in spite of themselves. That law was the weak point in the Compromise. Had the South been willing to lose the thousand slaves a year who escaped North (protecting itself, perhaps, by a small government insurance), the Compromise might have endured much longer. 

It was with regard to the disturbing effect of this part of the Compromise on the Northern conscience that Lowell exclaimed: "To tell us we ought not to agitate the question of slavery (when it is that which is forever agitating us) is like telling a man with the ague to stop shaking and he will be cured." 

In his " 

Higher Law" speech (page 402) Seward had warned the South in advance: "You are entitled to no more stringent laws, and such laws would be useless. The cause of the inefficiency of the present statute is not at all the leniency of its provisions it is the public sentiment of the North." And 

Emerson called the law "a law which every one of you will break on the earliest occasion a law which no man can obey, or abet, without loss of self-respect and forfeiture of the name of gentleman."

The law could be applied to Negroes who had been living for years in the North in supposed safety since the breakdown of the law of 1793 (page 383). Thousands of these now abandoned their homes for hurried flight to Canada, and others were seized by slave hunters. More attempts to recapture slaves took place in 1851 than in all our history before, but 

---

THE FUGITIVE SLAVE LAW 

405 66 every seizure now caused a tumult, if not a riot. Even proslavery men in the North could not stand for slave hunting at their own doors. Legislatures refused to United States officials the use of State jails, forbade State officers to aid in executing the law, and enacted various "personal-liberty laws." These laws promised to any man seized as an escaped slave those rights of jury trial and legal privilege which the Federal law denied him. (Some of these State laws amounted to downright nullification; and in 1859 the Wisconsin legislature deliberately used the words of the Kentucky Resolutions of 1799.) The "Underground Railroad"1 was extended, and, in several cases, fugitives were rescued from the officers in full day by mobs" of such high-minded gentlemen as Thomas Wentworth Higginson, Samuel J. May, and Gerrit Smith. All attempts to punish such open defiance of the law broke down, because no jury would convict. In February, 1851, a mob of Negroes rescued a fugitive out of the hands of Federal officers in Boston and carried him in triumph through applauding streets, where, fifteen years before, Garrison had been dragged in ignominy by a White mob. And when another fugitive (Burns) was sent back to slavery, after bloody riots, and a cost to the government of $100,000, it took 1100 soldiers and a battalion of artillery to convey him through those streets which were draped in mourning. 

Still, in the campaign of 1852, the platforms of both Whigs. and Democrats indorsed the Fugitive Slave provision; and when Charles Sumner in the Senate moved its repeal, he found only three votes to support him. In the presidential election, too, General Scott, the Whig candidate, who was believed to be more liberal than his platform, was defeated by the Democratic Franklin Pierce, who gave the Compromise hearty support. 

The tendency among respectable classes at the North to cling to the Compromise was especially notable in the Eastern colleges, where there were many students from the South. Andrew

1 D. White says that in the Yale of the early fifties (when he was a student there) "the great majority of older professors spoke at public meetings in favor of proslavery compromises." 

The two great Yale professors of the day who opposed the Fugitive Slave Law, he adds, were generally condemned for "hurting Yale" by driving away Southern students. 

One feature of the election of 1852 was the prominence of a new political party - the American party, or the Know-nothing party. From the time of the Philadelphia Convention, bitter attempts had been made now and again to limit the political influence of immigrants. To this "native" prejudice there was added, after the Irish immigration of the late forties (page 396), a silly fear of "Catholic" domination. The new party was a secret society whose purpose was to exclude from office all except native-born. Members below the highest grade of officials were pledged to passive obedience to orders, and were instructed, when questioned as to party secrets, to reply, “I know nothing." The movement was bigoted in character and un-American in methods; but for a time it gained considerable strength in Eastern and Southern States, and elected several congressmen.

II. THE REPEAL OF THE MISSOURI COMPROMISE 

What slim chance there was that the North might quiet down under the iniquity of the Fugitive Slave Law was dissipated by another audacious measure in the interests of slavery. 

Missouri, Arkansas, and Iowa were the only States formed, so far, from the Louisiana Purchase. The vast Platte country, or Missouri Territory (map facing page 319) had not even Territorial organization. Immigrants to California were pouring across it; and in December, 1853, Stephen A. Douglas of Illinois, chairman of the Senate Committee on Territories, strove to set up the long-needed government. His Kansas-Nebraska Bill 

¹ A distinguished scholar, author, and diplomat, - the first President of Cornell University and in later years Minister to Russia, Ambassador to Germany, and United States delegate to the First Hague Conference.

THE KANSAS-NEBRASKA BILL 

407 proposed that a vast district there should be divided into two new Territories - each on a squatter-sovereignty basis as to slavery.

This district had been solemnly guaranteed to freedom by the great Compromise of 1820. But Douglas and President 

Pierce argued that the recent Compromise of 1850 (which had specifically applied only to new territory just acquired) really repealed the older Compromise and implied squatter sovereignty for all future Territorial governments. The South had not thought of asking such a boon-but now, after a gasp of astonishment, it applauded wildly. Most Northerners looked upon the move as a wanton violation of a sacred pledge.

The bill carried by a close vote, in the House, 113 to 100. 

Douglas tried to make it a party measure, but it ended as a sectional measure (map facing page 408). All Southern Congressmen but nine voted for the bill. All Northern Whigs voted against it, and half the Northern Democrats, though the President used all his power to whip them into line. (The 

Northern Democrats who voted for it, almost to a man, lost their seats at the next election.) 

The struggle for "Bleeding Kansas" was then transferred to the country at large. From Missouri thousands of armed slave-owners poured across the line to preëmpt land — which, however, few of them made any pretense of really settling. 

From the North, especially from distant New England, came thousands of settlers, financed often by the "Emigrant Aid Society" and armed with the new breech-loading Sharpe's rifle, to save Kansas for freedom. In like fashion, far-off Georgia sent her contingent of the "Sons of the South" religiously dedicated to the cause of slavery. To the North the Southern immigrants all appeared as " Border Ruffians," while the favorite term of the South for the Northern immigrants was "Hessian mercenaries." But once more slavery proved its weakness. 

In spite of the neighborhood of slave territory, it was not easy to move slave plantations to a new State, especially to one not

COMPROMISE BREAKS DOWN, 1850–1860 

particularly adapted to slave labor. The free-State settlers soon predominated in numbers. 

The first Territorial legislature, however, was carried by a disreputable invasion from across the Missouri line. A preliminary "census" had shown only 2905 legal voters in the Territory; but on election day five thousand Missourians, with guns on their shoulders, revolvers stuffing their belts, and bowie knives protruding from their boot-tops, seized all but one of the polling places and swamped the "free-State" vote. The legislature, so elected, passed stringent laws to protect slavery. The free- 

State settlers refused to recognize this government (January, 1856), and it was also denounced as fraudulent by the honest and fearless governor, Andrew H. Reeder (who had been appointed as a strong proslavery man). But President Pierce removed

Reeder and supported the proslavery legislature with troops. 

Actual war followed in Kansas between rival "governments," and bloody murders were committed both by raiders from Missouri and by free-State fanatics like John Brown.¹ 

In the debate on the Nebraska bill, Sumner had declared, "It puts freedom and slavery face to face, and bids them grapple." 

And said Emerson: "The Fugitive law did much to unglue the eyes; and now the Nebraska bill leaves us staring." That measure brought together the discordant antislavery elements throughout "Anti-Nebraska men the country into a new political party. (Free Soilers, Northern Whigs, Northern Democrats opposed to Douglas' measure) joined under the name Republican. This "third party" took from the Free Soilers the program of prohibiting slavery in all Territories. It adopted from the 

Whigs, who rallied to it in large numbers, their broad-construction views. It recognized its Democratic element by nominating as its first candidate for President a young officer belonging to that party, John C. Fremont. The first Republican National Convention (1856) contained representatives from all the free States and from Maryland, Delaware, and Kentucky. The platform asserted that under the Constitution neither Congress nor any Territorial legislature had authority to establish slavery in a Territory, urged a railway across the continent, and pledged liberal aid to commerce by river and harbor improvement. (At the same time it asserted that Congress had no right to interfere with slavery in the States. Republican leaders reviled Abolitionists almost as violently as the Southerners did.)

In the election of 1856 Fremont carried all the Northern States but four. The Know-nothings carried Maryland. The Democrats elected their candidate, James Buchanan, by 174 electoral votes to 114. The Republicans, however, in this first contest, mustered 1,300,000 votes, to 1,800,000 for the Democrats. The 

Whig party had practically vanished.

III. THE SUPREME COURT AND SLAVERY 

Then (March, 1857) came the Dred Scott decision. Dred

Scott was the slave of an army officer. In 1834 his owner had taken him to an army post in Illinois and, later, to one in what is now Minnesota; then, back to Missouri. Slavery could not legally exist in Illinois because of the Northwest Ordinance, or in Minnesota because of the Missouri Compromise. So, some years later, certain abolitionists persuaded Scott to sue for his freedom on the ground that he became free legally when taken into free territory. 

The case finally reached the Supreme Court. That august body held that Scott was still a slave and had no standing in court; and two thirds of the Court concurred in the further opinion of the Chief Justice (Roger B. Taney) that neither Congress nor Territorial legislature could legally forbid slavery in a Territory. The Constitution, said the Court, sanctioned property in slaves, and every citizen of the Union must have his

COMPROMISE BREAKS DOWN, 1850-1860 

property protected in any part of the common national domain. 

Only a State could abolish slavery. 

This was a sweeping adoption of Calhoun's doctrine, and the precise reverse of Republican doctrine. According to this dictum, the restriction upon slavery in the Missouri Compromise had always been void in law. Quite as clearly, the opinion denied the "popular sovereignty" idea. But in exchange for this ground which it was told to surrender, the South was offered more impregnable proslavery ground; while the Republican party was branded as seeking an end wholly unconstitutional by any means. It must surrender, or defy the Court "that part of our government on which all the rest hinges."

Without hesitation, the Republican leaders defied the Court. 

Said Seward in the Senate: "The Supreme Court attempts to command the people of the United States to accept the principle that one man can own other men; and that they must guarantee the inviolability of that false and pernicious property. The people . . . never can, and they never will, accept principles so unconstitutional and abhorrent. 

We shall reorganize the Court, and thus reform its political sentiments and practices, and bring them into harmony with the Constitution and the laws of nature." Lincoln, in public debate, even accused the Court of entering into a plot with Pierce, Douglas, and Buchanan; but a little later he said more temperately: We offer no resistance to the Dred Scott decision; but we think it erroneous, and we shall do what we can to have it overruled." To the same effect the influential Springfield Republican said: "In this country, the court of last resort is the people. They will discuss and review the action of the Supreme Court, and, if it presents itself as a practical issue, they will vote against it.” 66 The congressional elections of the next year showed great Republican gains. The campaign was made famous by a series of joint debates in Illinois between Douglas (the "Little 

Giant") and Abraham Lincoln, candidates for the Senate.

Lincoln was defeated, but he attained his deliberate purpose.

For fifty years, "stump-speaking" had furnished recreation and education in the West. In the early frontier days, whole families traveled horseback or in jolty farm wagons a long day's journey to hear their favorite orator demolish a despised opponent. In those early days the crowd did not wear white collars, as many of this audience did; but then this audience of 1858 had gathered for the most part by rail or were townsfolk. 

The figure of Lincoln and that of Douglas (who stands next him, ready to reply or question) are excellent likenesses. Douglas was a powerful and wily debater, who had well won his title "The Little Giant." He was also a warmly loved leader; and since the passing of Clay and Webster, he had been generally looked upon as America's foremost statesman. Lincoln was as yet little known outside Illinois, but there at home he was as popular as Douglas was. Each side has its bands and its mottoes. A Lincoln man has hoisted a banner bearing the significant title, "Abe the Giant Killer." A 

Douglas man has raised a defiant reply, "The Little Giant Chawing up Old Abe." Lincoln's supporters appeal to the women and to the old Whigs (who had been strong in this district) by the banner stretched between two trees, in the background, proclaiming, - Westward the Star of Empire takes its Way. 

The Girls link on to Lincoln, Their Mothers were for Clay."

ABRAHAM LINCOLN IN 1860. 

February 27, 1860, Lincoln made a powerful address at Cooper Union in New York City. The favorable impression that he made there was one factor, a few months later, in swinging some New York votes to him in the wavering nominating convention (page 423). This photo (an ambrotype) was taken just after the speech. After his election he let his beard grow, and his face also soon showed deep marks of strain and sorrow.

THE LINCOLN-DOUGLAS DEBATES 

His acute and persistent questions forced Douglas to choose between the new doctrine of the Supreme Court - to which the South now clung vociferously - and his own old doctrine of squatter sovereignty which was certainly as far as Illinois would go. If Douglas did not oppose the Court, he would lose the Senatorship and Northern support for the presidency in the next election to which men's eyes were already turned. 

He was driven to maintain that, despite the Dred Scott decision, a Territorial legislature could keep out slavery by unfriendly legislation." This "Freeport doctrine " was at once denounced bitterly by the South. Lincoln had made it impossible for Northern and Southern Democrats to agree upon Douglas-far their best vote-getter-for their candidate 66 in 1860. 

4II 

Even more significant was the moral stand taken by Lincoln. The real issue, he declared, was the right or wrong of slavery — not any constitutional theory. "It is the eternal struggle between these two principles right and wrong-throughout the world. They are the two principles which have stood face to face from the beginning of time, and which will ever continue to struggle. The one is the common right of humanity: the other is the divine right of kings." Slavery, he affirmed, “is the spirit that says, 'You work and toil and earn bread, and I'll eat it.' No matter in what shape it comes, it is the same tyrannical principle.”

IV. THE KANSAS STRUGGLE FOR STATEHOOD 

In 1857 the free-State men won the Kansas elections so overwhelmingly that the proslavery organization could no longer expect open support from Washington. The expiring legislature, however, provided for a proslavery convention, which met 1 If Senators had been chosen by popular vote, as now, Lincoln would have won.

The "Lincoln candidates" for the legislature (which was to choose the Senator) received 190,000 votes, to 174,000 for "Douglas men."

But the Democrats had been in control of the legislature for some years, and had "gerrymandered" the State so skillfully that a majority of their candidates were elected. A graphic account of Lincoln's famous Freeport debate is given in Churchill's novel The Crisis.

COMPROMISE BREAKS DOWN, 1850–1860 

at Lecompton (November, 1857). President Buchanan had purchased for that body the privilege of meeting in peace by promising that its work should be submitted to popular vote. This pledge was not honestly kept. The convention arranged a "constitution with slavery" and a "constitution with no slavery," — which last, however, left in bondage the slaves then in the Territory. At the promised election, the voters were permitted merely to choose between these two constitutions: they were given no opportunity to reject both. 

The free-State men kept away from the polls; and the “ constitution with slavery" carried overwhelmingly, six thousand votes to six hundred. The new free-State legislature, however, at once provided for a new and proper expression of opinion. This time the proslavery men abstained from voting, and the two constitutions together received less than two hundred votes, to more than ten thousand against both of them. Still, the South and the Administration at Washington strove violently to secure the admission of the State with the "Lecompton constitution," claiming the first election as valid. 

This attempt to rob the people of their will was defeated in Congress by the honest opposition of Douglas, who remained true to his doctrine of popular sovereignty. The Slave Power did succeed, however, in getting Congress to submit the Lecompton constitution a third time to the people, with a bribe of public lands if they would accept it. Kansas refused the bribe, 11,000 to 2000. Even then the Senate would not admit the State with its "free" constitution. Kansas statehood had to wait till 

1861, when the Southern Senators had left Congress. Meantime, however, Minnesota (1858) and Oregon (1859) came in, to confirm Northern supremacy in the Senate. 

V. THE SLAVE POWER OFFENDS FREE LABOR 

In one vital matter at this same time the Slave Power set itself against the material interest of "free" labor. As early as 1845, Andrew Johnson of Tennessee (page 342) introduced in

THE SLAVE POWER OFFENDS LABOR 

413 

Congress the first "Homestead bill " to give any homeless citizen a farm from the public lands. Several times such bills passed the House. But larger free immigration into the public domain would end all chance to set up slavery there. So the 

Slave Power, formerly favorable to a liberal land policy, now defeated all these bills in the Senate.

This new attitude of the South helped to make the poor men of the North see the fundamental opposition between free and slave labor, and it angered especially the rapidly growing immigrant class, who desired free land above all else. Both these classes were attracted, too, by the position of the antislavery parties on this matter. The Free Soilers declared in their platform of 1852, in full accord with the 

Labor parties of twenty years before: "The public land of the United States belongs to the people, and should not be sold to individuals or granted to corporations, but should be held as a sacred trust for the benefit of the people, and should be granted in limited quantities, free of cost, to landless settlers." (6 In June of 1860 the House again passed a Homestead bill giving any head of a family a quarter section after five years' residence thereon. (There were only 7 Northern votes against the bill, and only 5 Southern votes for it!) Just afterward, the Republican platform "demanded" that the Senate also pass that "complete and satisfactory measure," and protested "against any view of the free homestead policy which regards the settlers as paupers or suppliants for public bounty." This time the

Senate did pass the bill, but Buchanan vetoed it. The honest poor man," argued the President with gracious rhetoric, "by frugality and industry can in any part of our country acquire a competency. . . . He desires no charity. This bill will go far to demoralize the people and repress this noble spirit of independence. It may introduce among us those pernicious social theories which have proved so disastrous in other countries." So a 

Homestead law had to wait until 1862 when the Slave Power had withdrawn from the government.
